name: Mississippi Today
title: Power is shut off at Jackson apartment complex, prompting city and community to step in
description: The Grand Chateau Apartments sit abandoned at 1576 W. Capitol St. in Jackson on Monday, July 27, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Dirty blankets lined the rails of the Grand Chateau apartments, left behind by residents after power to their homes was shut off by Entergy last week.
The owner of the apartment complex said the building was supposed to be vacant. But when power got disconnected, at least a dozen people still living there were left vulnerable to the heat.
City officials have stepped in to help provide the nearly one dozen residents escape the near triple-digit temperatures by giving them access to a cooling center and, now, temporary housing.
“Nobody needs to live in those circumstances. So I got into action and helped those people get out,” said Ward 2 City Council Member Tina Clay.
She visited the apartment complex, located on West Capitol Street, Friday night and called the situation heartbreaking. That’s when she stepped up not as a city council member, she said, but as a concerned citizen. 
Jackson City Council member Montyne “Tina” Clay listens during a council meeting at City Hall in Jackson on Tuesday, April 21, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Other city residents began bringing water and ice for the complex’s residents. The situation became more alarming when one resident had to be transported to the hospital for heat exertion. 
Soon after, efforts began to relocate residents from the dilapidated brick building. Jackson Mayor John Horhn secured a cooling tent with the help of state health officials. The cooling center opened Monday at the Jackson Police Training Academy on St. Charles Street, nearly two miles from the apartment complex, and is available to all Jackson residents. 
The city identified emergency funding to help relocate displaced residents. By Sunday, the complex was empty and residents were split among Matt’s House, a shelter for women and children, and temporary hotel housing. Stewpot Community Services is working alongside Matt’s House to shelter those affected. The nonprofit also donated 25 cots to the city’s cooling center and is helping to provide meals.
“These hot days are dangerous for all of us, but especially for those who have no reprieve from the high temperatures,” the Rev. Jill Buckley, executive director of Stewpot, said in a statement from the city. “We are glad to work with the city to provide relief for our neighbors.” 
Jackson police will provide 24-hour security at the Grand Chateau.
In a statement, Entergy said the power was disconnected after alleged signs of meter tampering were discovered. Power will remain disconnected until the property owner completes the necessary repairs. It remains uncertain when power will be restored.
Grand Chateau property owner Ramesh Ramchandran said eviction notices were handed out in May 2025, and units at the property were supposed to be unoccupied. 
Ramchandran told Mississippi Today that various efforts were made to renovate the property after residents were evicted. He said security issues caused delays. 
According to Ramchandran, the building was supposed to be boarded up and utilities cut off. However, squatters have been a longtime problem and added to the renovation delays.
A look at some of the units at the Grand Chateau Apartments at 1576 W. Capitol St. in Jackson on Monday, July 27, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
On Monday, wooden boards covered most of the complex’s windows. Some boards had notices from the city to vacate the premises within 30 days of July 24. 
Entergy also stated that the complex still had two active accounts at the time of disconnection. 
Ramchandran said he has previously called on the city to help in the renovation process.
Ward 5 City Council Member Vernon Hartley disputed Ramchandran’s claims. He said the city had tried to contact Ramchandran as late as September regarding code violations. Hartley added that the city can only do so much when it comes to matters regarding private property. 
“The City of Jackson cannot be just caretakers for everybody’s circumstances. We want to help in time of need, but that help has to be balanced,” Hartley said. “We’re limited by funding, and we’re also limited by law.”
Hartley added that city officials are trying to identify similar situations across Jackson.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Officials urge patience as Fox Cities respond to tornado
description: Parts of the city of Menasha and the nearby village of Fox Crossing remained inaccessible Tuesday after an EF3 tornado — the third highest classification meaning a “severe” tornado with wind speeds between 136-165 miles per hour — struck the Fox Valley Monday afternoon.  Downed powerlines and blocked streets have shut down access to the […]
text:
A set of metal bleachers was lodged in the fence of a Menasha baseball field by a tornado that ripped through Fox Valley communities on Monday. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Parts of the city of Menasha and the nearby village of Fox Crossing remained inaccessible Tuesday after an EF3 tornado — the third highest classification meaning a “severe” tornado with wind speeds between 136-165 miles per hour — struck the Fox Valley Monday afternoon. 
Downed powerlines and blocked streets have shut down access to the communities while emergency response crews continue to assess the damage and restore power and water. Officials say they’ve had zero fatalities and no serious injuries reported. 
“Just looking at the twisted metal and rooftops of some of the industrial buildings along the highway, it’s hard to describe the level of damage,” Winnebago County Executive Gordon Hintz told the Wisconsin Examiner. “We’ve had tornadoes in Wisconsin before, but in an urbanized area, the level of destruction is just incredible and we’re going to need time and patience and hopefully with everybody’s support we can get people back on their feet.”
A Madison Gas & Electric truck drives past downed powerlines in Menasha. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
Wanda Tracy, a spokesperson for Winnebago County, said Tuesday afternoon that responders were still in “discovery mode” to assess the damage of the storm. 
At a Tuesday evening media briefing, Menasha Police Department spokesperson Matthew Roe said that 68 people were transported to area hospitals Monday with tornado-related injuries, referring to them as  “walking wounded.” He added that crews have conducted two searches of the area to try to find people who might be trapped in their homes and assess the damage to roads and powerlines. 
A curfew is in place in Menasha from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. and parts of both Menasha and Fox Crossing remain under boil-water orders and thousands of people still don’t have power. 
Hintz said that although much of the area was devastated, the timing of the storm was “lucky” because most people aren’t home at midday on a Monday. 
“We have considerable challenges however,” he said. “Roadways are blocked with debris, there are downed power lines presenting both a danger and risk. Some people can’t access their  property, and if they can there’s no power and it may be several days until power is restored.” 
“It’s a mess and we’re going to need some patience,” he added. 
Community response
Residents and businesses across the Fox Valley quickly jumped into action following the storm, with community organizations working to distribute bottled water and assistance to families. 
“It’s amazing to see people come to support, even those affected,” Rebecca Rockhill, executive director of the northeast Wisconsin Red Cross, told the Examiner. 
Rockhill was managing a shelter established at Christ the Rock Community Church in Menasha where 38 people spent the night Monday following the storm. She said that more than 60 people had arrived at the site Tuesday to get meals, resources and charge their phones. 
Hotels throughout the region were fully booked Tuesday.
A Wisconsin State Patrol Officer directs traffic around downed powerlines in Menasha. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
Rockhill said that the best way to support the Red Cross recovery efforts is through financial donations to help purchase equipment such as tarps, rakes and garbage bags to help with cleanup. 
Down the street at the former UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities campus, Carolyn Desrosiers, CEO of Volunteer Fox Cities, was leading the effort to coordinate the more than 1,000 volunteers who came to help. Pallets of bottled water sat outside the campus planetarium building. She said that the first donation of the day came from an 11-year-old boy who came to give his allowance.
“We’re focused on helping organize the helpers,” she said. “It’s awful to wait but help is on the way.” 
Desrosiers added that people who want to help should go sign up at the coordination center to register and get a safety briefing so they learn what is needed, how to stay out of the way of work crews and stay safe around the downed powerlines. 
Roe said at the Tuesday evening briefing that the most needed donations were Lysol wipes, diapers, cleaning supplies, hearing and eye protection.
Disaster relief
Gov. Tony Evers announced a state of emergency for the region on Tuesday. 
“We are continuing to assess the devastation and destruction Wisconsin is seeing, especially in the Fox Cities, and we are committed to doing everything we can to help every family, business, and community affected recover,” Evers said in a statement. “This emergency declaration will ensure every available resource is deployed so we can respond quickly to the needs on the ground, and I want to thank the neighbors, emergency and first responders, local partners, and volunteers who are already working to help to restore essential services, clean up neighborhoods, and assess the damages. Together, we will recover and recover stronger, and I ask everyone to keep the families and communities affected in your thoughts over the coming days and weeks as they rebuild.” 
Hintz told the Examiner the emergency declaration will help move resources and that he’s making a request for National Guard troops to come bolster the “capacity to clean up.” 
“We need more manpower and equipment to clear some roadways to get the utility and power back on for people that have a home to return to,” he said. 
On Tuesday, the Winnebago County website displayed banners directing people to the tornado response and to federal disaster relief for the major flooding that hit the region in April. 
In recent months, the federal disaster relief system has been under a microscope due to President Donald Trump’s unwillingness to provide funds to areas represented by Democrats.
Pallets of bottled water sit at the volunteer coordination site on the former UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities campus after an EF3 tornado hit the region July 27. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
Rep. Lee Snodgrass (D-Appleton) told the Examiner that there’s an effort among legislators of both parties to “nudge that along at a federal level.” 
“When a disaster strikes a community, partisan politics are put aside locally and we try to come together as a group and help our neighbors,” she said. 
Climate Change 
The tornado hit the state just weeks after wildfires in Canada and northern Minnesota blanketed Wisconsin with smoke while record-breaking heat domes pushed temperatures dangerously high. 
Wisconsin has also seen an above average number of tornadoes and severe storms this summer as climate change shifts the country’s weather patterns. 
Snodgrass said that on Tuesday, one of her staff members was at the National Conference of State Legislatures summit in Chicago where he attended a panel on disaster management and mitigation. 
“This is part of the reason why Democrats so desperately want a trifecta,” she said, referring to hopes that the party can win both houses of the Legislature and the governor’s office this year. “The time to do something about this was 20 years ago. To stave back the occurrence of these natural disasters we’re going to have to make some pretty impactful legislation move forward.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah may be home to a nuclear innovation campus, Department of Energy announced
description: A campus to develop nuclear technologies may be coming to Utah, as the U.S. Department of Energy shortens its list of potential hosts for new “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” the federal agency announced Tuesday.  Apart from Utah, other four states — Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho — are in the running to build campuses that, […]
text:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announces Utah will be applying with the U.S. Department of Energy to host a "nuclear lifecycle innovation campus" in a remote area in northwest Tooele County during a news conference there on March 27, 2026. (Photo Courtesy of the Utah Governor's Office)A campus to develop nuclear technologies may be coming to Utah, as the U.S. Department of Energy shortens its list of potential hosts for new “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” the federal agency announced Tuesday. 
Apart from Utah, other four states — Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho — are in the running to build campuses that, according to the Department of Energy, “could support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and disposition of waste.”
Utah has campaigned hard for a campus, with Gov. Spencer Cox inviting reporters to a remote site in northwest Tooele County in late March to show a portion of the state’s vision for it, arguing then that the facility would help “build the safest, most complete nuclear energy ecosystem in the country.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Today’s agreement with the U.S. Department of @ENERGY is an important step in a competitive process exploring the potential for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus in Utah,” Cox said in a social media post on Tuesday. “We’re grateful for @SecretaryWright‘s leadership and look forward to continuing the conversation about how Utah can help strengthen America’s energy security and nuclear supply chain.”
Utah to apply with feds for a nuclear campus in remote Tooele County

The Utah campus is not a done deal yet. The Department of Energy did not provide a specific timeline for when the agreements with states will be final.
During that March event, Utah leaders were still fine tuning the details of their application, but shared they were contemplating using a wide swath of “thousands” of acres in Tooele County for the campus.
Cox said then that the site was “uniquely suited” for the project. 
“The geology, the arid climate, existing infrastructure, distance from major population centers, and some of the very best people on planet Earth, make it one of the most practical locations for this kind of work,” he said.  
However, environmental advocates from HEAL Utah worry the project may bring high-level radioactive waste to the state. According to Utah’s proposal, the state “is prepared to support DOE in advancing a safe, secure, and compliant approach to managing the first-ever long-term storage solution for (high-level waste) and (used nuclear fuel).”
“I can’t in good conscience say that we won this bid because it really feels like losing,” Lexi Tuddenham, executive director of HEAL Utah, said on Tuesday.
“The Utah office that led this said that they wanted and were willing to take both temporary and permanent high-level waste storage. So that means that it will be shipped from around the country. It will be shipped and buried here in our land forever,” Tuddenham said. “And those issues have not been dealt with, nor have they been truly rolled out in a way that involves people who will be dealing with those health effects potentially for generations.”
In support of the campus, the Utah Legislature also passed a law this year authorizing the state’s Office of Energy Development “to pursue development of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus” to prepare for the competitive process the Department of Energy issued.



Let us know what you think...


 


According the bill text, the scope of the campus may include “facilities for fuel fabrication, uranium conversion and enrichment, and the reprocessing of used nuclear fuel,” as well as the deployment of advanced modular reactors and micro-reactors and the “development of secure, long-term pathways for used nuclear material consistent with national security and environmental safety standards.”
The Utah campus, if materialized, may also host other nuclear-adjacent products, like isotopes, heat, or nuclear supply chain manufacturing. 
Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis also celebrated the news of Utah’s selection, arguing that it represents “another vote of confidence in our state’s future.”
“This is an incredible opportunity to strengthen American energy dominance, bolster our domestic nuclear supply chain, and create new high-paying jobs right here in Utah,” Curtis said in a statement.
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright signed memorandums of understanding with all five shortlisted states to continue to explore pathways to build the campuses, the Department of Energy said in a news release. The proposed projects have the potential to generate about $10 billion in state and local taxes and to create nearly 25,000 jobs, the agency said.
“These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth, create thousands of high-paying jobs, and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance,” Wright said in a statement.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Advocates gather at vigil for ICE shooting victims in Helena
description: HELENA — About 75 people gathered at a vigil at Hill Park in Helena on Monday night for two men killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents earlier this month in Texas and Maine. Attendees delivered a eulogy for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, while also expressing frustration with federal immigration […]
text:
Advocates stand in a 200 square foot box at a vigil for people who have been killed by federal agents this year. Indivisible Helena hosted the event at Hill Park on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)HELENA — About 75 people gathered at a vigil at Hill Park in Helena on Monday night for two men killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents earlier this month in Texas and Maine.
Attendees delivered a eulogy for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, while also expressing frustration with federal immigration policies.
The event was hosted by Indivisible Helena and sought to remember people who have been killed by federal agents since President Donald Trump retook power and made deportation and arrests a top agency priority at ICE. The group made 26 signs, one for each of the people who have died in ICE Detention in 2026.
At the Helena event on Monday, which lasted for about an hour in the smoke and heat, religious leaders and advocates spoke about the frustration they felt with the country’s immigration policies and how those in ICE custody are being treated.
A woman stands with a sign for Renee Good at an Indivisible Helena event on Monday, July 27, 2026 at Hill Park in Helena. Good was killed earlier this year by an ICE agent in Minneapolis. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
As part of the event, a 200 square foot marked box was set up, which advocates at the event said was the same size as a holding area at an ICE facility in Helena. That facility, which the Montana Free Press reported held some ICE detainees from a Bozeman immigration sweep earlier this month, was also accused of overcrowding in an Upper Seven Law lawsuit. ICE facilities across the country have also been accused of overcrowding.
Last year, the Helena Police Department stopped a man at the behest of ICE last year, but it was not who ICE was actually looking for, an incident that angered many in Helena. The man was later deported by federal authorities.  That led to a city commission immigration ordinance being passed — and then rescinded following pressure from the state— with long, intense and well-attended public meetings on the topic.
“People are pretty disgusted with ICE,” said Taylor Chriske-Hall, who attended the event as a member of Montanans for Palestine.
There’s also frustration with local politicians, who Chriske-Hall said were nowhere to be found at the event.
“There’s not an effective mechanism for us to take action except working together in the community,” Chriske-Hall said. “I mean, we cannot rely on our votes. We cannot rely on our representatives to protect us. Like we have to protect us. We have to come together.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: See Louisiana’s ‘I Voted’ sticker for this year
description: The work of a New Orleans artist, internationally known for his works that celebrate the city’s culture and architecture, is featured on this year’s version of the “I Voted” sticker handed out at Louisiana polling locations.
text:
New Orleans artist Terrance Osborne created the image for this year's "I Voted" sticker made available for elections. (Image courtesy of Louisiana Secretary of State)The work of a New Orleans artist, internationally known for his works that celebrate the city’s culture and architecture, is featured on this year’s version of the “I Voted” sticker handed out at Louisiana polling locations. 
Terrance Osborne joined Secretary of State Nancy Landry to unveil his design at the Old Governor’s Mansion. The inspiration for the artwork was what Louisiana would look like if you could see its sound, Osborne said.
“What an honor it is to be the artist, especially looking at the artists that have come before me,” Osborne said in a news release from Landry’s office. “When people vote and get their ‘I Voted’ sticker, they’re excited — they put it on their shirt, and it shows that they’ve officially voted. To be a part of that, of that symbol of voting, is something that I couldn’t be more excited about.”
Louisiana has provided “I Voted” stickers on election days since 2016, starting with a Blue Dog image from artist George Rodrigue. Other Louisiana artists chosen for the sticker include Rodrigue protegé Tony Bernard of Lafayette, Becky Fos of New Orleans and Shreveport’s William Joyce.
Osborne is a graduate of the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts and Xavier University. He taught art at Alice Harte Elementary in New Orleans until Hurricane Katrina, after which he and his family relocated to Georgia. 
After two years in Georgia, Osborne and his family moved back to New Orleans, and he’s worked full-time ever since. He’s produced a collection of Katrina-related works and has been featured six times as the official poster artist for the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival. 
Osborne’s art has been featured through partnerships with Nike, Coca-Cola, the NBA, Heineken, Raising Cane’s,  Hancock Whitney, the Zulu Organization and Tulane University.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: SD runoff voters talk decision-making, party switching, ‘the lesser of two evils’
description: Lucy Burdick didn’t really vote in favor of anybody in Tuesday’s runoff election for the South Dakota Republican Party’s nomination for governor. She voted against somebody. “Today we have two choices,” said the 71-year-old Burdick, of Fort Pierre. “Not Toby is who I picked.” She was talking about her opposition to Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, […]
text:
A voter fills out a ballot at a Brandon polling place during the runoff election for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Lucy Burdick didn’t really vote in favor of anybody in Tuesday’s runoff election for the South Dakota Republican Party’s nomination for governor.
She voted against somebody.
“Today we have two choices,” said the 71-year-old Burdick, of Fort Pierre. “Not Toby is who I picked.”
She was talking about her opposition to Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, who qualified for Tuesday’s runoff by finishing first in a four-way June 2 primary. Doeden failed to reach 35% in that election, which threw him into Tuesday’s top-two contest with the primary’s second-place finisher, Gov. Larry Rhoden.
South Dakota Republicans go to polls in historic runoff for governor nomination

The South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office planned to begin releasing runoff returns after polls close in western South Dakota at 8 p.m. Central, 7 p.m. Mountain on Tuesday.
Burdick said she dislikes Doeden’s pledges to eliminate or phase out property taxes, which she said would “hurt the counties.” All property tax revenue in the state goes to counties, schools, cities and other local governments.
Burdick said in the primary, she voted for U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who finished third.
Ronald Millar, 71, of Sioux Falls, also voted for Johnson in the primary and said his runoff vote was “more of a vote against Toby Doeden rather than a vote for Larry Rhoden.”
He described Doeden as “more of a sound bite guy than someone who has an understanding of policy.”
“It also came down to trust and the ability to collaborate with others,” Millar said. “I don’t always agree with Rhoden, but he has shown he is willing to listen to and work with others in making decisions about what is best for South Dakota.”
Alfred Slaathaug, 75, of rural Brandon, said he switched his registration from Democrat to Republican so he could vote for “the lesser of two evils” in the runoff, which was only open to Republican voters.
He was one of potentially thousands of party switchers voting Tuesday, judging by the 7,382-person rise in registered South Dakota Republicans during the six weeks between the primary and the runoff registration deadline.
“I changed my party just to vote for Rhoden,” Slaathaug said. “I don’t trust Doeden at all.”
The winner of the runoff will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a former legislator. The last time South Dakota elected a Democratic governor was 52 years ago in 1974.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Republican governor nomination runoff Voter Guide: Runoff for Republican governor nomination.]
South Dakota Searchlight reporters also encountered Doeden supporters Tuesday at the polls.
Kris Kluver, 47, of rural Sioux Falls, described Doeden as an “outsider who can bring a different perspective.” Kluver said he previously voted for state House Speaker Jon Hansen, who finished fourth in the primary.
Dawn Geerdes, 58, of Brandon, voted for Doeden in the primary and the runoff and said Doeden “really wants to make South Dakota a good place.”
“There wasn’t anything that didn’t appeal to me about Rhoden,” Geerdes said. “Doeden just had more of what I was looking for. It was a tough race in my head and heart. I was going back and forth.”
At a polling place in Pierre, 55-year-old Scott Isburg said he voted for Rhoden in the primary and the runoff. Isburg said he trusts that Rhoden will “run government in a way that’ll actually work.”
“I was a little bit concerned with some of the potential policies from Toby, whether they would work or not,” Isburg said.
South Dakota Searchlight’s Meghan O’Brien, Joshua Haiar and Makenzie Huber contributed to this report.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Walz selects farmer, ag leader, ex-Republican as Nebraska lieutenant governor pick
description: Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont announced a corn and soybean farmer and ex-Republican on Tuesday as her pick for lieutenant governor.
text:
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the Democratic nominee for Nebraska governor, center, announces her pick of Humboldt farmer Ben Steffen as her choice for lieutenant governor on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, on a farm north of Elkhorn. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)ELKHORN, Neb. — Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the 2026 Democratic choice for Nebraska governor, announced a corn and soybean farmer and ex-Republican on Tuesday as her pick for lieutenant governor.
Walz announced the selection Tuesday of Ben Steffen, who farms near Humboldt, while at a supporter’s farm north of Elkhorn. She described Steffen as “salt of the earth” and humble, honest and an “all-around good person.” He is the Richardson County chair for the Nebraska Farm Bureau, chair of his county planning commission, chair of his local water district board and chair of the Nebraska Rural Radio Association. He previously served as president of Ag Builders of Nebraska.
“Like me, he was not interested in politics, but he shared the desire to do what he could for his community, whether it was through public service or helping others thrive,” Walz said.
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the Democratic nominee for Nebraska governor, and Humboldt farmer Ben Steffen talk to reporters after Walz announced Steffen as her pick for lieutenant governor on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, on a farm north of Elkhorn. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The lieutenant governor is the right-hand to Nebraska’s governor and, in their absence, acts as the state’s chief executive. They preside as president of Nebraska’s one-house Legislature.
Running mate’s background
Steffen grew up on his parents’ dairy farm near Humboldt in southeast Richardson County. He continues to farm on the same land that has been in his family for more than 130 years with his wife, Paula Sue. In 2022, they made the difficult decision to sell their dairy cows. 
Walz, a former teacher, also grew up on a small hog farm north of Fremont in Fontanelle. She was elected to the Legislature in 2016 and served two four-year terms.
Steffen said that when Walz called him this summer and asked him about joining her ticket, he was in his field planting corn. He said he “just about drove my tractor in the ditch.”
“It’s humbling to be considered,” Steffen said.
He said his upbringing instilled in him the values of hard work, honesty, personal responsibility, faith and giving back to others. He testified before Congress on behalf of farmers in 2013 at the invitation of former U.S. Sen. Mike Johanns, R-Neb., a former Nebraska governor who had been a U.S. secretary of agriculture under President George W. Bush.
“My story is like many of yours,” Steffen said Tuesday. “When there’s a problem we Nebraskans raise our hands to help. We come together, we find common ground, we work through our differences.”
Pillen campaign, NEGOP fire back
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen’s reelection campaign manager, Taylor Sliva, and the Nebraska Republican Party were quick to downplay Steffen. Both noted Steffen spoke at a recent “No Kings” rally against Trump.
In contrast, Jane Kleeb, chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party, was quick to elevate Steffen over Pillen’s running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, who is a longtime prosecutor, Lexington native and Nebraska National Guard veteran. The NEGOP disavowed the comparison and noted Pillen is a farmer. His family continues to run the hog farm operation he built in Columbus.
Pillen taps longtime prosecutor Joe Kelly as running mate

“Your guy complains in the media, speaks at ‘No Kings’ rallies and like your other candidates is a glorified activist,” the NEGOP said Tuesday on X.
Steffen laughed at the description and told the Examiner he bailed hay for four days straight to make time for Tuesday’s event and that while doing so, he was on the phone and plugged his baler three times. His wife, Paula Sue, then told him: “I’m taking the phone away so we can get the hay finished.” Steffen said he is still coughing from grain dust after scooping grain bins this summer and highlighted his background as a former school board member, churchgoer and director of his church choir for 35-plus years, plus his marriage of 40 years.
“If those aren’t conservative family values,” Steffen said, “go ask Jim Pillen what is.”
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the Democratic nominee for Nebraska governor, center left, poses with her pick of Humboldt farmer Ben Steffen as her lieutenant governor choice on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, on a farm north of Elkhorn. To Walz’s right is her husband, Chris, and to Steffen’s left is his wife, Paula Sue. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Steffen was a registered Republican through the 2024 primary election and was a registered Democrat by the 2024 general election, according to the Richardson County Clerk’s Office.
Steffen did donate to the Nebraska Democratic Party sooner, according to the Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission. He gave $1,500 to the party two days after the May 2024 primary. In 2024, he gave $500 to a Democrat running to represent his Legislative District 1 and $250 to the Nebraska Farmers Union Political Action Committee. He donated $250 to Walz in January. The NADC did not list any other contributions.
‘Political hogwash’
Alongside her new running mate, the Walz-Steffen pair directed criticism at Pillen, at times by name, and Walz said that if things were going so well, she and Steffen wouldn’t be running.
Walz described the state as being at a “crossroads” with the “least transparent” administration in Nebraska that has led with “financial mismanagement” and brought economic development “crawling almost to a halt.”
“Our governor is ignoring the crisis he created,” Walz said. “I’ve worked a lot of jobs in my life … and if I performed any of them like that, I would have been fired.”
State Sens. Brad von Gillern of the Elkhorn area, chair of the Legislature’s Revenue Committee, Rob Clements of Elmwood, chair of the Appropriations Committee, and Speaker John Arch of La Vista, from left. Oct. 30, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The state budget is projected to be in the hole by more than $1 billion over the next three fiscal years, including $200 million in the current budget year that ends next June 30. Lawmakers will need to address that in the spring, a problem Walz calls the “Pillen budget crisis.”
Pillen told reporters last week Walz doesn’t know what she’s talking about.
“I would call that somebody that doesn’t have a clue what the facts are,” Pillen said last Wednesday. “Doesn’t have any ability to study and really learn what’s going on, and just trying to grab headlines. Political hogwash.”
Tax policy
Pillen has also taken pride in cutting income taxes in 2023 in a bill from former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, which Walz ultimately voted for. Voters elected Linehan to Legislative District 39 in 2016 over Democrat Bill Armbrust, whose farm Walz and Steffen were at Tuesday.
Walz was elected to adjacent Legislative District 15 in 2016 over a Republican appointee in a district that heavily backed President Donald Trump. Both Walz and Linehan were reelected in 2020 before being term-limited after 2024.
Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference at the end of the Legislature’s special session to address property taxes that began almost one month prior. To his far left is then-State Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of the Elkhorn area, chair of the Legislature’s Revenue Committee. Aug. 20, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Linehan has again endorsed Pillen. She chaired the Revenue Committee for six years, beginning in 2019, while Walz chaired the Education Committee in 2021 and 2022. The pair championed reading legislation together in 2024, though they didn’t always see eye-to-eye.
Walz and Steffen said they want to focus on and deliver property tax relief, a promise Pillen also made in 2022 and made again for 2026. He has struggled to find enough legislative support to deliver the amount of sweeping reforms he desires but has vowed not to give up.
Steffen said Pillen has failed to focus on daily issues, and “everyone knows he can’t deliver on property tax relief, especially when he has a billion dollar budget hole.”
“Pillen’s administration has failed,” Steffen said.
Walz previewed her platform last week — “Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans” — but hasn’t yet detailed how she would address property taxes. Steffen repeated Walz’s call that doing so will require growing Nebraska’s economy and ensure Nebraska is welcoming for businesses, families and people.
‘A winning team’
Walz told the Nebraska Examiner that the duo met while she was running as the lieutenant governor pick to then-state Sen. Bob Krist of Omaha in 2018. Krist is a Republican turned independent turned 2018 Democratic nominee. He’s now a registered nonpartisan again.
“I view the lieutenant governor as a true partnership,” Walz said Tuesday, “someone who will fight for Nebraskans every single day and treat the role with the gravity that this moment demands.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican at center, is running for reelection against former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Steffen said he took time to consider his decision but ultimately found it easier to make with Walz at the helm. He said that ever since he met her, he’s seen Walz as a “breath of fresh air” who cares about others and wants to bring people together. Steffen, a pilot, said he and Walz will travel Nebraska and meet Nebraskans where they’re at in the coming months.
“Lynne Walz is the leader this moment calls for, and it’s because her leadership is a complete contrast to our current governor,” Steffen said.
The last Democrat to win the governor’s race was Ben Nelson, who won reelection in 1994. He was also the last Democrat to win a statewide office, when he ran for one final term to the U.S. Senate in 2006. Republican voters today nearly double the number of Democrats in the state.
However, Walz has said she doesn’t hear concerns on the ground about her being a Democrat.
“I know that we have a winning team,” Walz said Tuesday. “I’m not optimistic, I know we do, not just for this campaign but to get this great state back on track and bring us back to the best versions of ourselves. I have the right partner in place to do this.”
Walz and Pillen will face off in November. Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Rick Beard of Omaha is also on the ballot, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha would also be on the ballot if he submits enough signatures by next Monday to qualify as a registered nonpartisan. As of Tuesday evening, his campaign website still said “coming soon.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota state senator facing election-related criminal charges ends his reelection campaign
description: Republican South Dakota state Sen. Tom Pischke, of Dell Rapids, ended his reelection campaign Tuesday as he continues to face felony charges for allegedly filing false or forged election-related documents. “I have always prided myself on conducting campaigns with complete transparency on every issue,” said a portion of a statement Pischke sent in response to[...]
text:
State Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on March 3, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Republican South Dakota state Sen. Tom Pischke, of Dell Rapids, ended his reelection campaign Tuesday as he continues to face felony charges for allegedly filing false or forged election-related documents.
“I have always prided myself on conducting campaigns with complete transparency on every issue,” said a portion of a statement Pischke sent in response to South Dakota Searchlight questions. “Unfortunately,” he added while citing the pending criminal charges, “I would not have been able to maintain that standard during the upcoming November election.”
Pischke’s withdrawal comes more than a month after prosecutors charged him with two felony counts alleging he submitted 16 candidate petitions for Minnehaha County Republican precinct committee positions without the candidates’ knowledge. 
Dell Rapids Republican lawmaker may get plea deal in election fraud case

The prosecution is playing out amid a long-running struggle over leadership of the county party. Obtaining a meeting quorum requires the presence of 20% of voting members, and filling more positions could make it more difficult for the county party’s leaders to obtain a quorum and conduct official business.
Pischke has pleaded not guilty, and lawyers involved in the case have said a plea deal is possible.
Pischke’s withdrawal leaves Republicans searching for a replacement candidate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. Republican county party central committee members who reside in his district have until Aug. 11 to make a selection.
Bryan Breitling, an independent from Dell Rapids, is the only other candidate on the ballot for the District 25 Senate seat. The district includes Moody County and part of Minnehaha County. 
“It has been an incredible honor to represent the wonderful people of District 25 over the past 10 years, and I look forward to whatever God has planned for me next,” Pischke said in his statement.
Another South Dakota legislator, Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, is facing a felony charge for allegedly causing intentional damage to a public road. He is scheduled for a court appearance this week in Butte County.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Puppy mill operator was consulted on the timing of inspections at her kennel
description: The owner of a southern Iowa puppy mill where 32 dogs were found to have been neglected is currently facing no criminal charges in the case. Newly released court records also show that in the months leading up to the recent seizure of the animals, federal officials repeatedly allowed the owner of the kennel to […]
text:
This dog was photographed by USDA inspectors in January 2023 at a kennel operated by Wuanita Swedlund of Iowa. (Main photo: USDA image courtesy of Bailing Out Benji; text-message illustration sourced from federal court records)The owner of a southern Iowa puppy mill where 32 dogs were found to have been neglected is currently facing no criminal charges in the case.
Newly released court records also show that in the months leading up to the recent seizure of the animals, federal officials repeatedly allowed the owner of the kennel to help schedule the government’s on-site inspections of the facility.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service sued Wuanita Swedlund of Farmington for allegedly barring federal officials from conducting inspections of her dog-breeding operations.
According to the USDA’s lawsuit, licensed breeders are required, during business hours, to allow inspectors to enter their place of business to inspect and photograph the property, the animals and business records. The lawsuit alleges Swedlund has failed to provide the USDA’s APHIS inspectors with access to her facility on five occasions when they visited the Farmington operation between November 2025 and May 2026.
As a result, the USDA claimed, APHIS officials were unable to inspect the business or view the animals in Swedlund’s care. The USDA asked the court to issue an injunction granting the agency access to the property.
While that case was proceeding in federal court, VanBuren County officials, armed with a search warrant, visited Swedlund’s facility on June 30, 2026, and took temporary custody of 32 dogs, one cat and one rabbit.
On July 10, 2026, citing the fact that Swedlund appeared to have either acquired additional dogs in violation of a previously issued temporary restraining order or hidden animals from inspectors during past inspections, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher issued the USDA’s sought-after injunction requiring Swedlund to let inspectors onto the property — although, by then, the animals had already been seized by the county.
“Swedlund’s noncompliance goes well beyond bureaucratic handwringing,” Locher wrote in his ruling. “The evidence shows that Swedlund has housed hundreds of dogs since acquiring her USDA license in 2023. She has consistently failed to provide her animals with adequate facilities, access to water, or access to medical care. It is evident that the animals in Swedlund’s care suffered needlessly — precisely the type of harm that the Animal Welfare Act sought to prevent. The public’s interest strongly favors a preliminary injunction.”
While that ruling settled the federal case brought by the USDA, the state court still had to determine the fate of the 34 animals seized from Swedlund.
On July 17, 2026, District Court Judge Joel D. Yates presided over a hearing at which deputies and animal welfare experts testified as to the condition of the animals and Swedlund’s facility.
That same day, Yates transferred ownership of the animals to the PAW Animal Shelter in Fort Madison, where they were already being treated, for eventual adoption. In his ruling, Yates said the evidence showed the “animals were neglected by not having access to appropriate food, potable water, sanitary conditions, proper ventilated shelter and necessary veterinary care.”
No criminal charges in the case
Swedlund, 35, said Tuesday her only regret about the seizure of the animals was the manner in which it was carried out. Rather than wait for her to be present, she said, authorities took the animals when her three children, age 11 to 17, were present. The experience, she said, left the children traumatized.
“They did it in front of the kids instead of having me there,” she said. “It hit them hard, actually, because some of them were emotional support animals. My kids have depression and anxiety, and this hit them pretty hard. For the first three days afterward, they didn’t sleep at all. (The county) wouldn’t even let me have a few dogs back just to help with the kids’ health.”
She said the animals she considered family pets were a rottweiler, a Yorkshire terrier, a pug, a chihuahua, the cat and the rabbit.
Swedlund has not been criminally charged with animal neglect or any other offenses related to the incident, and says that as far as she’s concerned the matter is settled and she’s done dealing with USDA inspectors and the county.
Court records show that while the USDA places great importance on the surprise nature of inspections at breeders and kennels, the agency’s inspectors repeatedly texted Swedlund during 2025 and 2026 to arrange for inspections at mutually agreeable times.
The records also show Swedlund declined to meet with the inspectors at the facility, citing work obligations at a Casey’s General Store. At one point, she even texted the inspectors photos of her work schedule at the retailer so they could arrange for an inspection that didn’t conflict with her work at the store.
In federal court filings earlier this month, Michelle Spatz, a senior trial attorney for the U.S. Department of Justice, told Judge Locher that unannounced inspections by the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service were “critical” to the agency’s work.
“In general,” Spatz told the court, “the unannounced nature of APHIS’ inspections is critical because it provides an accurate picture of the level of compliance and general welfare of the animals on a day-to-day basis.” She explained that when breeders and dealers have advance notice of an inspection, they “could conceal their failure” to comply with certain regulations, in part by simply transferring or euthanizing animals that show signs of illness or injury.”
Inspectors tried to schedule inspections
Text messages from USDA inspectors, included as exhibits in the federal court case, show the inspectors repeatedly messaged Swedlund about setting up pre-scheduled visits and inspections.
“We have an appointment 10:15 today,” an inspector twice texted to Swedlund in February 2025. Swedlund did not respond.
On Sept 9, 2025, an inspector texted Swedlund, “Hi Wuanita, are you available for inspection today?” Swedlund did not respond, according to the court records.
On Nov. 20, 2025, an inspector texted Swedlund, “Are you available for inspection today, Wuanita?” Swedlund replied, “Sorry, can’t talk … At work.”
On Jan. 8, 2026, inspectors again tried to gain access to the facility, texting Swedlund, “Please call when you can.” Swedlund replied, “I’m at work at Casey right now.” The inspector responded, “So you’re not available for an inspection?”
On Feb. 12, 2026, Swedlund sent an inspector photos of her work schedule at Casey’s and explained, “Trying to get days off so we can do an inspection.”
“Thank you, Wuanita,” the inspector replied. “It doesn’t look like there’s much time in your schedule for an inspection.”
A few days later, Swedlund told the inspector she’d have March 2, 6 and 10 off, indicating an inspection could be done then.
But then, on March 6, Swedlund texted the inspector that she was called into work and also had a doctor’s appointment that day.
On May 5, the inspector messaged Swedlund, “Hi, Wuanita, are you available for an inspection today?”
“No,” Swedlund replied, adding that her work schedule had changed.
Swedlund: ‘All my animals were healthy’
Swedlund said that the problem with arranging for an inspection was that she always left her 17-year-old child in charge of the kennel while she was working at Casey’s, and her child didn’t have the authority to let in the inspectors.
As for her future plans, she said she wants “to get out of town,” but also has plans to buy the property she now occupies from owner Steve Kruse — another Iowa breeder with a history of Animal Welfare Act violations. Once she owns the property, she said, she can sell it and use the proceeds to buy property in a more rural area of Iowa.
She said she feels the court proceedings were stacked against her, and that she wasn’t treated fairly. “All my animals were healthy,” she said.
Court records indicate the USDA first issued Swedlund a license in July 2023. Since then, the records show, she has been cited for numerous violations of the Animal Welfare Act, some of which were tied to the deaths of eight puppies from three different litters.
In that case, the USDA alleged Swedlund told inspectors she had found three dead bulldog puppies after feeling a strong, cold draft at the front of their enclosure. Inspectors reported Swedlund had placed duct tape over the hole that caused the draft, but the tape was peeling away at the time of the inspection and the cold draft could still be felt.
Three more puppies from a litter of Rottweilers were found dead, the USDA says, and one puppy was severely injured and later euthanized after a husky broke into an enclosure housing a sheepdog and her newborn litter. A week later, another of the puppies from that litter was apparently eaten by its mother.

name: National
title: Obamacare enrollment declines in 49 states
description: In 49 states, the number of people enrolled in Obamacare plans has declined since Congress made coverage more expensive by allowing federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year. The lone exception was New Mexico, the only state that has used its own money to fully replace the expired aid, according to a […]
text:
The owner of an insurance agency that offers Obamacare plans stands outside his storefront in Miami, Fla, in 2021. In 49 states, the number of people enrolled in Obamacare plans has declined. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)In 49 states, the number of people enrolled in Obamacare plans has declined since Congress made coverage more expensive by allowing federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year.
The lone exception was New Mexico, the only state that has used its own money to fully replace the expired aid, according to a new analysis by KFF, a health policy research group.
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that overall participation in the health insurance marketplaces created under Obamacare, officially called the Affordable Care Act, had declined by nearly 3 million people, to about 19.2 million from 21.8 million in 2025. That 2025 figure, the highest ever recorded, was the culmination of six years of steady increases.
In announcing the figures, the Trump administration blamed much of the growth since 2021 — the year former President Joe Biden took office — on “improper, phantom and fraudulent enrollment.” It said the number of people in those categories peaked at 5.6 million last year, and that this year’s decline was the result of its efforts to eliminate enrollees who misstated their income to gain access to free plans.
But KFF connected this year’s decline to the expiration of the enhanced federal subsidies. Designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, the subsidies were made available by the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021 and later extended through the end of 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act.
The enhanced subsidies were available to everyone, regardless of income. Additional federal aid provided to some of the lowest-income households entirely eliminated premium payments for some people. Congressional leaders let the subsidies expire on Dec. 31.
Some states are helping to make Obamacare plans more affordable

Under the Affordable Care Act, each state can either use the federal government’s online insurance marketplace, HealthCare.gov, or operate its own state-run exchange. In states with their own exchanges, including some that used their own money to partially replace the expired federal subsidies, the average enrollment drop was 6%, according to KFF. In states using the federal marketplace, the average decline was 15%.
Enrollment fell the most in Ohio and Oklahoma (32%), Arizona (30%), South Carolina (29%), Indiana (28%), Michigan and Minnesota (27%), and Louisiana and Mississippi (26%).
Enrollment in Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Idaho, Illinois, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Texas was flat or fell by less than 5%. In New Mexico, enrollment grew by 14%.
Justin Lo, a KFF senior researcher who co-authored the report, said in an email that the number of fraudulent enrollees in Obamacare is likely in the “hundreds of thousands,” rather than the millions. Higher estimates, he said, are based on “suspicious patterns that could be explained by fraud or by legitimate factors, the most notable of which is greater subsidies making coverage more affordable.”
“We had a huge growth in the marketplace uptake because a lot of people were seeing that they could now qualify for very cheap plans,” Lo said. “So now, when we’re looking at the loss…it’s people who had marketplace coverage now having to evaluate whether they want to continue it.”
Obamacare premiums likely to surge again next year

The KFF report examined not just the number of people who enrolled in Obamacare plans this year compared with last year, but also how many maintained that coverage as the year went on. Many people, the group noted, enroll but then end up dropping coverage when they can’t make the first premium payment.
This year, Mississippi had the lowest rate of enrollees maintaining coverage past January, at around 61%, while South Carolina, Louisiana, Indiana and Oklahoma also had rates below 70%. In New Mexico, California, Nevada, Vermont, and Idaho — all states with their own marketplaces — at least 95% of enrollees kept their coverage.
Lo said it’s hard to predict how enrollment figures may look in a year, as some insurers that currently offer plans on the marketplaces “are reassessing their positions and their commitment” to participating.
“So, if insurers are pulling out, people who are seeking marketplace coverage might have fewer choices,” Lo said.
Obamacare insurers are proposing a median premium increase of 14% for 2027, which would be a double-digit hike for the second year in a row, according to a new analysis of preliminary rate filings. Rates should be finalized later this summer.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Federal judge voids Johnston’s land seizure under eminent domain
description: U.S. District Court Judge Melissa DuBose on Tuesday ruled Johnston's attempt to seize land for a new town hall and public safety complex violated constitutional requirements, handing a victory to developers planning a 252-unit affordable housing project.
text:
A Providence federal judge has tossed the town of Johnston's attempt to take land from a family-owned homebuilding corporation for a new municipal complex. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)A Providence federal judge on Tuesday invalidated the town of Johnston’s 2024 attempt to seize 31 acres of land by eminent domain from a family-owned homebuilding company in order to build a new public safety complex and town hall.
Rhode Island U.S. District Judge Melissa R. DuBose ruled that the town failed to meet basic constitutional requirements when it sought to take over the site of a planned 252-unit affordable housing complex on George Waterman Road. Dubose wrote that Johnston officials acted without pledging “the public faith and credit” to provide just compensation and without establishing clear enforcement procedures.
Johnston mayor dodges an affordable housing complex with a silver bullet

“When a municipality elects to invoke the power of eminent domain, it must proceed in the manner prescribed by law, and the town did not do so here,” DuBose wrote in her 20-page ruling.
On March 10, 2025, the Johnston Town Council voted 5-0 to begin the legal process of condemning the site after obtaining an appraisal that found the property was worth $775,000. Two days later, the town transferred title to the property to itself by eminent domain and filed a petition in Rhode Island Superior Court seeking permission to deposit estimated just compensation into the court registry.
A Superior Court judge later ordered the town to change the land records back to the family-owned homebuilder corporations of Santoro and Salvatore Compagnone — whose families have owned the land since the 1980s.
The town maintained that its eminent domain authority derived independently from its home rule charter, which was ratified by the Rhode Island General Assembly.
“The town proceeded to condemn the property relying on nothing more than a charter provision that, standing alone, cannot bear the constitutional weight the town has placed on it,” DuBose wrote.
On the same day in December 2024 that the Santoro family met with the town’s Planning Board for a pre-application meeting for their income-restricted apartment complex, Johnston Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr. issued a public letter opposing the proposed housing development. Polisena warned that the town would “fight back” using “all the power of government” available to stop the project.
Polisena made no secret of his desire to move forward with plans for a new public safety complex and town hall to replace the town’s aging buildings.
The Santoro family claimed neither they nor their lawyer received constitutionally adequate notice of the filing, the transfer of title or the proceedings in state court before the transfer was recorded. They filed a federal lawsuit against the town, identified as SCLS Realty, LLC, and Sixty Three Johnston, LLC.
“Eminent domain is one of the most powerful tools a government may wield against a property owner, but that power comes with real legal limits,” said Kady Valois, an attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation, which represented the Santoro family in the case. “The Town of Johnston didn’t follow those limits — it tried to seize private property by making up its own procedures, exercising a power it does not possess under both Rhode Island law and the U.S. Constitution. A taking without lawful authority is, as the court concluded, ‘void ab initio.’”
Rhode Island Current reached out to Polisena for comment about the town’s plans for the site after Tuesday’s ruling. An email response from his deputy chief of staff, Dominique Turner, had a statement attributed to Polisena.
“On page one of the decision, the court states that it ‘does not question the exercise of that authority,’ thereby acknowledging the town of Johnston’s power to exercise eminent domain,” the statement reads. “The town will follow the court’s guidance regarding the proper procedure moving forward.”

name: WyoFile
title: Another Weston County clerk resigns — this time 3 weeks before an election
description:
The clerk’s office in Newcastle has been under significant strain since a 2024 ballot miscount led to multiple investigations and criminal charges.  
The post Another Weston County clerk resigns — this time 3 weeks before an election appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Weston County Clerk Michael Tooman resigned Tuesday, three weeks before the primary election and less than two months after a district court judge appointed him to the position. 
“I was becoming a focal point for questioning the validity of the election, and we badly need a good election in Weston County,” Tooman told WyoFile on Tuesday. “And so I just removed myself.”
The clerk’s office in Newcastle has been under a significant strain since 2024, when former clerk Becky Hadlock caused an initial ballot miscount that sparked public outcry, a legislative subpoena, several investigations and multiple criminal charges. 
Hadlock resigned in April, one day after she was arrested and charged with two felonies related to her conduct during and after the 2024 general election. In May, Hadlock reached an agreement with prosecutors that reduced one felony to a misdemeanor and dismissed the second charge in exchange for a guilty plea. The deal helped her avoid any jail time.
Tooman was appointed in June to fill the vacancy until voters selected a new clerk in the 2026 election. That process, however, was also not without controversy. A district court judge stepped in after county commissioners failed to make a selection from the three nominees provided by the Weston County Republican Party. 
“I was court ordered in the first place,” Tooman said Tuesday. “The commissioners weren’t willing to choose me from the three names, so it’s already controversial.”
Tooman said he would not “go into specific details because they’re not relevant,” but he became a “distraction” after he had Weston County GOP Committeewoman Ann Slagle “come and help me because she was an election judge to help set everything up.”
Local residents objected to that, Tooman said. 
“Even though there’s nothing that I did illegally or immorally or unethically. [It] doesn’t matter — perception. The number one rule of politics, whether you like it or not, perception is reality,” Tooman said. 
Tooman also withdrew as a candidate from the race, which leaves deputy clerk Amber Green running unopposed in the primary election. In the meantime, she’s now serving as interim clerk. 
“She’ll do a good job,” Tooman said. “I’m very confident that she’ll handle it. I really am. If I wasn’t, I wouldn’t have resigned.”
Green declined to comment Tuesday to WyoFile but confirmed that the public testing of election machines scheduled for today had been postponed and that her office is working with the secretary of state’s office to keep things on track for the Aug. 18 primary election. 
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

title: Courts issue conflicting rulings on Trump executive order restricting vote-by-mail
text: A federal appeals court ruled Tuesday that the federal government can continue implementing President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting vote-by-mail, reaching the opposite conclusion that another appeals panel decided over the weekend.The conflict appeared to make it even more clear the issue will have to be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court, which already has been asked for its opinion on Trump’s sweeping order that would have a huge impact on states just a little more than three months before the midterm elections.A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said Tuesday the executive order, which directs the U.S. Postal Service to collect from states lists of eligible voters who intend to vote by mail at least two months before an election and the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of voting-age citizens in each state, can proceed because the agencies have not yet written rules implementing the order.A D.C. trial judge in May denied several voting rights groups’ request to block the order, saying the groups had not yet been harmed.Judges Patricia Millett and Robert Wilkins, who were appointed by President Barack Obama, and Gregory Katsas, whom Trump appointed, affirmed the decision.They wrote that the executive order, which Trump signed March 31, is not self-executing and specifically tells the USPS and DHS to write the prescribed rules in a way that is consistent with the federal laws the groups say the order violates.“We affirm because, while Plaintiffs have identified a number of serious questions concerning the lawfulness of proposed actions if implemented on the threshold of the upcoming federal election, this case likely is unripe for review in its present posture,” they wrote.Their order directly contradicts a ruling the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals published Saturday in a case brought by Democratic officials from 23 states and the District of Columbia. That opinion held that states would be harmed if the order was allowed to proceed because state elections officials would immediately have to shift significant resources to prepare to meet the order’s requirements, even without final rules from USPS or DHS.The Trump administration appealed that ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the justice assigned to the 1st Circuit, requested briefs on whether the court should hear the case by Aug. 3. In a social media post, the voting rights legal group Democracy Docket, which is not affiliated with the case, called Tuesday’s ruling “a loss for voters” and said the administration under it could build a citizenship roster and withhold mail-in ballots from states that do not share citizenship data.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Report on reducing environmental risks of cancer travels across the state
description: BOONE – In a conference room at the Ericson Public Library Tuesday, cancer survivors, farmers, elected officials and community activists from Boone County discussed the things they have done to reduce their exposure to carcinogens and the things they hope will change in Iowa to help lower the state’s high cancer rates.  The discussion in […]
text:
Iowa Environmental Council led a conversation in Boone about its report on environmental risk factors and cancer. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) BOONE – In a conference room at the Ericson Public Library Tuesday, cancer survivors, farmers, elected officials and community activists from Boone County discussed the things they have done to reduce their exposure to carcinogens and the things they hope will change in Iowa to help lower the state’s high cancer rates. 
The discussion in downtown Boone was part of a series of community conversations led by the Iowa Environmental Council about the information in the “Environmental Risk Factors and Iowa’s Cancer Crisis” report the council released in March. 
Kathy Toms, a Boone County resident, said she started removing the toxins she could control from her life five years ago after a breast cancer diagnosis. Now she prioritizes foods, beverages and household products that are free of chemicals she feels might have contributed to her cancer. 
“I don’t want to fight again,” Toms said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Boone County, according to figures from the Iowa Cancer Registry, has a cancer incidence rate and a cancer-related mortality rate higher than the state or national averages. 
The conversation in Boone was the eighth stop for the council in its tour around the state to present the report, which analyzed more than 250 studies and included the perspectives of hundreds of Iowans that participated in public forums.
Kerri Johannsen, Iowa Environmental Council’s senior director of policy and programs, said the council is hosting the conversations in areas that have especially high cancer rates, or where the council has a local partner to help host the event. 
She said that while the Tuesday event in Boone was full of folks who have been engaged with this issue, usually the room is split when presenters ask who has called their elected officials or submitted an opinion article to their local papers on the issue. 
Johannsen said the council is listening to the concerns and solutions brought forward by attendees who often bring different perspectives than researchers. 
“What do we all want to do together, because this is impacting everybody,” Johannsen said. “Everyone has to be at the table, or we’re not going to make progress.” 
Johannsen asked the room if they knew someone who had cancer — every hand was raised in response. She was again met with a room full of raised hands after asking if those gathered felt like the state had a “long way to go” in addressing the connection between environmental issues and cancer. 
Diana Wright, a Boone County resident at the event, said she wants to see more action on Iowa’s water quality issues. 
“We’ve got a huge water quality issue in the state, and we’ve got a huge cancer issue,” Wright said. “I want to make sure I’m understanding the science, and then we need to advocate to do something about it because I think there’s a lot of stuff out there that could be preventable, and we need to have the will to make the changes.”
The report, which was done in collaboration with the Harkin Institute at Drake University, started as a look at water quality in Iowa and its relationship to Iowa’s cancer incidence rates. Iowa is one of two states where the rate is rising, instead of declining. 
The final report looked at pesticides, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, nitrate and radon – all of which, the report concluded, have links to the types of cancers that are higher in Iowa than in other states. 
The report points to Iowa’s vast agricultural landscape, livestock industries and the application of fertilizers, which can cause elevated concentrations of nitrate in the water, and pesticides. 
Toms, who raises grass-fed cattle, said she felt that the presentation focused largely on agricultural applications of fertilizers and pesticides and didn’t emphasize that the same products are used in urban areas as well. 
“It’s more than just the farm families,” Toms said. “Towns have a responsibility too.” 
Other environmental risks, like PFAS, can enter waterways through wastewater streams and impact humans through things like non-stick cookware, certain types of clothing, cosmetics and other products. 
Radon is a naturally occurring gas that is emitted during the breakdown of soil and rock, and is the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The report shows that Iowa homes have higher radon rates than other parts of the country. 
The Iowa legislature passed a law this spring that requires new homes to be built with radon mitigation systems, in an effort to lower Iowa’s cancer instances.
Wright said there are policies that could be enacted to help with Iowa’s water quality, but she felt things like “power and profit” get in the way of making significant changes. 
“The only ones that get traction are the ones like radon mitigation,” Wright said. “No humans caused the radon issue, so those are easier to deal with.” 
Wright said she recently tested for radon and installed a radon mitigation system in her home. Another attendee, Margaret Liston from Ogden, said she installed a reverse osmosis system in her home to help limit her exposure to potential toxins in the water. 
Johannsen told attendees that the goal wasn’t to memorize the powerpoint, or the statistics about environmental risk factors, but to know “with confidence” that this is an issue in Iowa. Then, she said, they can speak to friends and family members, or even push for change at a higher level. 
“The most powerful thing any person can do is to talk about how this has impacted their own lives or the lives of their kids, their parents, their neighbors, etc.” Johannsen said. “Those stories are going to move policymakers.” 
Future community conversations on the report can be found, at the Iowa Environmental Council’s website.

title: Medgar Evers Library reopens to ‘an explosion of excitement’
description: Hundreds of children from area daycare centers were treated to music, storytime, face-painting, play activities and snacks during the reopening celebration of the Medgar Evers Library, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The Medgar Evers Library reopened Tuesday during a day packed with activities for Jackson children.
Mississippi Today previously reported that multiple branches in the Jackson/Hinds Library System had maintenance issues, including the Evers branch in northwest Jackson.
The library closed for two months for air conditioning repairs. David Burks Jr., vice-chairman of the Jackson/Hinds Library System’s board of trustees, confirmed that the building has a new HVAC system.
“People come here for everything, so we wanted to make sure we got it up and running,” he said during a back-to-school event at the library.
The library will be open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Monday to Thursday, and from  9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday and Saturday.
On their first day back, the library held a Back-to-School Bash. Branch manager Anne Sanders said at least 400 children from the area attended for a day of music, food and fun.
