name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rep. Analilia Mejia marks 100 days in office as another election nears
description: Rep. Analilia Mejia has been in office for 100 days after winning a special House election in April. She’s seeking reelection in November.
text:
Rep. Analilia Mejia has been in office for 100 days after winning a special House election in April. She’s seeking reelection in November. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Analilia Mejia described her first 100 days in Congress in one word: jarring.
“One would think that in such a space, there would be more discussion, there would be a genuine debate on issues that are of such importance, like the lives of American people we send abroad to fight in wars or how affordable housing, healthcare, gasoline is for everyday American families,” Mejia told the New Jersey Monitor. “It’s been jarring to see that it’s not.”
Mejia, a Democrat and former union organizer, won the special election for New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District in April following her surprise win in a crowded Democratic primary against some opponents who had support from the district’s establishment Democrats.
Since taking office on April 20, she said she’s co-sponsored more than 80 bills, including Medicare for All and the John Lewis Voting Rights Act, along with legislation aimed at universal childcare and revamping the Supreme Court by establishing term limits for justices and enforcing a code of ethics.
She touted a task force she launched centered on the 14th Amendment as one of her signature efforts. President Donald Trump’s attempt this year to argue the amendment does not guarantee citizenship to children born in the United States to parents who aren’t citizens was rejected by the U.S. Supreme Court last month.
But she said the accomplishment she’s proudest of is less about legislation and more about her constituent outreach: telephone town halls, in-person meetings, and regular updates keeping the district’s residents informed about her time in Congress.
“I’ve tried to think about what I wanted or what I want as a constituent, which is information, transparency and explanation on votes, and integrity,” she said. “That’s what I’ve tried to deliver to the people of my district.”
The district was formerly represented by Mikie Sherrill (D), who resigned from Congress last year to become governor.
Reps. Frank Pallone, Analilia Mejia, and Rob Menendez exit Delaney Hall after visiting the detention center in Newark on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Mejia was sharply critical of Trump’s immigration policy and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during her campaign earlier this year. When Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall became a national flashpoint within weeks of Mejia’s swearing-in — detainees said they launched a hunger strike over conditions inside — Mejia made frequent visits to the facility with other members of Congress. She said she came away alarmed with what she found, including detainees cramped during meals before dawn and detainees with chronic illnesses who lacked medical attention.
Mejia, who is the second Latina to represent New Jersey in Congress, said people “don’t have to speak Spanish or identify as an immigrant to feel the humanity and reject the chaos.”
“The bottom line is that we need to ensure that the facilities that our U.S. government are utilizing not only meet the needs of individuals, but that we’re not incentivizing the long-term detention of people who would be best served in the community,” she said.
Mejia is running for reelection in November against the same Republican she faced in April’s special election, Randolph Councilman Joe Hathaway. That election is for the two-year term that begins in January.
In an interview, Hathaway criticized Mejia’s response to the Delaney Hall unrest, saying her visit to the facility during Memorial Day weekend was used to “stoke the flames of rioters” and to make social media videos to placate her “radical base.” That weekend, federal immigration agents fired pepper balls at protesters rallying outside the facility.
“Before she was a congresswoman, she would have been out there because she’s an activist. That’s what she does,” he said. “That is not what we need in Congress.”
Hathaway argued that her record shows she’s governed as an ideological activist rather than a pragmatic, bipartisan legislator.
“For the people of NJ-11, her term has been a complete and abject failure — an F in all ways,” he said. “When you look at the legislation she’s supported, it falls right in lockstep with these radical socialist candidates. She’s paving the way for what we see in New York and Colorado with these anti-law enforcement, anti-government socialists.”
Joe Hathaway speaks at Morris County GOP headquarters in Morris Plains on Feb. 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Mejia dismissed the attacks as personal rather than substantive.
“It just shows that because Joe Hathaway has no legs to stand on, he defaults to name-calling. I’m a mom with two kids. I’m familiar with it, and I see it for what it is,” she said.
She also pushed back on the idea that she’s governing from the left, pointing to her support of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, a new law that creates competitive grant programs for towns to increase housing supply, cuts regulatory red tape, and restricts large institutional investors from buying single-family homes.
“My opponent is content to raise costs by following Donald Trump in this illegal war, in eliminating energy tax credits, in fighting against affordable housing,” she added. “I’m trying to ensure that our Constitution is upheld.”

description: A bipartisan committee of Wisconsin legislators has signed off on a $250,000 funding deal for WisconsinEye, the livestream service that covers the state Legislature. The Joint Committee on Legislative Organization approved the funds, to be paid out $50,000 per month starting Aug. 1, on a 9-1 vote, the nonpartisan Legislative Council announced Tuesday. The co[...]
text:
From left, Assembly Minority Leader Greta Neubauer and Assembly Speaker Robin Vos speak at a joint press conference in January announcing an agreement to fund WisconsinEye. That bill died after passing the Assembly, but this week a committee of leaders from both parties approved funding the livestream service through the end of this year. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)A bipartisan committee of Wisconsin legislators has signed off on a $250,000 funding deal for WisconsinEye, the livestream service that covers the state Legislature.
The Joint Committee on Legislative Organization approved the funds, to be paid out $50,000 per month starting Aug. 1, on a 9-1 vote, the nonpartisan Legislative Council announced Tuesday. The committee is made up of six Republican and four Democratic leaders of both the Senate and the Assembly.
Sen. Dan Feyen (R-Fond du Lac), the assistant Senate majority leader, cast the only vote against the proposal.
The funding is to support WisconsinEye so it can provide livestream coverage of floor sessions in the Legislature as well as public hearings and votes held by Senate and Assembly committees, as it continues to seek long-term funding to operate.
WisEye President Jon Henkes welcomed the vote Tuesday, saying that it provided “a strong statement of support” in both chambers “for unfettered citizen access to state government proceedings,” with both Republicans and Democrats signing on.
“They’ve put action to their words that transparency is essential to our democracy, and we are extremely grateful,” Henkes said in a statement.
Henkes said the sum was sufficient for WisconsinEye to maintain operations through December, including its coverage of events in the 2026 election campaign as well as coverage of the Legislature’s joint study committees, which are discussing a variety of topics with future policy implications.
The vote also provides “an existing foundation of ongoing support” that will be important to charitable donors and WisEye program sponsors, according to the WisconsinEye statement.
The streaming service is counting on the new Legislature that takes office in January 2027 to reach a bipartisan agreement for future partial funding for the service.
WisconsinEye launched as an independent nonprofit in 2007 to livestream and archive government meetings and legislative sessions. The service has operated on donations and runs independently from the state Legislature.
WisconsinEye’s management announced in November 2025 that it needed additional revenue to support the service’s $900,000 annual budget after donations fell behind in the last couple of years.  The service went dark for nearly two months at the end of December, resuming in February.
Two separate proposals to fund the service passed earlier this year, one in the Assembly and the other in the Senate, but neither one got a vote in the opposite chamber.

WISDOM hosts a forum with seven gubernatorial candidates. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The five Democratic candidates for governor of Wisconsin will face off in the only televised debate ahead of the Aug. 11 primary Tuesday evening at 7 p.m.
The candidates are former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, Joel Brennan, former state Department of Administration chief, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, state Rep. Francesca Hong and state Sen. Kelda Roys.
The meeting of the candidates comes on the first day of in-person early voting with two weeks to go before Election Day. Recent polls show Hong leading the race. 
The winner of the primary will likely face U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the presumptive Republican nominee in November. 
The debate, which will run until 8 p.m., will be hosted by WISN 12 on the Marquette University campus and moderated by Gerron Jordan and Matt Smith, WISN 12 journalists and hosts of “Upfront.” There will not be an in-person audience. 
According to WISN, the debate will air on WISN 12 along with local ABC affiliates across the state including WBAY in Green Bay, WKOW 27.2 in Madison, WXOW 19.2 in La Crosse, WQOW 18.2 in Eau Claire and WAOW 9.2 in Wausau. name: VTDigger
title: Vermont schools are on the slide
description:
Vermont has spent a decade comparing its schools only to itself. Set against the rest of the country, that comfort disappears.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont schools are on the slide.
text:
Dear Editor,
For years, the reassuring answer to worry about Vermont’s schools has been a comparison: Vermont scores above the national average. That was true for decades. This year it survives on one of four federal checks — and the national average itself has been falling. Vermont has been falling faster.
I pulled together a public dataset putting nearly every Vermont district’s test results on the federal National Assessment of Educational Progress scale, using Stanford’s Education Data Archive, so they can be compared honestly with districts across the state and over time. The short version:
In 2013, Vermont students scored about nine-tenths of a grade level above the 2019 national norm. By 2025, they scored half a grade below it — and most of that lead was gone before the pandemic closed a single school. The median Vermont district has fallen from the 78th percentile of U.S. districts to the 40th since 2013.
It is not money. Vermont spends $1.64 for every dollar the nation spends per student: $28,818 against $17,619 in the latest federal accounting.
And the slide shows up in numbers that districts already publish. Fewer than half of Vermont’s graduates now continue to college within 16 months, down from about six in 10 in the 2019 count. More than one student in four is chronically absent.
My own district, Washington Central, illustrates the trap of local comparison. It still leads Vermont; its edge over the state average has more than doubled. Against the country, it fell from the 86th percentile to the 71st. And adjusted for the community it serves — family income, adult education, poverty, employment and family structure — its advantage over what communities like its own typically score is gone entirely: 81st percentile in 2013, 50th in 2024. A district can look excellent in the Vermont mirror while the rest of the country walks past it.

READ MORE

None of this is an indictment of teachers or students; test scores measure the opportunities that communities provide as much as anything a school does. But it is an argument that Vermont’s school debate — consolidation, funding formulas, governance — is being conducted against the wrong yardstick. 
The comparison that matters is not “better or worse than the Vermont average.” It is “better or worse than the country,” and on that comparison Vermont has been losing ground for more than a decade.
Matt Rkiouak
Middlesex, Vt.

description: Drivers with low incomes will soon be able to pay less to travel on two of Washington’s newest tolled roadways. After months of conversation, the Washington State Transportation Commission approved a new program last week offering a 50% discount on tolls on the state route 509 and 167 expressways in the Puget Sound region. People […]
text:
In December 2026, Washington plans to begin offering offer a toll discount for drivers with lower incomes on State Route 509 expressway (above) and the State Route 167 expressway. (Photo courtesty of Washington State Department of Transportation)Drivers with low incomes will soon be able to pay less to travel on two of Washington’s newest tolled roadways.
After months of conversation, the Washington State Transportation Commission approved a new program last week offering a 50% discount on tolls on the state route 509 and 167 expressways in the Puget Sound region. People can sign up this fall, with discounts available starting in December.
With current toll rates on those routes ranging from $1.20 to $2.40 in peak hours, eligible drivers who commute daily on the expressways could save a couple hundred dollars a year.
This will be the state’s first foray into permitting some drivers who use a Good to Go! pass to pay lower tolls based on income. The discount does not apply to the fee for those who pay by mail. 
This program could eventually expand to the Highway 520 bridge, Interstate 405, and Tacoma Narrows Bridge.
“We have been advocating for a low-income toll policy for a long time. I’m really happy that we’re taking a pragmatic step forward,” said Commissioner Debbie Young before the panel voted. “Our hope is that we will expand this to the other toll facilities around the state and other people in need.”
Where it’s happening
A provision in the current state transportation budget directs the commission and Washington State Department of Transportation to “design and implement a toll relief” program. 
What was developed will launch on two segments of the Puget Sound Gateway project, a $2.8 billion undertaking to improve access to the ports of Tacoma and Seattle and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.
The discount will apply on the first leg of a four-lane expressway that will eventually run from Interstate 5 to where Highway 509 ends near the airport.

CONTACT US




For State Route 167, the reduced rate will only cover the six-mile expressway being constructed between Puyallup and the Port of Tacoma. It will be available when tolling starts in December on the initial two-mile stretch from Interstate 5 in Fife to the port.
How it will work
This program is only for two-axle vehicles such as passenger cars, vans and trucks.
To qualify, a person must have a household income of no more than 200% of the Federal Poverty Level. In 2026, a single person would be eligible if their annual income does not exceed $31,920. For a family of four, the maximum is $66,000.
The Washington State Department of Transportation will administer the program, including verifying eligibility.
A person will need to provide documentation to show they’re eligible or that they are already enrolled in other income-qualified programs. 
They also will need to show they have a vehicle registered in Washington and the name on the registration matches theirs. They will be able to apply online or by mail. Approval is good for a year, after which a person would need to re-enroll.
Transportation commission staff received comments from 1,700 people on the program during a multi-week online open house with another 149 sharing their views in emails.
Overall, more people expressed support than opposition. Supporters said they would like to see discounts offered on more of the state’s tolled facilities. Some also said they would like to see a larger discount and eligibility expanded to cover more people, Aaron Halbert, a financial analyst with the commission, told the panel.
Among opponents, the “number one” theme centered on fairness that all drivers should pay the same amount, he said. Some expressed concern that toll rates will rise when the program starts. Halbert said that will not happen, as the potential costwas accounted for in the rate-setting process.
‘Better than nothing’
Commissioner Matt Ransom said when the program is up and running, it should be aggressively audited to be responsive to concerns that were raised, including that some ineligible drivers may try to game the system to get the discount.
“While the program may not be perfect, it’s not overly ambitious and fraught with what could be complex implementation hurdles,” said Ransom. “With that said, I’m very empathetic to those that need relief, and I believe the legislative intent was to provide relief.”
Commissioner Nicole Grant of King County threw a little cold water on the conversation as she reluctantly backed it.
“Even if it’s just $1.50 a couple times for a poor person, for the very low income, of course I’d vote yes on that,” she said.
But, she said, as one who lives next to the project and knows how people in the community actually feel about it, “I can’t celebrate it and I can’t celebrate the policy because it’s inadequate.”
The 509 expressway runs through a “poor and racially diverse neighborhood” in south King County, she said. Residents will have to pay the toll “for the rest of their lives” and deal with traffic from what is intended to be a heavily-used freight corridor.
“I’m going to vote for it because it’s better than nothing,” she said. “But I don’t think WSDOT has shown respect to the community. They’ve shown respect to shipping corporations and to the freight industry. Those are industries. Those aren’t people.”SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

title: Byron Donalds wants to ax ultra-processed foods in school
description: Gubernatorial candidate U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds is advocating for a plan similar to one the Florida Legislature has declined to advance — removing ultra-processed foods from school lunchrooms. Donalds, a Republican and former member of the Florida House, wants ultra-processed food, artificial dyes, and “harmful additives” removed from school meals. “When a k[...]
text:
School lunches are to focus of Byron Donalds' latest platform point. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Gubernatorial candidate U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds is advocating for a plan similar to one the Florida Legislature has declined to advance — removing ultra-processed foods from school lunchrooms.
Donalds, a Republican and former member of the Florida House, wants ultra-processed food, artificial dyes, and “harmful additives” removed from school meals.
“When a kid sits down in a cafeteria, parents want to know what’s on that tray. When they fill a cup at the fountain, we want to know what’s in that water,” Donalds said in a news release. 
“Florida doesn’t have to wait on Washington to catch up. We already grow the food and we already have the farmers ready to supply it. This isn’t radical, it’s what every parent expects at their own kitchen table, and it’s what Florida is going to deliver to every Florida student.”
Ag commissioner says Legislature should chop ultra-processed school lunches

Still, Florida lawmakers last year sounded like they prefer to wait for Washington.
During the 2025 legislative session, Sen. Jon Martin, R-Fort Myers, introduced SB 1826, which would’ve defined the term “ultra-processed food” and prohibited schools from serving or selling it.
That bill was heard in the Senate Agriculture Committee, but amid concerns from lobbyists in the food and beverage industry it died. He did not introduce the bill again in 2026. 
Those lobbyists suggested that banning certain ingredients would leave consumers questioning their confidence in the food supply.
In addition to those concerns were logistical ones, including finding new food suppliers and buying food that would likely cost more on already-tight cafeteria budgets. Well-established school food suppliers would likely either have to create separate products meeting Florida standards or schools would have to find new suppliers. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In October, in advance of the 2026 legislative session, state Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson said he was dedicated to addressing students’ “diet of ultra-processed foods,” particularly in Florida school lunches.
Following a report from President Donald Trump’s Make America Healthy Again Commission, Simpson said that, pending federal action, he “is committed to defining and addressing ultra-processed foods during Florida’s upcoming legislative session.”
“Schools that receive federal lunch subsidies are required to follow a meal pattern that limits added sugars, sodium, and carbohydrates, but do not set limits on UPF consumption, leading to excessive intake of sugar, processed carbohydrates, processed fats, and sodium among children,” the MAHA report states.
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services hosts the Farm to Schools program, which focuses on getting Florida farm products into school lunches.
He wants to ramp up that program with “a dedicated appropriation to build the supply chain clean food standards need.”
Donalds billed the plan as a commitment to agriculture producers.
He also wants to require schools to post menus and ingredients on the internet and to “guarantee every Florida child access to clean, tested water at school and at home.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand presents ‘distinctions’ with opponent’s positions during cancer forum
description: Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said he would support increasing pediatric cancer research funding, raising taxes on tobacco and nicotine products and ensuring access to cancer-preventing vaccines — but warned advocates Tuesday these actions will require GOP support. Sand, a Democrat who currently serves as Iowa state auditor, met with organizers and volunt[...]
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate running for Iowa governor in 2026, spoke to American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network advocates at The Empire in Des Moines July 28, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said he would support increasing pediatric cancer research funding, raising taxes on tobacco and nicotine products and ensuring access to cancer-preventing vaccines — but warned advocates Tuesday these actions will require GOP support.
Sand, a Democrat who currently serves as Iowa state auditor, met with organizers and volunteers with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network at The Empire in Des Moines Tuesday for a “coffee cancer chat.” It was part of a  nonpartisan series of events the group is holding with candidates on the ballot in 2026 to ask them about their plans to address high and rising cancer rates in Iowa.
Businessman Zach Lahn, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, is also set to speak with ACS CAN advocates as part of the series in August.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sand told advocates at the event he believed there were important “distinctions” between him and Lahn when it came to the issue of cancer. The Democratic said his opponent was someone “who wants to ban all future mRNA vaccines,” and who was part of “the campaign on behalf of a dark money group in Montana to try to prevent Medicaid expansion there.”
“I think that Iowans are ready for balance,” Sand told reporters after the event. “… I go back to some of the positions of my opponent. He would ban some of the most promising cancer treatments that are out there today. That is the wrong direction. He cheered on some of the cuts at the federal level to cancer research. That is the wrong direction. Balance and common sense that you get from forcing both parties to work together is a path towards actually addressing real issues with real solutions.”
Dan Capodilupo, director of communications for Lahn’s campaign, said, “Zach has been loud and clear from day one of this campaign that Iowa is facing a cancer crisis. He has been the most vocal candidate in the entire state about solving this crisis and has spoken at length on numerous occasions about his specific plans.”
Sand also criticized Lahn’s running mate, state Rep. Derek Wulf, as “someone who voted to defund water quality monitoring in the state of Iowa” — a major concern as many Iowans and researchers say there may be links between high nitrate levels and the state’s cancer rates. But Capodilupo said the Democratic candidate’s running mate, Dave Muhlbauer, is also a subject of scrutiny on the issue of water quality.
“The Sand Campaign has no room to talk about water quality,” Capodilupo said in a statement. “Rob’s own running mate was fined by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources. The Muhlbauer family’s cattle feedlot was investigated and fined $7,000 for allowing manure-contaminated runoff to pollute local streams. Rob is projecting onto our campaign and ignoring the elephant in the room, when it comes to his running mate.”
Several cancer patients and survivors, as well as caregivers and medical professionals who treat people with cancer, told Sand about their personal experiences battling cancer and asked the Democrat about policy and funding commitments related to cancer research, prevention and healthcare if he were to become governor.
Bogdan Buzdugan, a pediatric cancer researcher at the University of Iowa’s Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center, said the funding for his research and for other forms of pediatric cancer often comes from patients and “parents continue to fund our research though their child has passed away.”
More support has come from the state in 2026, when the Iowa Legislature approved up to $3 million in pediatric cancer research funding by implementing a 5-cent tax on vapes and alternative nicotine products. But Buzdugan said, “especially if you talk to any senior researcher, especially in the cancer department at University of Iowa, $3 million is almost nothing.”
Sand said if elected governor, he would support expanding funding for pediatric cancer research. He gave “credit where credit is due” to Republicans who advocated for increasing pediatric cancer research funding this year, highlighting support from Rep. Jason Gearhart, R-Strawberry Point, but said the state should be providing significantly more in research funding.
“Nebraska has done over $20 million,” Sand said. “And I’m a very proud Iowan. I think that we all should want to beat Nebraska in cancer research. So that should be table stakes to us, as we look at what Nebraska did for their kids. And for kids in general — of course, since cancer research doesn’t follow state boundaries, but we should say, ‘Oh, you put in that much, we can beat that.'”
Though the GOP-led Legislature did approve a 5-cent vape and nicotine product tax, other legislation raising taxes on these products by a more significant margin — as well as a proposal to increase the tax on tobacco products — did not reach Gov. Kim Reynolds’ desk in 2026.
Advocates at the event asked if Sand would support a $1.50 per pack tax increase on cigarettes as well as a 50% tax on tobacco and nicotine products by wholesale price — taxes the organization has argued would serve as a deterrent to tobacco and nicotine use, and reduce lung cancer rates. Sand did not commit to these numbers, but said he supported finding a compromise with GOP state lawmakers on raising these taxes.
“I know that there is support, in both chambers and in both parties, to make sure that our tobacco tax in Iowa and for nicotine products is at a more competitive level, right?” Sand said. “And when we do that, we can also make sure that we are discouraging people from using those products, which again is helping them stay healthier as well as helping everyone else keep healthcare costs low. Now I say to everybody, everywhere I go, you’re never going to get 100% of what you want. … But I am here to tell you that I want to learn more about that and try to find it a level that we can put it at that is going to help improve healthcare outcomes for Iowans, and and put us in a place where we also aren’t just sending everyone somewhere else to go get it instead.”
Sand said he believed it was important to be realistic about what he could deliver. While he said he supported easy access to the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, which has been linked with significantly lowering instances of cervical cancer especially when a person is vaccinated before age 17, he said it was unlikely the Legislature would want to change a law signed this year restricting minors from receiving the HPV and hepatitis B vaccines without parental consent.
“I’m going to be working with the same Legislature that just voted to pass that, I can’t imagine them putting a bill on my desk that would reverse it,” he said.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Proposed WV natural gas plant to generate power for Dominion Energy customers in Virginia, PJM grid
description: Dominion Energy, a Virginia-based company, is proposing to construct a new natural gas-fired power plant in Grant County, which would be connected to the existing coal-fired plant near Mt. Storm, according to a Tuesday news release from Gov. Patrick Morrisey.
text:
A look inside the Mt. Storm Power Station, a coal-fired power plant in Grant County that could be combined with a newly proposed natural gas plant owned by Virginia-based Dominion Energy. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office via Facebook)Dominion Energy, a Virginia-based company, is proposing to construct a new natural gas-fired power plant in Grant County, which would be connected to the existing coal-fired plant near Mt. Storm, according to a Tuesday news release from Gov. Patrick Morrisey.
The new energy plant, if constructed, could add 2.6 gigawatts of natural gas-generated power to the region in addition to the 1.6 GW already produced by the coal-fired Mt. Storm Power Station, which the company plans to keep online as part of the new Mt. Storm Combined Cycle Station.
When asked via email on Tuesday whether the power proposed to be generated by the Mt. Storm Combined Cycle Station would be used in West Virginia, Jeremy Slayton, a spokesperson for Dominion Energy, said, it will “serve (Dominion Energy’s) customers in Virginia.”
“… But excess energy can be utilized by the PJM grid, which includes West Virginia,” Slayton continued. 
Ed Baine, the executive vice president of Utility Operations at Dominion Energy, said in a news release Tuesday that the proposed project “will further enhance Mt. Storm’s positive impact on the economy and grid reliability for decades to come.”
“The project demonstrates our continued commitment to West Virginia and supports the state’s energy goals,” Baine said in the statement.
Dominion Energy is headquartered in Virginia, and serves millions of electric customers there and across the Carolinas. Excess power potentially produced at the West Virginia facility will go to the PJM grid, which delivers power to West Virginia and 12 other states.
Dominion estimates that the new Mt. Storm Combined Cycle Station could create 1,400 local construction jobs as well as 150 permanent jobs once the project is completed.
Last week, Dominion filed an application with the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection to modify its existing air quality permit to include the newly proposed natural gas plant. In the application, the company said that commercial operations at the new combination plant could start by 2033.
Per the modified application, the proposed plant will operate on four combustion turbines, which would burn natural gas that is piped in. A source for that gas was not indicated in the filing. Diesel would be stored on-site in two 4-million-gallon fuel storage tanks, to be used as backup power in generators when gas is not available.
Proposed annual emissions for the new site include:

More than 9.85 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions
2,917 tons of carbon monoxide
1,114 tons of volatile organic compounds
752 tons of nitrogen oxides

According to the modified application, the newly calculated emissions would mean up to 75,000 more tons of greenhouse gases could be emitted each year, as well as 40 more tons of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides. Carbon monoxide emissions could increase by 100 tons annually compared to current emissions at the Mt. Storm Power Station.
Dominion Energy wrote in its modified application that the new natural gas plant is necessary due to a projected increase in energy demand on the PJM grid, largely due to the expected creation of new data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities.
PJM predicts that, by 2030, peak demand on the grid will grow by 32 gigawatts. By 2045, that could increase to 70 gigawatts of need due to some power sources being taken offline. A majority of the forecasted increases in peak demand — which could mean higher utility rates and less reliability for customers that depend on the grid for power — are due to the addition of data centers. By 2030, for example, all but two of the 32 gigawatts in increased peak demand is estimated to come from data centers being added to the grid.
The proposal for the new plant was lauded by Morrisey, who said it will help the state reach goals he set in his “50 by 50 Power Generation Plan.” Under that plan — announced by Morrisey last year — the governor wants to see the state increase its energy generation to 50 gigawatts by 2025, largely by investing in coal- and natural gas-fired projects to offset future energy demand deficits on the grid.
In his news release on Tuesday, Morrisey said the state is already 20% of the way toward that goal.
“West Virginia is demonstrating that we can lead with coal, natural gas, nuclear energy and other forms of reliable energy that power America’s future,” he said. “These investments strengthen our position as America’s energy state, create good-paying jobs, and help ensure we can meet the nation’s growing demand for reliable, affordable power.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Water wars: Oklahoma residents fight for lake water
description: HINTON – A brown ring of dirt where waters once stood covers white rocks partially encircling Cedar Lake. It is an emotional reminder to residents of this rustic and blue collar community 45 miles west of Oklahoma City that their way of life and livelihoods are dramatically changing. Generations of families have celebrated the Fourth […]
text:
A water level marker at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)HINTON – A brown ring of dirt where waters once stood covers white rocks partially encircling Cedar Lake.
It is an emotional reminder to residents of this rustic and blue collar community 45 miles west of Oklahoma City that their way of life and livelihoods are dramatically changing.
Generations of families have celebrated the Fourth of July and other holidays on the beaches of the lake, which has served as a baptismal pool for children and grandchildren.
What began as a hunting club in the 1950s is dotted with original small cabins, newer residences and expansions. Pink and red Crape Myrtles and cedar trees dot the land, which is home to about 400 residents, about half who live there year-round.
Its red dirt and partially paved roads meander past a community garden, chapel and volunteer fire department.
But the residents say their idyllic lifestyle has been threatened by a well-connected political family, whose decision to erect a dam on a tributary feeding the lake has slowly caused levels to dramatically drop and have begun drying up the water wells it feeds.

They said their pleas for assistance from the state agency tasked with ensuring the state’s water resources are being adequately managed and used, have been ignored. Instead, they said the Oklahoma Water Resources Board has slow played a year-old complaint they filed seeking to have the two dams removed. 
“I’ve worked 71 years, all my life, to have lakefront property just to watch it dry up,” said Don Machacek, who lives in Oklahoma City but owns property at the lake.
A lack of action
Documents obtained by Oklahoma Voice through an open records request show that the state agency in May 2025 received its first anonymous complaint about the dams, which were erected upstream of the small lake that can hold up to 325.8 million gallons of water. 
Even as lake levels continued to drop and residents called repeatedly seeking assistance, emails indicate the agency was discussing the issue for months behind-the-scenes, and had quietly provided several extensions to the representatives of the owners of the dams.
A view of Dam No. 6 on the Coffee property affecting Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
After more than a year of inaction, Cedar Lake residents were outraged when the board earlier this month abruptly proposed allowing the dams to continue holding water while the owners went through the process of obtaining a permit. 
The Oklahoma Water Resources Board, which consists of nine members appointed by the governor, was prepared at the meeting to vote on an agreement with no public discussion, but tabled consideration until September after angry Cedar Lake property owners showed up at the public meeting to voice their disagreement.
Cedar Lake residents said while the property owner is listed as Coffee Grounds LLC and C&F Ranch, they believe the board’s reluctance to force the dams to be removed is because the property is connected to V. Glenn Coffee, a former powerful state senator who is now a paid senior legal consultant to the state Senate Republican Caucus. 
Coffee, who is an attorney, is listed as manager of the two entities and the respondent to the water board’s proposed agreement to allow the dams to remain, according to records. 
A former president pro tem of the Senate, Coffee backed bills that made it more difficult to file lawsuits and collect damages. He is also a former Secretary of State under former Republican Gov. Mary Fallin. He became well versed in Oklahoma’s water rights laws and worked helping resolve a major water rights dispute. That dispute involved the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations, the state of Oklahoma and Oklahoma City over transferring water from a major reservoir in southeastern Oklahoma to the capital city.
Coffee declined requests for interviews, but had previously told Oklahoma Voice that once his family became aware of the complaints, they hired two engineering firms and an attorney to guide them. 
His attorney did not return a phone call seeking comment, but told the board the dams were safe and well constructed. He disagreed with statements made by property owners and their attorney.
Oklahoma Water Resources Board leadership said after the meeting that it could not answer questions due to the “large number of requests.” The agency provided a statement, but did not respond to follow up questions.
State law allows dam owners to obtain a permit after dam construction, and the dams upstream of Cedar Lake do not pose an “immediate threat” to public safety, the statement said. 
Several residents disagree, saying if dams failed property owners downstream would suffer.
The agency’s solutions include establishing a rural water district for Cedar Lake, incorporating the community to make it eligible for financial support for a municipal water system, linking the community to a nearby rural water district, or obtaining expanded surface or groundwater rights to help improve lake levels. 
“None of these are going to be a ‘quick fix’ but we are exploring all options and meeting regularly with attorneys for the community,” the agency’s statement said.
A view of the low water level in the swimming area at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)From left, Mandy Taylor-Griffin, Charles Corey and Tammy Cramer look at Corey’s dock sitting on dry land at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Charles Corey’s dock sits on dry land at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)A dock sits on dry land at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)A dock sits above the water level at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)A view of Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Cedar Lake advocates sit at a Oklahoma Water Resources Board meeting on July 21, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)Anneliese Herren wears stickers showing support for Cedar Lake at a Oklahoma Water Resources Board meeting on July 21, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)Tammy Cramer’s dock is now on dry land as lake levels have dropped at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Docks are several feet above the water level at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Anneliese Herren sits next to her water well at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
 
Water experts weigh in
Cedar Lake property owners asked Carol Becker, a hydrologist with about 35 years experience, to take a look at their situation. 
Becker holds a master’s in hydrology and has done work for the Oklahoma Geological Survey.
“There is no rocket science going on here,” she said.
Becker released her findings last week. 
It is “very obvious” that the two dams constructed upstream are capturing runoff from almost 40% of the watershed, she said. Water that would normally flow into Cedar Lake has been impounded, resulting in a lake level drop, Becker said.
She found that since 2022 the groundwater levels in Cedar Lake have “steadily declined” and have reached “historically low levels” and that many water wells have dried up or have limited supply.
Cedar Lake recharges an aquifer, which is located below it. That feeds the water wells that residents rely on, she said.
She said only after the two dams were constructed on the tributaries that feed the lake did residents begin experiencing water issues. Becker’s report found the first dam was built in 2005 while the other was completed in 2019.
Becker discounted drought as a major contributor to a decrease in lake levels and well water.
“I find it really hard to believe that somebody would build the dams above … a community and think that it wouldn’t affect them,” she said.
One of the lakeside residents who has seen the problem with the aquifer up close is Anneliese Herren, who has lived there for about 12 years. 
“When it gets to the point where the mud comes up, I just turn it off,” she said.
Using the washing machine and taking showers has become difficult, she said.
“Day by day, it is a guessing game,” she said, adding that she once went three days without a shower.
She has a water softening system, but can’t use it.
A dock sits above the water level at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
“Calcium deposits are showing up in my sinks, in my shower,” she said. “It is everywhere because there is really hard water out here.”
Attorney Christine Pappas is policy and education coordinator at the Water Institute at East Central University where she chairs the department of Politics, Law and Society.
At Oklahoma Voice’s request, she reviewed a copy of the Water Resource’s Board proposed agreement with the dam owners.
She said the agreement was noticeably silent when it came to the impacted residents.
“It seems the water rights issue should be considered in the consent decree,” Pappas said.
“You could divert water as long as it is for a beneficial purpose, if you are not impairing downstream users,” she said. “Usually, they would make you stop taking the water.”
Pappas said a remedy for property owners is to file a lawsuit in district court.
Praying for a solution 
But longtime Cedar Lake resident Tammy Cramer said homeowners don’t have the money to hire an attorney to take it to court, where it could take years to find a resolution.
Residents said they have spent the bulk of the $35,531 they raised themselves to pay for an attorney to represent them before the state board.
Meanwhile, their quality of life continues to worsen.
“We pray about it because we are Christian people,” said Julie Lamb, a resident. “We don’t want any conflict with people. We just want to be entitled to our lake water.”
Docks that until a few years ago floated on the lake are now sunken into dry land.
Terry Smith and his wife Rhea have lived at Cedar Lake for a few years, but have been enjoying the waters for 20 years.
Like other residents, the Smiths have had to buy water to be hauled in because their well water levels have plummeted.
“It’s slow to recover,” Smith said. “It hasn’t gone dry. We’re very protective of it. We try not to use too much.”
The two said they worked their entire lives so they could retire at the lake. They bought a home they could afford and have been fixing it up, Rhea Smith said.
But, they’ve had to replace a well pump and say their dock is now damaged.
The low water levels have affected Kacee Corey’s family dynamics and livelihood, she said. Their family has had property at Cedar Lake for 22 years, she said.
“My grandkids don’t want to come out anymore,” said Corey.
Her family can no longer fish from their dock because the receding water levels have left it sitting too far from the lake and surrounded by trees, she said.
“It’s a beautiful piece of property and it’s not being loved anymore and used,” Corey said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Auditor: $111 million spent on Hurricane Helene emergency camps
description: A new rapid response report from the North Carolina auditor found that more than $111 million was spent on 55 camps set up in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene to help victims and storm responders. The 1,100 page report released Tuesday focuses on services provided by the disaster response contractor SLSCO (SLS). The audit notes […]
text:
Depot Street in Asheville flooded during Hurricane Helene. Extensive flooding and storm damage required the state to establish camps and comfort stations for rescue crews and storm survivors.  (Photo: Courtesy of Carly Brown)A new rapid response report from the North Carolina auditor found that more than $111 million was spent on 55 camps set up in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene to help victims and storm responders.
The 1,100 page report released Tuesday focuses on services provided by the disaster response contractor SLSCO (SLS).
The audit notes that North Carolina Emergency Management spent more than $516,500 per day over the seven-month period that the camps were operational.
“A one-night stay in a single bed cost roughly $800,” the auditor’s report highlighted.
SLS provided turnkey base camps in western North Carolina following Helene. A state audit questions the costs. (Photo: SLS)
The audit also examined the costs of food over the seven-month period, amounting to $6.5 million.
Did the prices amount to price gouging?
The audit doesn’t say.
What the audit does detail is that the rates charged by SLS for disaster response services were set by pre-existing contracts executed between SLS and NCEM in 2023, before Hurricane Helene was ever in the forecast.
The Texas-based company told the state in its May 2022 proposal it could provide ready-to-use camps and additional services within 72 hours of an emergency. Virginia, Louisiana, and Florida have also used the company for disaster response.
In the aftermath of Helene, SLS submitted invoices to the state totaling more than $111 million between September 27, 2024, and April 30, 2025. Almost half of that was spent for base camps in western North Carolina.
An endless list of emergency needs 
Twenty-two months removed from the storm, it’s easy to forget how much damage Helene caused. Landslides and flooding interrupted power and internet service, leaving thousands of roads and bridges impassable. Asheville was without drinking water for 53 days.
The base camps were configured to serve as community care stations, staging areas, points of supply distribution, medical support facilities, and shelters for the thousands of emergency responders.
Study: Hurricane Helene caused spike in homelessness in North Carolina

State emergency management leaders coordinated with local governments and recovery organizations to determine the best location for each camp. Access to running water was a key factor in determining whether laundry, shower, or restroom services could be provided. The price per camp varied based on the size of the set-up, with a discount provided in the pre-existing contract for larger set-ups.
One high-priority invoice from October 2024 from the N.C. Department of Public Safety to SLS requested a base camp to be established at Burnville Elementary School. The $2.3 million camp was needed so 100 linemen would have a place to stay while they worked for months restoring power to the county.
Another invoice requested SLS to provide toilet trailers and handwashing stations for Mitchell County Schools because Spruce Pine’s water and wastewater was not expected to be fixed for weeks.
DPS responds 
In a July 8, 2026, response to the draft audit, state Public Safety Secretary Jeffrey Smythe acknowledged that “disaster contracts by their nature can be expensive but are necessary actions to take when life safety is concerned.”
Public Safety Secretary Jeffrey Smythe (Photo: NCDPS)
FEMA viewed each of the invoices and deemed the associated costs “necessary and appropriately procured.” The costs have been fully reimbursed to the state, according to DPS.
The lengthy audit concludes by recommending that N.C. Emergency Management consider tracking the usage rates and per-use cost of showers, restrooms, laundry facilities, and meals.
“Such tracking could give the State valuable data that could be used to negotiate improved costs for disaster-related support services in vendor contracts,” the auditor’s office wrote.
Smythe said the department will continue to make disaster purchases in line with FEMA and national best practices.
“While capturing the specific number of meals, showers, or beds used may be helpful in day-to-day commodity procurement, disaster procurement is based on supporting the needs of local communities, of [state] partners, and of emergency responders in a time of significant stress and when life safety and sustainment is the priority,” Smythe concluded.
Click here to read the full audit.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: What did Mike Lindell’s campaign spend its money on in June and July? Tough to say.
description: Republican primary voters who want to know how pillow mogul Mike Lindell is spending his campaign dollars won’t have much to go on based on the final pre-primary campaign finance report, which was released Tuesday by the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board. The campaign’s last reported expense for the MyPillow CEO’s campaign was on June 30 […]
text:
Mike Lindell supporters listen as he speaks at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)Republican primary voters who want to know how pillow mogul Mike Lindell is spending his campaign dollars won’t have much to go on based on the final pre-primary campaign finance report, which was released Tuesday by the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board.
The campaign’s last reported expense for the MyPillow CEO’s campaign was on June 30 — $545 to reimburse mileage, according to the campaign’s pre-primary finance report. It reported no expenses in July.
GOP-endorsed candidate Kendall Qualls and House Speaker Lisa Demuth are also running for the Republican nomination for governor in the Aug. 11 primary election. Early voting has already begun.
Lindell and his running mate, Phillip Parrish, told the Reformer on Tuesday that the campaign has spent about $200,000 recently, but it only got billed for the charges in the past few days — after the campaign finance reporting period. The $200,000 in expenses should show up in the next campaign finance report, Lindell said.
“The majority of the expenditures didn’t shake loose until just only in the last few days,” Parrish said. Lindell said the majority of the campaign’s recent spending has been on yard signs.
Lindell is leading the latest polls and prediction market odds, underscoring how changes in technology and media have empowered unconventional candidates. Lindell’s pillows and ubiquitous TV appearances have made him a household name. He secured the endorsement of his pal President Donald Trump earlier this month, and Lindell promotes himself for hours a day on his own LindellTV network.
Lindell has raised over $726,000 in campaign donations this year, and his campaign had $88,000 in cash as of July 20, according to the campaign’s latest finance report.
Demuth has the most cash on hand compared to her Republican primary opponents, with over $456,000. The campaign has raised over $550,000 this year.
Qualls’ campaign has over $67,000 in cash and has raised over $410,000 this year.
Whoever wins the GOP gubernatorial primary will have to quickly pivot to running against Minnesota’s most prolific fundraiser: Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
The senior senator has raised over $9.3 million since launching her bid for governor at the end of January. The Klobuchar campaign has about $4.5 million cash on hand.
Klobuchar’s campaign has spent about half of what it’s raised in donations already this year, with the majority of the spending going toward digital ads, mailers and campaign consulting.
Klobuchar’s staggering cash advantage will likely be compounded by outside spending by DFL-aligned allies like the Alliance for a Better Minnesota.
In addition to the governor’s race, all 201 seats in the Minnesota Legislature will be on the ballot in November, so the rival legislative caucuses and political parties are fundraising and will spend big to gain control of state government.
Both legislative chambers feature just a handful of competitive districts, which means voters in those battlegrounds can expect a torrent of mail and digital advertising in the months to come.
House Democrats have raised $2.8 million this year and have spent little of it so far. The campaign has about $2.5 million in cash.
House Republicans have raised about $1 million so far this year and have over $1.7 million cash on hand.
In the Senate, Democrats are hoping to widen their current one-seat majority. Senate Democrats have raised nearly $3 million this year and have about $3.7 million in cash.
Senate Republicans reported raising nearly $1.5 million this year and have over $3.2 million cash on hand.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Loss of Haitian workers will impact CT healthcare, officials say
description: One CT official said patient health could be impacted by the loss of Haitian workers in an industry already struggling to find staff.
text:
Elected officials gathered with immigrant advocates and staff of a Manchester nursing home on Tuesday to bring attention to how the revocation of Temporary Protective Status from Haitians in Connecticut will affect the state’s workforce and residents, specifically in the healthcare industry.
“It’s my job to track what happens with our economy, and I and other people who do work across the country are really worried about the impact that this has on our labor force, and about the impact that this will have on our labor market at a time when we are stretched for people to work in jobs like in the facility behind us,” said Comptroller Sean Scanlon, standing in front of the Westside Care Center.
TPS provides protection for people fleeing armed conflict and environmental disaster. Haiti was first designated for TPS after a devastating earthquake in 2010 that left more than 300,000 people dead and more than a million homeless.
Losing TPS means that Haitians, many of whom have lived here for more than a decade, can no longer legally work in the U.S. and can be deported. The Trump administration is reportedly planning to deport scores of Haitians.
“These are registered nurses, LPNs, CNAs, home care workers, group home workers. These are people who make the full chain of care,” said Stephanie Deceus, vice president of SEIU District 1199, which represents workers at the Westside Care Center nursing home, along with other facilities throughout the state. “They care for our parents. They care for our grandparents. They care for our neighbors. They care for some of the most vulnerable people in our communities.”
Staff members at Westside Care Center in Manchester listen to a speaker during a news conference regarding the expiration of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and it’s impact on the workforce on Tuesday, July 28. Credit: Sarah GOrdon / CT Mirror
Matthew Barrett, president and CEO of the Connecticut Association of Health Care Facilities, said some facilities had lost as many as 13 workers as of Tuesday due to the end of TPS for Haitians. He said his organization had been surveying its membership and found at least 100 people impacted by the end of the program. Most of those were certified nursing assistants, but there were also three nurses, a registered nurse and some housekeeping workers.
“Even if it’s one or two employees, that’s too many,” in the midst of a staffing shortage that worsened post-COVID pandemic, Barrett said.
Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, who is a physician, said the loss of staff will affect patient health.
“What this would mean for individuals is the ones who need their treatment, the medications, they will not get this in time. The ones who need their bed changed, they will not get that in time. That is going to develop more infections, skin infections,” he said, “leading to skin breakdown,” also known as bed sores or pressure sores.
Those conditions can lead to increased hospitalizations, Anwar said. “The hospitals are overwhelmed. This is a decision that is going to result in a healthcare disaster for the well-being of the people in our state of Connecticut,” he said.
Scanlon urged members of Congress to pass a bill that would extend TPS for Haitians. The Safe Environment from Countries Under Repression and Emergency Act, or SECURE, was introduced by U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and dozens of other Democratic senators. A similar proposal was passed by the House in April.
“This is about people, and this is about the kind of people that have been working hard in buildings like this to care for your loved ones and have been a part of our communities for a long time,” Scanlon said. 
Immigration Attorney Dana Buchin speaks during a news conference regarding the expiration of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and its impact on the workforce at  Westside Care Center in Manchester on Tuesday, July 28. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
The Supreme Court upheld the end of TPS for Haitians in June, cementing the administration’s decision to close what some say is a legal loophole that allows migrants to remain in the U.S. for long periods of time. 
But critics say that TPS is ending for Haitians at a time when that country is racked by extreme gang violence and has one of the highest homicide rates in the world. The U.S. Department of State has assigned Haiti a level 4 “do not travel” warning and tells Americans not to go to Haiti “due to the risk of crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited healthcare.” North Korea, Iran and South Sudan carry the same level of risk, according to the ratings.
At Tuesday’s press conference, attorney Dana R. Buchin urged Haitians who have lost TPS to meet with an immigration attorney to assess whether other pathways to remain in the U.S., like asylum, might apply to them.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Judge hearing testimony in case over Arkansas’ initiative process restrictions
description: A federal judge who prevented Arkansas from enforcing new limits on the initiative and referendum process heard testimony Tuesday as he weighs whether to permanently block the restrictions. The case stems from a lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Cole Jester in 2025 by the League of Women Voters of Arkansas. Two ballot question committees, […]
text:
Bill Dollar (center back) and his wife Marla (back right) speak with visitors to the downtown Fayetteville Square on May 14, 2026 as they collect signatures for ballot initiatives. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A federal judge who prevented Arkansas from enforcing new limits on the initiative and referendum process heard testimony Tuesday as he weighs whether to permanently block the restrictions.
The case stems from a lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Cole Jester in 2025 by the League of Women Voters of Arkansas. Two ballot question committees, Protect AR Rights and For AR Kids, were later allowed to intervene in the case. 
The groups, who collected signatures to qualify their three proposed constitutional amendments for the November ballot, argue the laws make it nearly impossible for Arkansans to propose their own constitutional amendments and laws and place them before voters. Supporters of the laws have said they’re needed to protect the process. 
Federal judge rules Arkansas initiative restrictions unconstitutional

U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks issued a preliminary injunction in November that temporarily blocked the state from enforcing some of the laws against parties involved in the suit, including two that require canvassers to request a photo ID from potential signers and inform them that petition fraud is a criminal offense.
Earlier this month, Brooks deemed some of the challenged laws unconstitutional, but took no additional action. He left the preliminary injunction in place and allowed a handful of claims in the case to proceed to a trial that began Tuesday morning in Fayetteville. 
Brooks is considering whether the requirements for all canvassers to be Arkansas residents and paid canvassers to be domiciled in Arkansas, and a prohibition on paying canvassers based on the number of signatures obtained, violate the First Amendment of the Constitution. Brooks was also considering whether the photo ID law and the law requiring potential signers to read a petition’s ballot title are unconstitutionally vague.
Attorneys on Tuesday morning questioned Bonnie Miller, president of the League of Women Voters of Arkansas and chair of Save AR Democracy, a ballot question committee that pursued a constitutional amendment aimed at strengthening the state’s direct democracy process. 
Miller, who has worked on other ballot measure campaigns, said paid canvassers are key to success because relying on volunteers can be limiting due to work and family schedules. 
The League could not recruit willing volunteers from out-of-state chapters because state law requires canvassers to be Arkansas residents, she said. 


Let us know what you think...


 

The League of Women Voters’ all-volunteer campaign was unsuccessful in collecting sufficient signatures to qualify their measure for the November ballot, said Miller, who argued the state’s initiative and referendum process isn’t accessible to Arkansans because of all the legislative restrictions.
“This process is not open to us,” she said. “It’s not a process for everyday folks, for volunteers, for grassroots orgs, and that’s who this process should be for.”
Jordan Broyles, an attorney representing the state, noted that Protect AR Rights was able to collect and submit the requisite number of signatures for another proposed constitutional amendment dealing with direct democracy despite the state laws Miller cited.
Protect AR Rights received more than $933,000 from the National Education Association that it used for paid canvassers. Save AR Democracy received about $5,300 in total contributions throughout its campaign, according to a June financial report. 
Protect AR Rights was the only group to submit signatures to the Secretary of State by the July 3 deadline. The secretary of state’s office has 30 days to notify sponsors if they’ve collected enough signatures for the November ballot or if they’ve qualified for more time to collect additional signatures. Samantha Boyd, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, said Tuesday they anticipate having the review completed by the weekend. 
Upon resumption of the trial midday, the hearing was expected to last through the late afternoon and perhaps into Wednesday morning.

description: Idaho is one of five states selected by the U.S. Department of Energy as a potential host site for new Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campuses, federal officials announced Tuesday.  The campuses are designed to strengthen and modernize the country’s nuclear fuel cycle. Officials say they will create thousands of jobs, expand manufacturing and attract financial[...]
text:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright (right) and U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, visited Idaho National Laboratory on Dec. 8, 2025, to tour the Advanced Test Reactor and several facilities at the Materials and Fuels Complex to highlight the Trump administration’s nuclear energy expansion goals. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson)Idaho is one of five states selected by the U.S. Department of Energy as a potential host site for new Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campuses, federal officials announced Tuesday. 
The campuses are designed to strengthen and modernize the country’s nuclear fuel cycle. Officials say they will create thousands of jobs, expand manufacturing and attract financial investment. 
Idaho-Wyoming nuclear industry partnership set to receive $31M federal award 

The other four states selected as potential host sites are Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Louisiana.
“These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth, create thousands of high-paying jobs and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance,” U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a written statement. “The innovative concept is a direct result of President (Donald) Trump’s leadership and ambitious directives to restore the domestic nuclear fuel cycle and get America’s nuclear industry growing again.” 
Wright signed memorandums of understanding with Idaho and the other four states to continue exploring options to host one of the new nuclear campuses, the U.S. Department of Energy said in a press release issued Tuesday.
  Idaho officials say they support US Department of Energy project

Idaho Gov. Brad Little and other elected officials welcomed the selection. They touted the presence of Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and said they would work hard to help Idaho be selected to host the new nuclear campus. 
State of Idaho seeks to become ‘preferred destination’ for nuclear energy investment 

“Idaho is honored to have been selected as one of five initial contenders to further explore the development of Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses,” Little said in a written statement. “For more than 70 years, Idaho has been at the forefront of nuclear innovation and we are grateful to President Trump, Secretary Wright, and the U.S. Department of Energy for recognizing our unmatched expertise and legacy. We look forward to working with (the Department of Energy) to continue advancing every stage of the nuclear lifecycle, strengthening our nation’s energy security, creating good-paying jobs and ensuring Idaho remains the home of America’s nuclear renaissance.”
The new nuclear campuses would be designed for a variety of nuclear activities, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel and the final disposition of used nuclear fuel, U.S. Department of Energy officials said. 
Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke said Idaho would make a great host for a nuclear campus. 
“Idaho has been synonymous with nuclear innovation since the earliest days of the atomic age, and today’s announcement is a recognition of decades of work by the scientists, engineers and communities at Idaho National Laboratory and across our state,” Bedke said in a written statement. “This is an opportunity to build on that legacy, bringing new investment, new jobs, and new technology to Idaho while helping restore America’s leadership in the full nuclear fuel cycle.”
“As this process moves forward, we’ll continue working with our federal and local partners to make sure Idaho is positioned to make the most of this opportunity for our workforce, our economy and our national security,” Bedke added.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Youth climate lawsuit seeks full Ninth Circuit hearing
description: A group of young plaintiffs, who sued the federal government alleging a series of executive orders threaten their constitutional right to life by exacerbating climate change, are still fighting their battle in court. After a three-judge panel on the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the lawsuit’s arguments in June over a lack of […]
text:
Eva Lighthiser, left, and other plaintiffs wait to enter Missoula's federal courthouse on Sept. 16, 2025. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)A group of young plaintiffs, who sued the federal government alleging a series of executive orders threaten their constitutional right to life by exacerbating climate change, are still fighting their battle in court.
After a three-judge panel on the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the lawsuit’s arguments in June over a lack of plausible link between their alleged injuries and the federal actions, the plaintiffs are asking the full Circuit Court of Appeals to rehear their case and “correct the three-judge panel’s abdication of law and duty,” according to a press release by law firm Our Children’s Trust.
“The panel’s decision is the first in American history to deny courts the power to review an unconstitutional executive order. That is not a small mistake. That is constitutional corruption,” said Julia Olson, Chief Legal Counsel and Co-Executive Director of Our Children’s Trust. “No president should be able to direct a sweeping fossil fuel agenda that endangers children’s lives and face zero judicial review. The full Ninth Circuit has the opportunity and the obligation to correct that.”
Lighthiser v. Trump is one of a series of youth-led climate change lawsuits brought by Our Children’s Trust, an Oregon-based advocacy law firm, which also successfully litigated Held v. Montana in 2023. The plaintiffs include young people from Montana, Oregon, Hawaii, California, and Florida.
Lighthiser, first argued before a federal judge in Missoula, alleged three executive orders Trump signed early in his second term will accelerate human-caused climate change and cause further harm throughout their lives.
The challenged orders included Trump Executive Orders 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” 14156, “Declaring a National Energy Emergency,” and 14261, “Reinvigorating America’s Beautiful Clean Coal Industry.”
Federal District Court Judge Dana Christensen said he had dismissed the case “reluctantly,” but the scope of the request from the 22 young people was “an unworkable request.”
The circuit court agreed, saying granting an injunction rolling back three Executive Orders would require “extensive judicial supervision of executive branch actions related to energy policy.”
In their petition submitted earlier this month, the plaintiffs argue that the panel disregarded Christensen’s finding that there was “overwhelming evidence” that the youth were harmed by climate change, and that the executive orders are worsening those harms. Instead, they argue, the panel ruled not on the harms themselves, but that the plaintiffs could not challenge a president’s “sweeping executive orders and their coordinated implementation in a single lawsuit.”
In its ruling, the circuit court said that granting an injunction to roll back the Executive Orders would require “extensive judicial supervision of executive branch actions related to energy policy.”
“Plaintiffs explicitly seek to undo everything from staffing reductions, to the revocation of research grants, to anticipated rule changes, to the type of language the current administration has used on government websites,” the memorandum states. “…The district court correctly recognized that disputes over such questions would inevitably result in the court ‘spending a lot of time together’ with the parties and holding hearings ‘until the expiration of [their] collective lifetimes.’”
The petition for full review identifies three potential errors in the panel’s decision — that it ignored the factual findings of the district court related to greenhouse gas emissions; that the U.S. Supreme Court has rejected similar circuit court reasoning over broad executive orders; and that other circuit courts have upheld the right to challenge executive orders on constitutional grounds.
The Constitution gave us the tools to hold our government to its promise,” lead plaintiffs Eva Lighthiser said. “We are 22 young people using exactly those tools, and we are asking the full Ninth Circuit to do its part. Two hundred and fifty years later, the promise still has to mean something.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s 17 governor candidates have raised nearly $9 million. This chart shows who gave it.
description: Money isn’t everything. But in politics, it sure helps. Candidates, generally, can’t run effective campaigns without it, and those who raise the most are far more likely to win. Donors’ identities can also tell the public about which constituencies and stakeholders are supporting particular candidates, and they also can hint at which special interests a […]
text:
The Alaska State Capitol in Juneau is seen on Apr. 24, 2026. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)Money isn’t everything.
But in politics, it sure helps. Candidates, generally, can’t run effective campaigns without it, and those who raise the most are far more likely to win.
Donors’ identities can also tell the public about which constituencies and stakeholders are supporting particular candidates, and they also can hint at which special interests a winning candidate might favor once in office.
In Alaska’s gubernatorial race, scrutinizing donors is especially helpful in understanding and assessing the field of candidates because of its huge size: No fewer than 17 people are vying to be the next head of the state’s executive branch.
Alaska currently has no individual limits on direct giving to campaigns, and with large donors stepping in to support their preferred candidates, the campaigns have collectively raised nearly $9 million. After an Aug. 18 primary, the field will be narrowed to four candidates and their lieutenant governor running mates.
Political campaigns in Alaska are required by state law to disclose their donors — and in fact, any anonymous cash a campaign receives must be forfeited to the state.
A recent round of fundraising disclosures filed last week offers new hints about the state of the race. This interactive chart, produced by data scientist and graphics developer Will Koeppen for the Anchorage Press, steps through campaign contributions, progressively adding categories of income until it shows the total raised by each candidate since they entered the race.
Note that independent Destry Payne Sr. and Republicans James William Parkin IV, Hank Kroll and Michael Gilbert aren’t shown, as each has raised less than $5,000.


The next round of financial disclosures for Alaska’s state elections are due on Aug. 11, seven days before the primary election.
Will Koeppen is a data scientist and graphics developer with deep Alaska ties. Read more of his work at willkoeppen.com.
 Methodology

Raw financial disclosure data was downloaded from the Alaska Public Offices Commission (APOC), the state’s campaign finance regulator. We grouped individual contributions by donor, matching records that likely belong to the same person — a process that isn’t always exact. Totals raised were checked against summaries provided by APOC.
