title: New panel begins work reviewing options for Georgia’s next election system
description: A committee tasked with helping select Georgia’s next statewide election system is scheduled to hold its first meeting next week as lawmakers, election officials and other appointed members begin to envision a QR code-free method of voting.  The use of ballot QR codes have been a contentious issue throughout the last several years in Georgia […]
text:
An election worker in Gwinnett County demonstrates how to insert a voter card into ballot-marking devices used by voters across Georgia. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderA committee tasked with helping select Georgia’s next statewide election system is scheduled to hold its first meeting next week as lawmakers, election officials and other appointed members begin to envision a QR code-free method of voting. 
The use of ballot QR codes have been a contentious issue throughout the last several years in Georgia politics. Proponents of hand-marked paper ballots have repeatedly called for ballots to be counted based on text that can be deciphered by humans, prompting state lawmakers to pass a bill a couple years ago preventing elections from being tallied using ballot QR codes after July 2026. 
However, legislators failed to appropriate the roughly $66 million needed to make the switch and did not postpone the deadline during the 2026 session, so Gov. Brian Kemp summoned lawmakers back to the Capitol earlier this summer for a special session to address the looming election deadline.
Ballot QR code bill headed to governor after Georgia lawmakers scale back hand-counting requirement

Under a new law passed in June, Georgia’s current election system — which uses machines to mark voters’ selections and then prints a completed paper ballot — will remain in place until 2028, giving lawmakers time to replace the voting machines. The law also established a special committee which will focus solely on hand-marked paper ballot voting systems and issue a report to state lawmakers by February 2027.
“As a former secretary of state and current governor, I know firsthand just how much our system of governance rests on being able to trust the results of the ballot box,” Kemp said. “I look forward to the recommendations from the committee on how we can preserve that trust.”
The governor’s appointees to the committee include former state Elections Director Chris Harvey, Paulding County elections supervisor Deidre Holden and Kemp’s executive counsel Sam Hatcher.
Several Republican lawmakers, including Sen. Max Burns of Sylvania and Rep. Victor Anderson of Cornelia, will also sit on the committee according to a press release issued Tuesday. Covington Rep. Tim Fleming, the Republican nominee in the race to become the next secretary of state, will also be a member. Rep. Scott Holcomb of Atlanta is the only Democrat who was appointed to the committee.
Victor Anderson. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Anderson, who also chairs the House committee that typically handles election bills, said he expected legislators from both chambers to be “pretty much in lockstep” with their goals for the panel.
“I don’t really see there being a House priorities or Senate priorities scenario in this committee,” Anderson said. “It’s more going to be what’s best for the voters in the state of Georgia.”
But Senate Democrats, who had raised concerns during the special session about being excluded from the committee, accused legislative leaders of “bad governance” over the panel’s composition. 
Georgia Senate Minority Leader Harold Jones speaks with reporters at the state Capitol in Atlanta. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“Both Democrats and Republicans care deeply about elections, election security and election integrity,” Senate Minority Leader Harold Jones said. “Shutting one side out of that conversation makes it ripe for partisan games and conspiracy theorist takeover.”
Joseph Kirk, the Bartow County elections director and president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, said he hopes the meetings will be fruitful, giving legislators a head start heading into next year.
“The more the committee can get done before the next legislative session, the more they can talk about what we’re looking for from the system — not what brand we want or what company, but what we need out of the system,” he said.
The committee will hold its first meeting in Atlanta on Aug. 7.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Coalition calling for a ‘healthcare cost freeze’ in Pa. as insurers request rate increases
description: Health insurers submitted their proposed rate increases, but advocates say consumers can't afford to pay more.
text:
A photo of the Capitol Main Rotunda on July 9, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Advocates are urging the state agency tasked with reviewing health insurer applications for rate changes to reject proposed increases for 2027 that would apply to plans purchased by individuals and small businesses. 
On average, insurers are asking for a 17.1% increase for individuals and 11.5% for small businesses, according to the Pennsylvania Insurance Department. 
The submissions include increases for Pennie plans available on the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Submitted premium increases range from single-digit growth to a 40% increase.
More than 600 Pennsylvanians signed a petition calling for a “healthcare cost freeze,” organized by the Affordable Healthcare Coalition, which is scheduled to be delivered on Wednesday to the agency’s Harrisburg office. 
 
To see a breakdown by plan and region, visit the Pennsylvania Insurance Department’s website.


“The proposed 17.1% average increase in monthly premiums for 2027 Pennie health insurance plans would place an unacceptable burden on Pennsylvania families,” said Antoinette Kraus, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Health Access Network, in a release. 
Pennie enrollees include gig workers, child care staff and others who don’t have access to employer-sponsored plans, she added, who “are facing double-digit premium increases while the cost of everyday necessities continues to rise.”
“If these proposed rates take effect, even more Pennsylvanians are likely to be priced out of essential health coverage and forced to make painful cuts to basic household needs,” Kraus continued. 
Coalition members include Kraus’ organization, Affordable PA, the Pennsylvania Association of Staff Nurses and Allied Professionals, Protect Our Care, Families Over Billionaires, Action Together NEPA and SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania. 

Pennie health insurance enrollment drops by 160K after federal subsidies expire


Companies must file their proposed rates for review and approval. State staff determine “whether each requested rate change is justified, ensuring they are not excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory,” according to the department. 
“These rates are higher than we’d hoped and reflect continued rising costs across the healthcare environment,” said Pennsylvania Insurance Commissioner Michael Humphreys in a release. “PID’s team will be closely examining each filing to ensure rates are reasonable and justified and not charging any more than necessary to deliver promised benefits.”
The increases come after Pennie enrollment dropped by 160,000 Pennsylvanians following the expiration of federal subsidies that caused premiums to more than double.
Coalition members say that companies are increasing premiums even as their profits soar, noting multi-million dollar compensation for many top insurance leaders. They’ve organized a website to collect public comments, which are due by Aug. 22, 2026. 
Final approved numbers will be publicized in the fall. Public comment can also be emailed to ra-in-comment@pa.gov.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: As another heatwave bakes Arkansas, schools and summer camps move indoors
description: With Arkansas temperatures hitting triple digits again Tuesday, football practices and summer camps are changing plans to avoid the worst of the heat. The National Weather Service has placed the entire state under a heat advisory, at a minimum, with large swaths of central and eastern Arkansas placed under a more severe extreme heat warning […]
text:
Campers and counselors at the Lake Nixon Summer Day Camp in Little Rock take refuge from the heat under a tree in this undated 2026 photo. (Photo courtesy of the Lake Nixon Summer Day Camp)With Arkansas temperatures hitting triple digits again Tuesday, football practices and summer camps are changing plans to avoid the worst of the heat.
The National Weather Service has placed the entire state under a heat advisory, at a minimum, with large swaths of central and eastern Arkansas placed under a more severe extreme heat warning until Tuesday evening. 
A graphic created by the National Weather Service showing the projected heat indices and temperatures between July 28 and Aug. 1, 2026. (Graphic courtesy of the National Weather Service)
Several cities have opened cooling centers, such as Fayetteville, Little Rock and West Memphis. More information about cooling centers is available by contacting your local city or county officials.
It’s the second week in a row that the Little Rock weather service office, which covers most of the state, has issued extreme heat warnings for east and central Arkansas.
The extreme heat will affect school athletics practices, at a time when many bands and football teams are beginning to prepare for their fall competition and performance schedules. 
“You’re going to have to practice early in the morning or later in the evening or indoors, just because the temperature is not going to be conductive to having outdoor activity,” said Bobby Swofford, an assistant executive director with the Arkansas Activities Association, which oversees interscholastic sports and activities for hundreds of Arkansas schools.
The association’s heat rules only apply to member schools.
The organization’s policy for acceptable practice temperatures, adopted by the association in 2019, has progressively stricter requirements the hotter it gets. It relies on wet bulb temperature readings, which takes into account humidity to simulate the human body’s ability to cool itself, and is different from the heat index. The wet bulb temperature is the lowest temperature air can reach with the evaporation of water with ambient air conditions.
The restrictions start at 82 degrees, with required rest breaks. Outdoor practices can’t be held when the wet bulb temperature is above 92 degrees.  
Andy Black, executive director of Lake Nixon Summer Day Camp in Little Rock, said he and his staff routinely emphasize the importance of drinking water throughout Arkansas’ hot and humid summers, but extra precautions are taken when the weather service issues heat advisories and warnings. Coolers with ice water and Gatorade have been stocked for the week, he said.
“I remember one counselor, she was really great about this, she would always ask all her campers to put their water bottles on top of their head before they went off and hiked off to their next activity, so they made sure they had them with them and that they were ready to go,” Black said.
Certain outdoor activities, such as hikes around the camp’s lake, are limited in heat like this, Black said. Frozen snacks like popsicles — usually reserved as a Friday treat — become a daily staple to help keep campers cool.
“One of our staff members is actually a professional magician, and so we have him doing three different magic shows tomorrow,” Black said Monday evening. “We’ve got two air conditioned spaces, and we’ll be rotating groups in and out of those tomorrow as well.” 
The camp hosts campers ages six to 14, with around 190 attending this week, he said.
The heat index in Clarksville and Pocahontas is expected to soar to 115 degrees Tuesday, with Little Rock expected to reach 114 and Pine Bluff 108. The weather service expected Mena would have the lowest expected heat index temperature in the state on Tuesday, at 103.
According to Climate Central’s Climate Shift Index map, Tuesday’s scorching temperatures were unlikely to occur in the absence of human-driven climate change. 
Southwest Power Pool, which manages the electrical grid for parts of Arkansas and 16 other states, received an emergency order from the U.S. Department of Energy allowing it to deploy backup power to stave off possible rolling blackouts because of the heatwave, which has sent temperatures sky-high across swaths of the country.
A weak cold front will sweep through Arkansas on Wednesday, lowering temperatures and bringing some chance of rain, according to the weather service, but heat indices are still expected to hover around 100 into Saturday in many parts of the state.
When the heat index gets above 91 degrees, precautions such as going inside and increasing fluid intake should be taken to avoid issues like heat exhaustion and heat stroke, according to the Mayo Clinic.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah ranks No. 1 overall state for a 4th year in a row — but it was dinged for its air quality
description: For a fourth year in a row, U.S. News & World Report has ranked Utah the No. 1 overall state in the nation, citing high performance in multiple categories including economy, fiscal stability and infrastructure.  However, Utah ranked low, No. 48, in one category — natural environment — due to air pollution and industrial toxin […]
text:
Downtown Salt Lake City is silhouetted as the sun sets over the Great Salt Lake on Wednesday, Aug. 20, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)For a fourth year in a row, U.S. News & World Report has ranked Utah the No. 1 overall state in the nation, citing high performance in multiple categories including economy, fiscal stability and infrastructure. 
However, Utah ranked low, No. 48, in one category — natural environment — due to air pollution and industrial toxin levels that exceed the national average. 
The 2026 Best States analysis released Tuesday compared all 50 states on how they serve their citizens across a range of categories, including healthcare, education, economy, infrastructure, opportunity, fiscal stability, crime and corrections, and natural environment. 
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox applauded the ranking in a prepared statement included in a news release issued by U.S. News & World Report. 
“Being named the No. 1 state is an honor, but what matters most is what that ranking represents: hardworking people, strong families, and neighbors who look out for one another,” Cox said. “Utah’s success has never been about government. It comes from Utahns who serve, build, innovate, and invest in the future. I’m grateful to everyone who helps make our state the best place to live, work, and raise a family.”

Here’s how the top 10 states ranked overall: 

 Utah
 South Dakota
 Minnesota
 North Dakota
 Nebraska
 New Hampshire
 Idaho
 Florida
 Washington
 Vermont

Diving deeper into the rankings
Utah ranked No. 2 for its economy, beat only by Texas, which leads the nation in job growth, GDP growth, net migration and youth population growth, according to U.S. News & World Report’s analysis. Idaho ranked close behind Utah as the No. 3 state for its economy. 
In fiscal responsibility, Wyoming ranked No. 1 ahead of Utah, which took second place, and North Dakota took third. Wyoming jumped to the No. 1 position in fiscal responsibility after placing No. 30 last year, largely driven by improvements in budget balancing as measured by the ratio of total revenues to total expenses, according to the analysis. 
Utah also ranked No. 4 for its infrastructure, beaten in that category by Nevada (No. 1), Oregon (No. 2) and Nebraska (No. 3). To evaluate infrastructure, the analysis looked at electricity prices, power grid reliability, renewable energy, internet access, and transportation metrics including bridge quality, commute time, public transit usage and road quality. 
For its infrastructure, Utah was dinged for a 4.7% renewable energy use score compared to a national average of 8.8%, but earned points for an average commute time of about 23.2 minutes (compared to a national average of 27.2 minutes), and 17.5% of its roads rated to be in poor condition (compared to a national average of 18.9%). 
Utah also ranked No. 7 for crime and corrections, with an incarceration rate of 186 per 100,000 residents (below a national average of 381), and a violent crime rate of about 230 per 100,000 residents (below a national average of 359). 
For 19th year, Utah ranks No. 1 in nation for economic outlook

In education, Utah ranked No. 6, with a high school graduation rate of 88.3% (above the national average of 85.8%). It also has relatively low student debt and higher-than-the-national average math scores. 
For healthcare, Utah ranked No. 18, with about 10.7% of its population lacking health insurance (compared to a national average of 11.3%), and an obesity rate of 31.2% (compared to a national average of 34.2%). It ranked No. 36 for healthcare access, No. 11 for healthcare quality and No. 14 for public health.
In the opportunity category, Utah ranked No. 24 in the nation, having lost points for affordability and equality issues due to housing costs and income, and employment disparities between men and women, people with disabilities and ethnic groups. However, Utah ranked higher for economic opportunity, with a median household income of $96,658 (compared to a national average of $81,604) and a poverty rate of 8.3% (compared to a national average of 12.1%). 
For its low natural environment ranking, Utah was penalized for having 169 days a year with unhealthy air quality, above a national average of 152, and a measurement of 3,006 pounds per square mile of industrial toxins, compared to a national average of 930. 
Policymakers react
The office of one of Utah’s top Republican legislative leaders, Senate President Stuart Adams, highlighted Utah’s longstanding ranking in a news release, which said it “reflects a strong foundation of economic growth, infrastructure, fiscal responsibility and opportunity that continues today.”
“Utah’s strength has always come from the people of Utah and their vision to look beyond today and build for tomorrow,” Adams said in a prepared statement. “Being recognized as the nation’s best state for a fourth consecutive year reflects our enduring values and the sound policies that have expanded opportunity, encouraged innovation and strengthened communities. We are proud of what Utahns have built together, and we remain committed to making our state the best place to live, work and raise a family.”
The Utah Senate’s top Democrat, however, issued a statement saying the ranking shows Utah has room for improvement, especially when it comes to affordability for working families and its air quality. 
“Utah has a lot to be proud of, but the reality is that most working families are still struggling to make ends meet and can’t access basic necessities,” Escamilla said. 
She also said the near-bottom ranking for Utah’s natural environment is “seriously concerning.” 
“A state defined by having some of the most extraordinary landscapes and national parks in the world should also be a leader in protecting our public lands and the resources we depend on for survival,” she said. 
Utah has long had poor air quality compared to the rest of the nation, largely due to its natural geography, with mountains that form a bowl around the Wasatch Front that can trap cold air in the winter, aggravating pollution levels. The shrinking Great Salt Lake also exposes dry lake bed, which exposes dust that can be blown into nearby communities.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Trump administration demands hospitals share emergency room records
authors: Amanda Seitz, Maia Rosenfeld, Darius Tahir
description: This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawn mowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, person[...]
text:
The Emergency Department entrance at Newport Hospital is shown in 2024, before reflecting the rebranding of the health system that owns it as Brown University Health. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawn mowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, personally identifiable medical records of all patients who seek help at their emergency rooms.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission, responsible for tracking and issuing recalls of dangerous products sold in the U.S., began discreetly pressuring hospital executives this year to share personally identifiable health data with a private contractor. But hospital lawyers and other industry experts have questioned the agency’s authority to collect, its ability to safeguard such a swath of sensitive information, and whether it has followed the legal process to overhaul its surveillance system.
After KFF Health News asked the CPSC about the new system, the agency announced the program on July 21. Left unmentioned, however, is the alarm it has raised among hospital executives, as well as the nature and extent of the agency’s data demands.
In a stark departure from its product-focused mission, the agency’s goal is to obtain millions of Americans’ medical records from emergency room visits for most injuries, from a broken bone to a childhood vaccine reaction or even a suicide attempt, according to documents and emails obtained by KFF Health News, as well as interviews with five people involved or familiar with the discussions.
A CPSC official also insisted in the emails that the institutions provide all ER patients’ identifiable information — such as names, addresses, diagnoses, and other personal details — to the contractor, Konza Health, for analysis. In correspondence with hospital executives, Konza representatives described participation as “mandatory” or “required.”

As a condition of viewing the correspondence, KFF Health News agreed not to republish some of the emails it obtained.
The CPSC wants at least 100 hospitals to start sending detailed medical records by the end of this year, according to an internal memo.
“The whole thing is troubling,” said Sharona Hoffman, a professor of health law at Case Western Reserve University who noted that giving a private entity access to a sweeping collection of data will introduce risks to patient privacy. “If this company really is collecting identifiable information, that is worrisome for patients.”
The new project was launched amid upheaval at the traditionally independent agency, which is without a governing board since President Donald Trump fired the CPSC’s three Democratic board members. Nearly 1 in 5 career staffers left the CPSC in the first 16 months of the new administration, according to a KFF Health News analysis of federal workforce data.
The initiative also comes as the Trump administration has sought unprecedented access to millions of Americans’ medical records, with the Office of Personnel Management requesting federal workers’ sensitive health information and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. using a private organization to collect more medical records for his studies on vaccines and autism.
Steve Roney, CPSC spokesperson, said in an emailed statement on July 10 that the CPSC is “modernizing” its surveillance system. Asked whether the CPSC will file complaints against hospitals that do not participate, he said only that while the previous system “operated as a voluntary program, the ability of hospitals to opt out limited the sample size and usefulness of the data.”
Roney also acknowledged that the agency had not yet notified the public, as “required by law.”
Federal law requires the agency to provide notice and a public comment period before requesting information from 10 or more entities, a step it has not taken despite plans for 100 hospitals to join the surveillance system. KFF Health News independently confirmed with over a dozen hospitals that they had been approached.
Federal public health authorities cannot legally mandate that private health data be reported. But CPSC officials have suggested publicly and privately that if hospitals decline to share data with the new surveillance system, they could be subject to strict penalties from a data-sharing regulation known as “information blocking.”
Yet some hospital executives say they are reluctant to share patients’ sensitive data because they’re concerned about a different violation — that of federal privacy law.
AI takes over
Dozens of ERs across the country already participate in the CPSC’s voluntary National Electronic Injury Surveillance System, or NEISS, through which trained hospital workers report injuries involving consumer products, almost always stripped of patients’ identifiable information. The system helps the CPSC identify products, such as baby loungers, toys, and household appliances, with a pattern of injuring consumers.
The new injury surveillance program goes much further.
At a toy industry trade event in February, acting CPSC Chairman Peter Feldman said the agency is “investing in AI-enabled workflows that improve the quality and quantity of injury surveillance data, while also building up digital infrastructure to handle a massive new volume of electronic health records.”
Konza Health, a Kansas-based organization that runs the state’s health data exchange, will automatically pull and analyze medical records of all patient visits from ERs nationwide. Konza won a five-year contract worth up to $15.9 million with the CPSC last fall.
In email correspondence with hospital technology officials, Konza Health President and CEO Laura McCrary also has described ERs’ participation as “required,” stipulating that they share patients’ records with identifying information.
McCrary told KFF Health News by email that the company is not using AI to process the records it receives, saying instead that Konza will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities.” Roney, the CPSC spokesperson, did not answer questions about the use of AI.
For years, agency officials have discussed moving away from human contractors and automating NEISS to save time and money.
But without workers on-site, hospital staffers may no longer receive training to determine what clinical information is important to include for the CPSC. In short, the changes could dilute the quality of the product safety data the agency collects.
“They want to suck in as much data as possible, but I’m not sure how thoughtful they’re being about what is collected and what is actually needed by the agency,” said former CPSC chair Alexander Hoehn-Saric, one of the Democratic appointees Trump fired last year.

Wanted: Injuries from vaccines and stingrays
The CPSC’s new data collection appears to contradict its own 214-page operating manual, which instructs hospitals not to include identifiable information “such as names, birthdates, or addresses” when reporting cases.
The agency is supposed to receive patients’ identifying information only when needed for follow-up investigations, which happens in fewer than 1% of reported cases, according to the manual.
The CPSC has also historically limited the records it collects to minimize privacy violations in case of a data breach.
The risk is not hypothetical: From 2017 to 2019, the agency improperly released personal health information of around 30,000 people, a disclosure that a top Republican at the time called “concerning.”
Konza, however, will receive even more sensitive information on many more people. McCrary said in a statement that Konza will remove patients’ names, addresses, and medical information “not needed by CPSC” before sharing records with the agency.
Leaving a private organization to collect sensitive information introduces risks, including that it could be stolen or used for business purposes, said Hoffman, the Case Western professor.
“Very often, they will use information for marketing because now they’re going to know what conditions people have,” she said.
Roney said that its contract with Konza, which has not been made public, prohibits the organization from selling or marketing the data it collects.
The CPSC’s manual also identifies types of ER visits that should not be reported to the CPSC, which has jurisdiction over only certain consumer products. Excluded injuries are those caused by food, illegal drugs, medical devices, alcohol, or plants, as well as injuries that did not involve consumer products — such as a cut from a rock or broken bones from a fall on the ground — and suicide attempts by adults.
But in a contract offered to one hospital and reviewed by KFF Health News, Konza set no such limits on the information it would gather from ER records and said it would hold on to patient health information for at least 30 days.

In an email sent to hospital technology officials, McCrary wrote that Konza would provide the CPSC with records when a patient is treated in the ER for any of more than 10,000 conditions. The expansive list of diagnostic codes Konza provided in the email includes injuries that do not involve consumer products.
Child injuries resulting from “poisoning by” vaccines or contact with stingrays, neither of which is regulated by the CPSC, are included in the list.
A limited number of hospitals once shared deidentified data on all injuries — regardless of product involvement — through the NEISS using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s injury-tracking program. But the CDC halted that data collection, after funding and staffing were cut last year, and has not restarted it.
Pressure on hospitals
CPSC Chief Data Officer Elizabeth Puchek, who joined the agency late last year after engineering U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ data system, has told hospitals in emails that they must seek an exemption from the program if they decline to share patients’ emergency room records with Konza.

The CPSC’s targeted outreach has included some of the nation’s largest urban and rural health systems, as well as small, publicly owned hospitals.
Staff members at Mary Greeley Medical Center in Ames, Iowa, said that Konza and federal officials told them their participation in the new program was mandatory. The hospital, which has long participated in NEISS, signed a new contract in April to share its ER records with Konza.
Yet the hospital is reevaluating its participation after being notified that the funds it received to participate in NEISS were “no longer available,” spokesperson Steve Sullivan said.
Several hospital executives, lawyers, and others have raised doubts about the CPSC’s claimed authority.
Harborview Medical Center spokesperson Susan Gregg said the Seattle hospital’s emergency room has “voluntarily submitted de-identified data for many years, but we are not obligated to report this information.”
In Boston, Mass General Brigham has declined to participate in the new program, with spokesperson Kelly Mitchell saying that “to protect patient privacy, we are unable to provide these medical records.”
Henry Ford Health in Detroit; St. Luke’s in Boise, Idaho; and Sanford Health based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota — which together handle over a million ER visits a year — are among the health systems that have been approached but not yet entered into an agreement with Konza, according to representatives. Several of the nation’s busiest hospital systems targeted for the program — including the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut, Nationwide Children’s Hospital and the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, and Baylor Scott & White Health in Texas — declined to answer questions about whether they’re participating.
Hoehn-Saric, the agency’s former chairman, said he was surprised that the CPSC would insist that hospitals provide identifiable records from all emergency room visits.
“This idea that they can simply demand patient information from a hospital and that the hospital would provide it — I really don’t understand the basis for that,” he said.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Despite $13M stopgap, Maine’s public defense agency expects another funding shortfall
description: Maine’s indigent defense agency is already projecting a $4 million shortfall for the upcoming year, three months after Maine lawmakers allocated $13 million in one-time emergency funding to help the agency pay contracted private attorneys.  The projected shortfall is due to years of chronic underfunding built into the Maine Commission on Public Defense Servi[...]
text:
The exterior of the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services. (Photo courtesy of Jim Billings)Maine’s indigent defense agency is already projecting a $4 million shortfall for the upcoming year, three months after Maine lawmakers allocated $13 million in one-time emergency funding to help the agency pay contracted private attorneys. 
The projected shortfall is due to years of chronic underfunding built into the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services budget, and its reliance on contracted attorneys, who take on the bulk of indigent defense cases and bill the agency at $150 per hour.
“We don’t have the ability to just stop spending money without violating people’s constitutional rights,” said Frayla Tarpinian in a commission meeting last week. “If they’re allowable expenses that are necessary for defense, we have a functional obligation to make the payments on those.”
Last year, a Superior Court justice ruled that Maine had violated defendants’ Sixth Amendment rights by not assigning them an attorney when they could not afford one. That same year, the list of indigent defendants waiting for counsel grew to more than 1,100. 
At the time, the state was still getting the relatively new network of public defender offices up and running, so the commission relied primarily on private attorneys to represent the people on that list. A year later, the backlog has shrunk to about 220 defendants, according to Tarpinian. 
“That was a huge success in this organization, and collectively there was a lot of work done by the attorneys to get that uncounted list down,” she said. But it’s also the reason for the projected increase, as cases take anywhere from six to 18 months to be resolved.
The commission’s $9 million annual budget does not account for the 2023 rate increase for contracted attorneys, which went from from $80 to $150 an hour. 
That same year, the state began to establish a more robust system of public defender offices, which now includes six physical locations across the state. 
But when that budget was presented to the Maine Legislature in early 2024, the offices were just getting set up, Tarpinian said. Although she was not part of the agency at the time, she said the budget assumed that by Fiscal Year 2027, which started in July, the offices would be fully functioning and the agency would not rely so heavily on contracted attorneys. 
“Part of it was they were overly optimistic in some of their projections,” she said. “The other piece of it, which I think is actually kind of more significant, is that they seriously undercounted the number of hours we had.”
Last year, the commission paid 325,000 attorney hours, which was a huge increase from previous years. Tarpinian said she does not see that number decreasing this year, although there are eight more staff positions that were funded through the supplemental budget that will eventually help the agency shift away from private attorneys.
Given that, the commission will be proposing a new budget with an increased annual baseline, which they will submit next month to the Department of Administrative and Financial Services.  Tarpinian did not disclose the amount of the proposed increase. 
“The last two years we’ve had to come back to the Legislature every session and beg for emergency funding to plug a gap,” Tarpinian said. “And so our goal is to make the ask that should take into account all of the factors, and will cover all of our expenses, so we don’t have to do this again.”
How the next governor and Maine Legislature will handle an increase in the commission’s baseline budget is yet to be determined, but there was broad bipartisan support for the $13 million stopgap funding last year. Commission Chair Joshua Tardy said during last week’s meeting that he plans to be in touch with all three gubernatorial candidates — Democrat Hannah Pingree, independent Rick Bennett and Republican Bobby Charles — about the commission’s budget and challenges. 
“I’m pretty confident that whoever goes into the Blaine House will have a receptive look at what our needs are, will look at progress we’ve made as a commission, and understand our baseline needs are critical,” he said.

title: Bipartisan US Senate proposal on AI ethics panel good step but incomplete, experts say
text: WASHINGTON — A proposed federal commission on artificial intelligence ethics could help address moral questions associated with the rapidly developing technology, but there are still some areas in which they believe the proposal falls short, experts say.   Sens. Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, and Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat, introduced a bill last week that would create a cross-party body of experts to “advise Congress on the ethical and policy implications of emerging technologies” such as artificial intelligence. According to a summary of the bill, titled the Human Dignity and Emerging Technologies Act, the federal government lacks an institution dedicated to studying the deeper ethics of AI and the threats it poses to human dignity.“Emerging technologies have the potential to improve everyday life and strengthen America’s position on the global stage,” Cruz said in a joint press release announcing the bill’s introduction. “But as these technologies continue to evolve, we should carefully consider the ethical questions they raise and ensure human dignity remains at the center of our policymaking.”The commission would inform “both Congress and the American people on the best path forward,” Warnock added.“As artificial intelligence continues to become a larger part of our society, we need to be clear eyed about addressing the potential problems and perils of this technology,” Warnock said.The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, which Cruz chairs.The proposed commission would have a wide focus but a narrow function, largely serving as a researcher and advisor for lawmakers. The legislation would authorize $2 million per year to the commission for the next five fiscal years. The panel would sunset in 2032, according to the bill summary, allowing Congress to reconsider its function and effectiveness.AI bioethicsThe proposed commission would focus on examining AI advancement as it relates to bioethics, a decades-old area of research that considers the ethical questions raised by emerging technologies. Vardit Ravitsky, president and CEO of the Hastings Center for Bioethics, a nonpartisan think tank, said bioethics is an effective foundation for AI policy. It can help shape a regulatory structure from the outset of a developing technology, giving regulators and courts guiding principles.“When we do the thinking ahead of time, and we have principles to guide the implementation, the rollout of the technology works better, more responsibly, more wisely, and then we can reap the benefits without running into so many problems,” she said in an interview.Ravitsky said she is “fully in favor” of the commission outlined in the Human Dignity and Emerging Technologies Act, especially because such a body could help address high-stakes concerns related to AI use in the medical field. Ravitsky teaches bioethics at Harvard Medical School, where she specializes in emerging technologies including genomics, reproductive technologies and health AI. Ethical questions in medicine include the level of disclosure owed to patients when AI is involved with their care and what to do about people treating chatbots like their personal therapists. “You quickly understand why this has to do with humanity, because we need to ask ourselves: ‘Are we going to allow AI to take over any kind of role in the health context, or do we want to limit AI to roles that don’t involve care,’” she said. Developers neededThe Human Dignity and Emerging Technologies Act outlines four main features for its proposed ethics commission. First, according to the bill summary, the committee would be bipartisan, consisting of 17 experts in fields including philosophy, ethics, religion, civil rights, social sciences, medicine, technology and science. Members would be appointed by “the President, congressional leaders and relevant congressional committees.”Ravitsky said she is in favor of having ethicists on the commission and believes maintaining bipartisanship is key. But she also recommends inviting AI developers and some representatives from the private sector to participate, given how quickly artificial intelligence is evolving. Without them, she said, “the conversation is very limited” because those involved “need some understanding of the technology.”Julian Jonker, an assistant professor of legal studies and business ethics at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, has his own concerns about the way in which the proposed commission’s members would be chosen. Although the process laid out in the bill represents “an attempt for bipartisan nomination,” because one party currently controls all three branches of U.S. government, there is still a chance the commission could end up “fairly partisan,” Jonker said.Opportunity to expand  Along with detailing plans for composition, the Human Dignity and Emerging Technologies Act directs its ethics commission to hold public hearings, issue reports and advise Congress and other relevant stakeholders on “AI, robotics, biotechnology, neurotechnology, emerging clinical technologies and other science or tech developments.” The commission would inform lawmakers about possible threats to human dignity posed by federal science and tech policy, and other congressional committees could call on the body to evaluate related programs. Jonker said it's “really laudable” that the bill is “tuned into the intersection of several technologies,” but he also pointed out that it seems to exclude some important social concerns surrounding AI by focusing mainly on bioethics.He identified issues such as labor displacement, deepfakes and the widespread use of online bots as among those the average American thinks about when considering AI’s impact on human dignity. The proposal also does not cover anything having to do with the environmental and economic consequences of AI buildup or data centers, he added. “I’m not saying that the commission has to cover everything,” he said. “But if this is the main way in which deliberation around the social impact of AI appears in Sen. Cruz’s framework, then we must note that it leaves out those things that I think are very prominent in most people’s minds right now.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Amore requests DMV audit after New Jersey mistakenly registered noncitizens to vote
description: Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore has asked the Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) to audit records covering the first two years of the state’s contract with the company now under scrutiny for a software glitch in New Jersey where 6,600 noncitizens were registered to vote. Amore’s request aims to confirm if any noncitizens […]
text:
Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore has asked the Division of Motor Vehicles to audit records tied to the state's transaction system after the same software mistakenly registered thousands of noncitizens to vote in New Jersey. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore has asked the Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) to audit records covering the first two years of the state’s contract with the company now under scrutiny for a software glitch in New Jersey where 6,600 noncitizens were registered to vote.
Amore’s request aims to confirm if any noncitizens who obtained identification cards or drivers licenses in Rhode Island between 2017 and 2019 were mistakenly registered to vote at the same time. The years span the first two years of the DMV’s current transaction system developed by Idemia Identity & Security USA LLC. 
Idemia is the same company behind the motor voter system in New Jersey where Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed July 21 that about 6,600 noncitizens were registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024 because of a malfunction at the state’s Motor Vehicle Commission. About 400 noncitizens went on to cast ballots in New Jersey elections, Sherrill said.
Amore says no signs noncitizens were registered to vote in Rhode Island

Amore’s call for an audit was done “to help maintain Rhode Islanders’ trust” in the state’s election systems, he said in a statement Friday.
“Rhode Islanders deserve clarity on this issue,” Amore said.
A spokesperson for the Rhode Island DMV acknowledged a request for comment but had no information on if and when an audit would start.
Idemia, a French-based biometrics and cryptography company, has denied responsibility, saying the state of New Jersey is responsible for the voter registration errors.
Idemia has been employed as a vendor for credentialing and software services by the Rhode Island DMV since June 2002. A company spokesperson did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the state’s potential audit.
Rhode Island Department of State officials met Friday with DMV employees and Idemia representatives, who demonstrated how the transaction system works. Amore said the demonstration confirmed that noncitizens applying for a DMV credential are not offered the opportunity to register to vote.
Noncitizens in Rhode Island are eligible for REAL ID and, since 2023, can apply for driver privilege cards and permits. Driver privilege cards which look like a state driver’s license, are not an eligible eligible form of ID for voting in the state..
Amore noted the DMV has conducted a regular audit of a randomized selection of driver records to ensure that database entries match paper records since 2019.
“To date, over 5,000 records have been audited, with no errors detected,” Amore said. “I believe strongly in our systems, processes, and the rule of law. And I welcome the opportunity to have direct dialogue with any elected official, community group, or voter who wishes to express their concerns.”
Amore’s call for an audit comes after he and other election officials across the country received a letter from the U.S. Department of Justice warning they could face criminal charges if they fail to prevent noncitizens from voting in the upcoming midterm elections.
Federal authorities have previously sought access to Rhode Island’s full voter rolls, which Amore denied. Instead, he offered the U.S. Department of Justice a copy of the state’s publicly available voter list as a substitute. The Trump administration responded with a lawsuit last December.
U.S. District Court Judge Mary S. McElroy on April 17 denied the Justice Department’s demands for an unredacted copy of Rhode Island’s statewide voter registration. That ruling was appealed by the Trump administration on June 4, though the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston has not yet taken up the case.
“The RI Department of State adheres to all federal and State elections laws and continues to ensure that Rhode Island’s elections are secure, fair, and accessible,” Amore said Friday.

The former Republican, who spent six months representing Colorado’s 4th Congressional District in Congress in 2024, has run for governor twice before, losing in primary elections in both 2018 and 2022.  The secretary of state’s office […]
text:
Greg Lopez, then a Republican candidate for Colorado governor, attends the Western Conservative Summit in Aurora on June 4, 2022. He will be on the 2026 ballot as an unaffiliated candidate for governor. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Former U.S. Rep. Greg Lopez will be on the ballot as an unaffiliated candidate for Colorado governor in November.
The former Republican, who spent six months representing Colorado’s 4th Congressional District in Congress in 2024, has run for governor twice before, losing in primary elections in both 2018 and 2022. 
The secretary of state’s office announced Tuesday that Lopez submitted a sufficient number of signatures to appear on the November ballot. Unaffiliated candidates for governor must submit 1,000 valid signatures from each congressional district in Colorado, and he comfortably cleared that requirement. The secretary of state’s office verified just under 12,000 of the signatures Lopez submitted. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser won the Democratic primary election for Colorado governor in June, defeating U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet. Victor Marx won the Republican nomination, and Jeff Peckman is running as a member of the Unity Party. The winner will succeed Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited.
Weiser is the heavy favorite in the race. Colorado has only elected one Republican governor since 1975, and Democrats are widely expected to hold on to the governorship and other statewide offices in a favorable midterm election this year.
Lopez became a self-described “placeholder” in Congress following former U.S. Rep. Ken Buck’s resignation in March 2024. Shortly afterwards, a small committee of Republican Party members nominated Lopez to finish Buck’s term, and he went on to defeat Democrat Trisha Calverese in the June special election. GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert of Windsor won election to a full term representing the 4th District later that year.
Lopez also previously served as mayor of Parker. 
Marx, who lives in El Paso County, is the founder of All Things Possible Ministries, a nonprofit that purports to do humanitarian work around the globe. Throughout his primary campaign, he declined to answer questions about the organization’s specific activities and scope of work. He also dodged questions about whether he’s killed people or how many.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG sues CYFD over reports that staff instructed foster teen to cross Mexican border
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Tuesday announced his office filed a lawsuit against the state’s child welfare agency following reports that agency staffers took a teenage boy out of the foster care system and told him to cross the U.S.-Mexico border to reunite with his estranged mother in Ciudad Juárez.
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, pictured on April 8, 2026, alongside the surviving aunt of a teenager who killed himself in 2025 while in state custody, at a news conference to announce the results of his agency’s investigation into the state Children, Youth and Families Department. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Tuesday announced his office filed a lawsuit against the state’s child welfare agency following reports that agency staffers took a teenage boy out of the foster care system and told him to cross the U.S.-Mexico border to reunite with his estranged mother in Ciudad Juárez.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a news release, the New Mexico Department of Justice said the lawsuit against the New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department, filed in the state’s First Judicial District Court in Santa Fe, came after the state Office of the Child Advocate reviewed the case and found probable violations of the child’s constitutional rights and reckless disregard for his health and safety.
“The State of New Mexico cannot claim to protect children while abandoning one of its own at an international border,” Torrez said in a statement. “This case is about more than one child. It is about whether the agency entrusted with protecting our most vulnerable children is following the law, honoring constitutional rights and putting the safety of children above bureaucratic expediency.”
A CYFD spokesperson did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment.
Torrez’s lawsuit alleges that CYFD officials gained custody of the teenager after determining he was abused and neglected, but dropped the case weeks later and drove him to the Bridge of the Americas in El Paso, where they instructed him to walk alone into Mexico and reunite with his mother. The suit alleges that the child’s mother had recently been deported following a drug conviction.
It also alleges that the teenager sought re-entry to the U.S. and that CYFD officials asked federal authorities to bar him from entering the country.
Court records show NMDOJ lawyers argue that CYFD has violated the state Children’s Code and the teenager’s constitutional due process rights.
In April, Torrez published an investigative report focused on CYFD, which alleged the department often prioritized family reunification at the expense of children’s safety.
At an interim legislative committee hearing last week, state lawmakers expressed outrage over the recent reports — one said the troubled child welfare agency appears to be “a breeding ground for predatory behavior.”
At that hearing, Torrez’s NMDOJ presented 50 proposed reforms for CYFD, including amending state law to require that the CYFD secretary have professional child welfare experience.

name: VTDigger
title: Judge finds Vermont’s federal grants can’t be rescinded if political priorities shift
description:
“This ruling is an important step toward protecting Vermont’s federal funding, now and in the future, from arbitrary termination based on the shifting priorities of the Trump Administration,” Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark wrote. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Judge finds Vermont’s federal grants can’t be rescinded if political priorities shift.
text:
A cyclist pedals along the bikepath at Waterfront Park in Burlington in June 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
New sidewalks or bike paths for seven municipalities in northern Vermont are on hold after an Environmental Protection Agency grant was halted abruptly last year when the agency determined the projects no longer aligned with the government’s goals.
The $877,000 grant for the Northwest Regional Planning Commission, which covers around 20 municipalities in Franklin and Grand Isle counties, was terminated less than a year after it was awarded, Catherine Dimitruk, the planning commission’s executive director, said in an interview last week. 
The environmental justice grant was geared toward a project constructing “equitable active transportation” in the region with the aim of enhancing biking and walking access and safety. 
The termination is a lost opportunity to build both infrastructure and community connections, said Jesse Bridges, CEO of United Way of Northwest Vermont, a partner organization on the grant. 
“We know that transportation remains one of the biggest barriers to health, financial security, and community resiliency — especially for our neighbors living in rural areas, where distances are greater and transportation options are often limited,” Bridges said in the emailed statement. 
It’s too late for the planning commission to recover that money, but Dimitruk said she hopes a judge’s ruling earlier this month will prevent the termination of active grants in the future for organizations that rely on federal funds. 
U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani’s July 17 ruling found that agencies cannot cancel already secured funding for states, including Vermont, based on changes in executive branch priorities. Court filings in the case included mention of the NRPC grant, according to the Vermont attorney general’s spokesperson.  
The judge found that relevant regulations “do not allow terminations of awards based on new program goals or agency priorities that an agency identifies after granting the award.”
The judge’s decision offers Vermont more protection against the kind of chaos the Trump administration triggered last year when Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency started canceling grants that were already promised, officials say. 
“This ruling is an important step toward protecting Vermont’s federal funding, now and in the future, from arbitrary termination based on the shifting priorities of the Trump Administration,” Attorney General Charity Clark wrote in a press release. 
This ruling comes as the Office of Management and Budget is considering a new proposal to change the rules that govern federal grants. The proposal would create a new process for political appointees to review grants to ensure that funding aligns with the president’s “policy priorities.” 

READ MORE

The OMB did not respond to requests for comment on whether the administration would appeal the decision and how this ruling could impact the proposed new rule, if at all. 
Vermont last year joined 20 other states and Washington D.C. in a lawsuit against the Office of Management and Budget and other agencies in the Trump administration. 
The multistate coalition asserted they had collectively lost billions of dollars of funding through the termination of thousands of awards in the first half of 2025, including funding for universities, school lunch programs and initiatives to combat hate crimes. This came after President Donald Trump created DOGE by executive order and directed agencies to review grants for termination. 
The suit did not aim to restore lost funding, but the ruling helps ensure that federal grants continue to support work in Vermont, Clark, the Vermont attorney general, said in an interview. 
“In a practical sense, this is extremely significant because we need these programs, and we deserve to have our tax dollars coming back to us here in Vermont,” Clark said. 
Specifically, the lawsuit sought clarity on a regulation that guides federal grants called the termination clause, which the administration cited when canceling grants. 
In 2020, the Office of Management and Budget introduced the clause and later revised it in 2024 to allow agencies to pull funding in part or entirely “if an award no longer effectuates the program goals or agency priorities.”
The OMB had asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the states’ concerns with grant termination were not specific or timely. 
In the ruling, Talwani wrote that there is an imminent threat of states’ losing at least some current grants if the court did provide clarity on the termination clause. 
“The court finds that the Termination Clause does not permit the termination of grants based on their inability to effectuate program goals and agency priorities identified after the award was made,” Talwani ultimately ruled. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Judge finds Vermont’s federal grants can’t be rescinded if political priorities shift.

name: WyoFile
title: Park County proposes prohibiting data centers in most areas
description:
Commissioners agreed that data centers would only be permitted in certain zones, and that full prohibition may lead to litigation. 
The post Park County proposes prohibiting data centers in most areas appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Park County commissioners are taking a hard line with data centers, in large part after hearing overwhelming public sentiment in opposition and due to simply not knowing enough about potential issues. 
The concerns about data centers have been a big topic recently, especially in southeastern Wyoming as the Cheyenne area has seen dozens of the large centers being built or in various stages of planning in the last few years. 
While Gov. Mark Gordon recently came out opposed to a moratorium at the state level, a number of primary election candidates have expressed opposition to any more data centers being built. 
“As governor, I do not support any state-mandated moratorium on building data centers in Wyoming,” Gordon wrote in part in a recent column. “The job of deciding whether to encourage the building of data centers falls, as it should, on the more than capable shoulders of our local communities within the constraints allowed by the Legislature. As with most development, it is the communities, counties, and local boards who do the heavy lifting in economic opportunity.”
Park County is taking up that mantle. As commissioners hashed out last week in updating development standards and regulations ahead of an adoption draft to take before the public, heavy-load electric users would be permitted nowhere in the county without a special-use permit — which requires public hearings. 
Data centers would not be allowed at all in most areas, however, including smaller residential and commercial zones. Commissioners are only proposing centers be allowed with a special-use permit in the county’s General Rural 20-and 35-acre zones and industrial zones. 
“At this time, based on public input and just the unknown, the recommendation [from the consultant] is to more widely prohibit them as opposed to allow,” Planning Director Joy Hill told commissioners during a work session last week. “The other thing is that it’s understood that we don’t really have the power and water sources potentially in Park County. I can’t confirm that. I don’t know the power needs. I know they can create their own power. I don’t know how much water they need and how often. I could not tell you. I do not have enough factual information about data centers generally to feel comfortable even advising you.
“I don’t think generally the public is favoring them.”
Commissioner Scott Mangold said as data centers are currently set up, Park County wouldn’t be a desirable place for one anyway, as he said the county doesn’t have the infrastructure to get one set up. 
“Now, if they become smaller or if they discover they can put them out in space, that’ll be fine, but for now the actual way the data centers are set up right now, Park County is not a good place for them,” he said. 
While that may be, Commissioner Lloyd Thiel said he’d still prefer some ability to at least apply, to which Mangold agreed, saying an outright ban could lead to the situation the commissioners found themselves in when they blocked a cell tower in the Wapiti Valley after an outpouring of community opposition. The cell tower company sued and won a court case, forcing the county to accept the tower. 
“I don’t think eliminating completely is the answer,” Thiel said. 
Hill said she didn’t know if that would even be legal to fully ban them, and also brought up the fact of property rights. 
“We have the property rights issue too,” she said. “If there’s somebody with 3,000, 5,000, 10,000 acres and they want to sell that to a [data center] company, will they have to go through the process? Absolutely. But would they have a right to do it?”
With the commissioners’ determination, there would be a path for a developer to build a data center in certain areas of the county, but the proposal would have to pass public, and commissioner, scrutiny.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Families should not be left wondering’ – School clothing allowance program out of funds in 7 days
description: West Virginia's school clothing assistance program isn’t accepting anymore applications due to running out of funds, according to the state Bureau of Family Assistance. The application window was open for a total of seven days.
text:
(Stock photo by Thanasis/Getty Images)West Virginia’s school clothing assistance program isn’t accepting anymore applications due to running out of funds, according to the state Bureau of Family Assistance. The application window was open for a total of seven days.
The program provides eligible families vouchers to shop for shirts, pants, shoes, coats and more before school starts. In the past, more than 80,000 children statewide have used the clothing allowance.
The program launched later than expected on July 20 while Gov. Patrick Morrisey reviewed the use of federal anti-poverty funds the state uses to pay for the school clothing allowance program.  
The West Virginia Bureau for Family Assistance posted online that, “The 2026 School Clothing Allowance application period has closed effective 11:59 on July 27, 2026, since program funding has been exhausted.”
Earlier this year, lawmakers approved $177 million in Temporary Assistance for Needy Family funding for the state Dept. of Human Services to spend this current fiscal year on programs, including the school clothing allowance program.
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell
“We appropriated the funding requested by the governor for the school clothing allowance from TANF funds, so it is difficult to understand why families experienced weeks of delays only to see the program close after one week,” said Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, who chairs the House Health Committee.
“This program exists to help children prepare for the school year, and families should not be left wondering why promised assistance from the federal government is no longer available. The Bureau for Family Assistance owes the public a clear accounting of how the funds were spent, why the program closed after one week and whether additional eligible families will have an opportunity to receive the benefit,” Worrell said. 
DoHS previously said that clothing allowance applications would be accepted until Aug. 15, or until the available funds are fully allocated, whichever occurs first. 
The department did not respond to an inquiry by time of publishing about how many children successfully applied for the allowance during the last 7 days while the program was open. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha
“The delayed voucher funds after only a week tells us that West Virginia families are struggling more than ever to make ends meet. Children deserve dignity at school, and I hope the administration will work with the Legislature to ensure all children are fed and clothed in our state,” said Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha.
Morrisey has been reviewing TANF funding after saying that the program faced a $43 million structural deficit due to increased COVID-era spending by DoHS. The governor’s administration has not yet publicly shared budget documents that could provide additional details about the deficit. 
Lawmakers based their TANF approval amount earlier this year on Morrisey’s budget request. During the budget process, DoHS officials never alerted lawmakers that the state could face a deficit in TANF funds, which also fund foster care services, Legal Aid, family support centers and more. 
DoHS announced on July 16 that the department was nearing completion of the review of TANF dollars. 
“Today, West Virginia receives approximately $98.8 million in federal dollars each year to support TANF-funded state activities but spends approximately $137 million annually on TANF programs,” DoHS said in a news release. “The difference has been covered using TANF reserve funds – essentially savings accumulated over previous years. At the current expenditure rate, those reserve funds will be exhausted in about 13 months.”
The statement continued, “Those reserve funds help these programs respond when demand unexpectedly increases – whether because more families qualify for assistance or an emergency creates greater need. Spending them down to zero would leave West Virginia without that cushion when families need it most.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Aurora council insists on cooperation from GEO Group over tuberculosis investigation at ICE facility
description: The Aurora City Council approved a statement Monday that demands the private company that runs the immigration detention center in the city cooperate with public health officials in an investigation of a tuberculosis case. “It’s in our interest to protect the public health of our community to be able to merely make a statement that […]
text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Aurora, operated by private prison firm GEO Group, is pictured on Jan. 30, 2025. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The Aurora City Council approved a statement Monday that demands the private company that runs the immigration detention center in the city cooperate with public health officials in an investigation of a tuberculosis case.
“It’s in our interest to protect the public health of our community to be able to merely make a statement that requests or demands that (The GEO Group) comply on behalf of our residents,” Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman told council members during a study session.
“This is really not how you feel about the issue of immigration or immigration enforcement or any particular entity,” he said. “It’s simply a public health question.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Adams County Health Department issued a public health order in late June to investigate a confirmed case of tuberculosis in the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center run by GEO. Since then, despite pressure from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment and other state officials, GEO has not granted access or given Adams County the information it needs to conduct a public health investigation into the case, as required by state law. Immigration advocates suspect there have been multiple cases, based on conversations with people detained in the facility, and The Guardian reported there could be a dozen cases.
Immigration advocates press for action on tuberculosis case at Aurora ICE facility

“Before recent legislation about oversight of civil immigration detention facilities, the state has long had, as the county has long had, authority to act in cases of a potential outbreak of an infectious disease,” said state Sen. Mike Weissman, an Aurora Democrat who sponsored a recent law requiring more frequent safety inspections at the facility for things like food standards and confinement conditions. Another state law requiring notification and public health investigations, specifically around tuberculosis, has long been in effect.
“For my part, I have vigorously encouraged the state to make use of that authority to protect public health in the facility and in the broader metro Denver community beyond that,” he told Newsline.
An unnamed ICE spokesperson said earlier this month that there was one person at the center on June 25 with tuberculosis, and that person was “treated, cleared, and removed from the country.” During an oversight visit on July 15, staff from U.S. Rep. Jason Crow’s office were told by immigration officials that they identified 61 people who were exposed to that initial case and that one person was being monitored.
“The fact is, GEO is not cooperative, and so we have an incident here. There could be other incidents down the road,” Coffman said.
In an earlier statement, Attorney General Phil Weiser said his office is ready to work with Gov. Jared Polis and other state health officials “to bring GEO into compliance with the law,” but that has not been backed up by enforcement efforts or litigation. The attorney general’s office has the authority to enforce a public health order issued by the state’s health department. On Monday, Coffman said he thinks the county and state “may be prepared to go to court to force (GEO) to comply.”
Adams County did not immediately responded to a request for comment on that claim. A Weiser spokesperson wrote in an email that CDPHE and the governor’s office are “taking the lead” on the situation. CDPHE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
