title: Alabama Department of Corrections: ‘Reasonable concern’ $1.25 billion prison will be delayed
description: The Alabama Department of Corrections said in a statement on Tuesday that there is a “reasonable concern” that the opening of a 4,000-bed men’s correctional facility in Elmore County could be delayed. The statement said that Caddell, the contractor responsible for building the $1.25 billion Gov. Kay Ivey Correctional Complex, may not meet an Oct. […]
text:
An inmate in the custody of the Department of Corrections. The Alabama Department of Corrections said Tuesday that there was a "reasonable concern" that a 4,000-bed men's prison facility would not be completed before an Oct. 15 deadline. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Department of Corrections said in a statement on Tuesday that there is a “reasonable concern” that the opening of a 4,000-bed men’s correctional facility in Elmore County could be delayed.
The statement said that Caddell, the contractor responsible for building the $1.25 billion Gov. Kay Ivey Correctional Complex, may not meet an Oct. 15 deadline to complete work on the project, based on the terms of a contract between the company and the ADOC.
“Based on these factors, ACIFA (Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority) has implemented contractual remedies available to it under the DBA (Design-Build Agreement), including requiring Caddell to implement extraordinary measures such as additional contractors or workers and additional shifts, as well as payment withholding,” ADOC said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The statement, released prior to a scheduled meeting of a legislative prison oversight committee on Wednesday, did not provide details about the reasons for the delay or how long it might last. A message seeking comment was sent Tuesday to Caddell and the Hoar Program Management, the firm responsible for managing the construction project. A message was also sent to the ADOC on Tuesday seeking further comment.
State lawmakers, including Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa and Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, the chair of the Senate’s General Fund committee, said Tuesday they were unaware of delays regarding the facility.
“The legislative leadership has been briefed that, based on some percentages of completion in some areas, there could be a chance that it could go past the Oct. 15 date,” said Rep. Rex Reynolds, R-Huntsville, the chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund committee. “But our posture is that we want to see this thing completed.”
Both Albritton and Reynolds said they do not expect the cost to the state to increase significantly based on the terms of the state’s agreement with the contractor.
“If there are delays, as I understand it, those delays would be at the cost of the vendor, not to the state,” Albritton said.
The opening of the Ivey Correctional Complex was initially scheduled for May of this year, but officials late last year pushed the date to October.
The Alabama Legislature in 2021 approved the construction of two new men’s prisons in Elmore and Escambia counties, each with 4,000 beds. The Elmore County prison will also feature a medical and mental health area that will have 720 beds.
Officials said two new facilities are needed because the state’s current prisons are outdated and require more money to maintain them for use. Critics say the prisons will not address overcrowding or widespread violence within the state’s correctional facilities.
Both the Elmore and Escambia sites were not supposed to add capacity but replace the aging facilities that are designated to be closed. However, lawmakers have become increasingly concerned that because of the growing prison population, the state may need to keep facilities open.
The Legislature appropriated $1.3 billion for the construction of the two prisons, but the Elmore County facility has consumed nearly all of that appropriation, due to inflation and higher than projected costs on portions of the prison. State officials in 2025 approved additional borrowing of $500 million for prison construction.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Paula Lewis resigns from Oklahoma City school board after historic tenure
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The longest-serving school board leader in Oklahoma City Public Schools’ history, credited with helping stabilize a once-turbulent district, resigned Monday evening. Paula Lewis and her wife recently purchased a larger Oklahoma City home outside of the school district’s boundaries, which requires her to step down from office, she told Oklahom[...]
text:
Oklahoma City Board of Education Chair Paula Lewis speaks during a board work session Nov. 18, 2024, at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The longest-serving school board leader in Oklahoma City Public Schools’ history, credited with helping stabilize a once-turbulent district, resigned Monday evening.
Paula Lewis and her wife recently purchased a larger Oklahoma City home outside of the school district’s boundaries, which requires her to step down from office, she told Oklahoma Voice in a one-on-one interview. She served on the Oklahoma City Board of Education for a decade and led it as the at-large board chair since 2017.
Lewis, 56, cited her growing pediatric therapy business and a desire to spend more time with family as other reasons contributing to her departure.
“I’ve just added to my life over 10 years and it’s gotten big and I’m blessed with it,” Lewis said. “Now, I have to have a place that can (support) it.”
She notified fellow board members and top district administrators Monday evening of her resignation, which took effect immediately.
With Lewis less than halfway through her term, the board must call an election to fill the vacancy, according to state law. Board chair is the only position elected by voters in all parts of the Oklahoma City district. The officeholder leads each board meeting and sets the agendas.
The board’s District 6 position is up for election in February, indicating that date as a financially and logistically feasible option for a board chair special election.
State law allows the board to choose an appointee to fill the seat until a new chair is elected. Another possible option, under state law and board policy, is permitting the vice chair to lead the board until a new chair is elected.
Vice Chair Lori Bowman said the board will decide how to proceed at its next regularly scheduled meeting Aug. 17. 
Bowman said she would be interested in running to succeed Lewis as board chair once an election is called.
Oklahoma City Board of Education Chair Paula Lewis, right, listens to Vice Chair Lori Bowman before a meeting Jan. 8, 2024, at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services. (Photo By Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
“It’s been an absolute privilege to work alongside her, and I’ve learned a lot by watching her and working with her,” Bowman said. “I just think that she has always kept kids and our students at the forefront of everything that she’s done, and it’s a great lesson in leadership.”
Superintendent Jamie Polk echoed that “Paula has kept one question at the center of her work: What is best for our students?”
“Working alongside her, I have seen her commitment to public education and to creating safe, equitable and high-quality learning environments across our district,” Polk said. “I am grateful for her leadership and partnership.”
Lewis ‘helped usher in stability’ in OKCPS
Lewis’ younger son, Reign, was in pre-K when she first ran for the school board’s District 4 position in 2016. Next month, he’ll start his sophomore year at Classen High School of Advanced Studies at Northeast, where he’ll stay enrolled after moving.
Her older son, Hunter, now married with a child, was Lewis’ first inspiration to run for office, she said. He was in middle school at the time and was beginning to struggle with his mental health, she said. 
Lewis, an occupational therapist, wanted to advocate for better mental health support for OKCPS students like Hunter, but once she was elected, she stepped onto a school board that was in “constant conflict.” 
Tense, disorganized board meetings would last several hours, she said. Members of the community frequently came to yell and protest. The district superintendent’s office had been a revolving door for years. 
The board’s chaos too often made front-page headlines, suffocating any positive news from coming out of the district, Lewis said.
After a year in office, she successfully ran for board chair on a promise to deliver stability and better communication from top leadership.
“You can’t drive student achievement unless you have a stable environment, and prior to Paula being board chair … we did not have stability,” said state Sen. Mark Mann, who served with Lewis on the board for seven years. “The district was in turmoil consistently for years. I think that would be her mark, is that she helped usher in stability in the district.”
The Board of Education governing Oklahoma City Public Schools meets Feb. 29, 2024, to address the resignation of Superintendent Sean McDaniel. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The board then went on to hire Sean McDaniel as the district superintendent in 2018. He would become one of the longest-tenured OKCPS superintendents in three decades until his departure in 2024 — a period in which he and the board led the district through the COVID-19 pandemic and massive school consolidations.
The 2019 consolidation plan, which closed 15 underutilized schools and reconfigured 17 more, caused “hard feelings” in parts of the Oklahoma City community, Lewis said. 
The plan also offered benefits, like every remaining elementary school being staffed with a counselor, nurse, art teacher and physical education program, she said. But for some, frustration over beloved schools shutting down overshadowed the trade-ups. 
“The positives don’t make up for a hurt feeling, and I don’t know that we did enough to acknowledge the pain that we caused,” Lewis said.
Trust among voters, though, was strong by 2022 when they approved a $955 million bond issue for facility upgrades in OKCPS.
Two decades before, public trust in the school system was too low for the district to pass bond issues on its own, Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt said. That’s why OKCPS in 2001 had to rely on a city government sales tax initiative, known as MAPS for Kids, to improve school infrastructure.
“Many leaders inside and outside of the district have been a part of changing that trajectory since 2001, but Paula has been at the helm of the board now for nearly a decade, so she certainly deserves a lot of the credit,” Holt said.
McDaniel’s relationship with the board, though, declined beyond repair by 2024, leading to his resignation. He cited “irreconcilable” differences with an unnamed board member.
The board chose to promote Polk from within McDaniel’s administration to succeed the departing superintendent.
Oklahoma City Board of Education Chair Paula Lewis, left, and Oklahoma City Public Schools Superintendent Jamie Polk, right, listen during a board work session April 20 at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Lewis said she considered leaving the board in 2024 at the end of her second board chair term, but instead chose to run for reelection to maintain continuity through the leadership transition. She defeated two challengers by capturing more than 50% of the vote in a February 2025 election.
Now is “about as good a time as you could get” to step away, Lewis said. Polk is entering her third school year as superintendent, and the board has an experienced vice chair in Bowman.
Although Lewis plans to stay active as a community volunteer, she said she has no plans to run for another elected office, at least not until her younger son finishes high school.
She’ll have more time to spend with family and to focus on her business without having to dedicate 12 to 20 hours each week on board chair duties.
“For me, it’s been a great journey,” she said. “Will there be things I miss? Probably. Am I excited for the next chapter? One hundred percent. Do I believe that the board is in a good place, a better place than it started when I got there? Yes, I do.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ culls some improper voter registrations, sends others to counties for review
description: Gov. Sherrill said Tuesday about 4,500 non-citizens will be removed from the voter rolls. About 2,100 more names will be reviewed by county election officials first.
text:
Gov. Sherrill said Tuesday about 4,500 non-citizens will be removed from the voter rolls. About 2,100 more names will be reviewed by county election officials first. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey has begun culling its voter rolls of non-citizens who were registered to vote after visits to the Motor Vehicle Commission, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Tuesday.
The governor’s comments, delivered at a celebration of a state-level voting rights law signed earlier in July, come a week after she announced about 6,600 individuals were registered to vote despite marking themselves as non-citizens during visits to motor vehicle agency locations between June 2023 and June 2024. Fewer than 400 of them later cast ballots, according to Sherrill.
“We are moving very, very quickly. We are already removing people from the rolls who are not properly on there as we identified the serious system error, and as far as the investigation, it is moving quickly,” she said at the Union Baptist Church in Trenton.
NJ Republicans target two laws as they seek probe into non-citizen voting reveal

In a statement sent later Tuesday, the governor said New Jersey had begun removing more than 4,500 registrations made solely due to what her administration has characterized as a technical glitch in the Motor Vehicle Commission’s systems.
Idemia, the vendor responsible for that system since it was awarded a contract to manage driver’s license printing under Gov. Chris Christie in 2010, has denied responsibility for the registration of non-citizens. New Jersey last week moved to end the longstanding Idemia contract.
In her Tuesday statement, Sherrill said the state would refer the roughly 2,100 registrations it is not automatically removing to county election officials to ensure eligible voters are not removed from the rolls.
“We are taking this extra step because our initial review indicates that a number of these individuals may be citizens,” she said. “That has been the case in other states where clerical and administrative voter registration errors have occurred, and we’re determined to get this right.”
It’s possible eligible voters inadvertently marked themselves as non-citizens or that some registered to vote while eligible have since been naturalized.
Two of the Senate’s top Republicans, Sen. Tony Bucco (R-Morris) and Sen. Kristin Corrado (R-Passaic), had called for the governor to share registration information with local election officials. Bucco is the Senate’s minority leader and Corrado is the ranking Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee.
“Promptly providing this information will allow local election officials to review the registrations, take any action authorized by law and demonstrate to the public that every reasonable step has been taken to protect the integrity of our elections,” they said in a joint statement Tuesday.
Republicans in New Jersey and nationwide have questioned Sherrill’s claim that a software glitch was responsible for registering thousands of non-citizens to vote. They are calling for an end or at least a pause on automatic voter registration at Motor Vehicle Commission locations.
Sherrill said her administration had sent letters to those who were improperly registered to vote.
Her administration has retained the law firm Chiesa Shahinian & Giantomasi PC to probe the registration issues. Jeffrey Chiesa, a state attorney general under Christie and a former GOP U.S. senator, is a partner at the firm.
The Trump administration last week demanded Sherrill hand over information about the non-citizens who were added to the voter rolls. She reiterated she would not share the registrants’ information with the federal government.
“I’m not in the habit of turning over private identifying information of the citizens of New Jersey. This federal government is weaponizing the government against individuals that disagree with them,” she said. “They weaponized my private data against me in my election, and so I am working to protect people and their private data here in New Jersey.”
During the campaign, the Trump administration released Sherrill’s full military service record, which included her unredacted Social Security number, in response to a public records request filed by a former GOP congressional candidate. The technician responsible for the release, who retired rather than face termination, told investigators from the National Archives’ Office of the Inspector General he did not know who Sherrill was and did not notice that the request for her information was not filed by Sherrill herself.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Voter subpoenas denied in recount of narrow Indiana Senate Republican primary
description: The Indiana Recount Commission rejected a request to question voters under oath about how they cast their ballots in what is now a three-vote margin from May’s Republican primary for an Indiana Senate seat.
text:
Republican state Senate candidate Paula Copenhaver, right, listens with her attorney William Bock as Samantha DeWester, an attorney for Sen. Spencer Deery, speaks during an Indiana Recount Commission meeting on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Recount Commission rejected a request to question voters under oath about how they cast their ballots in what is now a three-vote margin from May’s Republican primary for a state Senate seat.
The commission’s 2-1 vote was a setback to Paula Copenhaver’s challenge to Sen. Spencer Deery’s lead following a rancorous campaign in which she had President Donald Trump’s endorsement because of Deery’s opposition to the congressional redistricting plan pushed last year by the president. 
The recount outcome, however, is not decided as the commission will meet again Aug. 18 to take up possibly more than 300 ballots the two sides have disputed.
Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales, the commission’s chair, sided with Democratic member Michael Claytor in voting to deny Copenhaver’s subpoena request.
Republican member Paul Mullin supported her motion to question 11 voters who disclosed in social media posts or to news reporters that they had cast Republican primary ballots to support Deery despite being Democrats or self-identified “progressives.”
Morales said in voting against the subpoena request that it wasn’t proper to question voters after they had cast ballots.
“This is the right thing to do, to make sure that we reject the motion to subpoena any voters because I don’t believe that’s the right thing to do,” Morales said. “I believe everybody has the right to go and vote, but they need to do it the right way. And the right way, again, is I encourage the General Assembly next session to close our primaries so we can avoid all of this.”
Copenhaver, the Fountain County Republican chair and staffer to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, said she intended to keep up the recount fight.
“Every Republican that voted in this Republican primary in this district should be upset to know that there were Democrats who voted in the Republican primary with no intention to support (the) Republican Party in the fall,” she told reporters after the commission meeting.
The ballot challenging process will continue, but Recount Director Evan Norris told the commission that a ballot review by State Board of Accounts auditors came up with no changes from the certified results that show Deery leading by a 6,337 to 6,334 margin.
The Deery-Copenhaver winner will face Democratic West Lafayette City Councilman David Sanders in the November election for the heavily Republican Senate District 23, which spans all or parts of six counties in the area between Lafayette and Terre Haute.
This story will be updated.

title: James Aren Duckett is executed on 1987 conviction for killing 11-year-old girl
description: Florida executed James Aren Duckett, 68, Tuesday for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee. He was declared dead at 1:19 p.m., according to a statement from the Florida Department of Corrections. The execution was delayed by more than an hour to await a ruling on Duckett’s requests for a stay of execution from […]
text:
Credit:  YouTubeFlorida executed James Aren Duckett, 68, Tuesday for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee.
He was declared dead at 1:19 p.m., according to a statement from the Florida Department of Corrections. The execution was delayed by more than an hour to await a ruling on Duckett’s requests for a stay of execution from the U.S. Supreme Court, which denied them.
Duckett became the 11th inmate Florida has executed this year. The man who could become the 12th such death-row inmate, Dominick Occhicone, is scheduled for execution at 6 p.m. If that takes place, it would be the first time two inmates were executed on the same day in Florida since 1964. Occhicone would also be the second oldest inmate executed in U.S. history.
Family members spoke with reporters shortly after Duckett was declared dead by lethal injection in Florida State Prison near Starke.
“Justice has finally been done,” said Tracy McFall, who was a cousin of the victim.
“My 11-year-old cousin was raped and killed and thrown in a lake like garbage. That man should have been executed and felt some kind of pain like he did my cousin. He got off way too easy…and it shouldn’t have taken 40 years for my aunt to see justice. I’m just glad that she’s still alive to see this closure.”
Duckett’s attorneys had unsuccessfully claimed he was innocent and that the state had botched the DNA testing that they claim would have exonerated him.
Duckett’s execution was the 30th in Florida since January 2025. In addition to Occhicone’s scheduled execution later Tuesday, Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 61-year-old William Silvia for Aug. 18. Silvia was convicted of the 2006 shooting murder of his wife, Patricia.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC voters support sports betting but don’t like prediction markets, new poll finds
description: North Carolinians are generally okay with sports betting, but a majority wants the state to ban prediction markets, according to a Meredith College poll released Tuesday.  The North Carolina General Assembly legalized online sports betting in 2024.  At 51%, just over half of registered voters said they were satisfied with the level of state regulation […]
text:
Kalshi photo illustration, Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)North Carolinians are generally okay with sports betting, but a majority wants the state to ban prediction markets, according to a Meredith College poll released Tuesday. 
The North Carolina General Assembly legalized online sports betting in 2024. 
At 51%, just over half of registered voters said they were satisfied with the level of state regulation of sports gambling. Only 11% said they were dissatisfied, while 38% said they didn’t know. 
The survey shows far fewer voters are comfortable with prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. Two-thirds of registered voters said they would support state legislation banning such markets, while 24% said they should be legal in N.C., and 8% said they didn’t know. 
At the same time, most registered voters in North Carolina don’t have much familiarity with prediction markets, according to the report. Fifteen percent said they were very familiar, 38% said somewhat familiar, and 47% said they were unfamiliar. 
Even though sports betting had a higher level of acceptance in the survey, respondents expressed concerns about its effects on specific groups of people. 
A majority of respondents, 58%, said they were concerned about illegal sports betting by individuals under 21, while 32% were unconcerned. 
For sports betting by young adults between the ages of 21 and 30, public opinion is divided: 47% of respondents expressed some concern and 43% expressed some level of unconcern. 
Stein order bans NC workers from insider betting on prediction markets

Exactly half of the participants said they were concerned about the impact of sports betting on college athletes, while 36% expressed little or no concern. 
“Concerns were substantially greater when questions focused on underage gambling, young adults, or college athletes than when respondents evaluated sports betting in general,” Meredith Poll director David McLennan said. “This pattern suggests that residents do not simply evaluate sports betting as an entertainment activity; they also consider its broader implications for families, communities, and higher education.”
In the most recent budget, Republican legislators raised the state tax on sports betting operators from 18% to 23%. They also imposed a new 6% tax on prediction market operators in North Carolina. The disparity in the rates led some Democratic critics of the provision to suggest that sports betting would move onto predictive markets in North Carolina to increase profits.
Meredith College conducted the poll between July 1 and 8. The sample size was 1,022 registered voters, giving a credibility interval of plus or minus 3%.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Medicaid extension in 2022 doubled postpartum medical visits, state officials say
description: Preliminary results from an ongoing New Mexico Department of Health evaluation show that a 2022 Medicaid expansion for new mothers doubled the number of visits they made to doctors' offices, which officials said is a promising sign as they seek to reduce pregnancy-related deaths.
text:
New Mexico Health Department officials said a 2022 Medicaid expansion that covers new mothers up to a year after giving birth resulted in twice as many postpartum healthcare visits. (Getty Images)Preliminary results from an ongoing New Mexico Department of Health evaluation show that a 2022 Medicaid expansion for new mothers doubled the number of visits they made to doctors’ offices, which officials said is a promising sign as they seek to reduce pregnancy-related deaths. 
New Mexico is one of 49 states that took advantage of a provision in the 2021 federal American Rescue Plan Act that enabled states to extend postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to a year beyond the end of a pregnancy.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The extension went into effect in April 2022 and promised to drastically change postpartum care in a state where Medicaid, a government health insurance program for low-income people, covers approximately 60% of all births. That’s among the highest rates in the nation, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. 
State Health Department officials are working on a comprehensive analysis of the Medicaid expansion that they expect to release in September. But they provided some early insights in a recent interview with Source NM that followed the release of new data on pregnancy-related deaths.
Since the expansion went into effect, according to state health officials, healthcare facilities statewide have seen twice as many visits from new mothers. Most of those increased visits have been to primary care providers or related to substance abuse disorder, though a “modest” number related to mental health. 
The health department declined to provide specific figures regarding the number of visits because officials are still finalizing their evaluation. Officials also are still evaluating whether the increased visits resulted in better outcomes for mothers or contributed to a post-pandemic decline in pregnancy-related deaths. 
But Kevin Peine, executive director at the NMDOH’s Centers for Public Health, said he can already declare the expansion a “success” that the state hopes to build on by increasing awareness of the expansion. 
“What we would like to see is even more women seeking care and not just one or two visits,” he said. “We want it to be a recurring thing to provide that support throughout the postpartum period.”
Expanding postpartum access to healthcare emerged as one of the key recommendations following the release of new data last week from the Health Department’s Maternal Mortality Review Committee, a multi-disciplinary volunteer board tasked with investigating deaths of pregnant mothers.
Mental illness, substance abuse driving New Mexico’s high maternal mortality, new data shows

The committee found that mental illness — and particularly substance abuse — was the biggest contributing factor to 74 pregnancy-related deaths of New Mexico mothers between 2018 and 2023.
The committee defines pregnancy-related deaths as those that occur due to pregnancy complications or from health conditions a pregnancy exacerbated. 
The data also show that nearly half of the deaths in that five-year period occurred in the “late postpartum period,” which state officials define as 43 days or longer after a child is born. According to the new data, 25.7% of deaths occurred between 43 and 180 days after birth, and a further 20.3% occurred between 181 days and 365 days after birth. 
Peine said the high number of “late postpartum” deaths demonstrates the need for prolonged access to care. While the Medicaid expansion enabled that access, Peine said some mothers may not realize they still have health insurance months after giving birth.
“Postpartum access to health care remains critical for improving outcomes,” Peine said. “Efforts to increase provider, patient and community awareness of the extension and covered services are necessary to ensure increased uptake in care in the postpartum period.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: DEEP agrees to stricter enforcement for Brookfield pipeline project
description: Leaving the door open to final approval, regulators said they would review the application to increase capacity along the Iroquois Pipeline.
text:
Opponents of a controversial natural gas expansion project in Brookfield celebrated this week after state environmental regulators agreed to reopen the public comment period and impose new enforcement measures to limit potential emissions.
On Friday, the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection concluded its monthslong review of the project by announcing that it would require the developer, the Iroquois Gas Transmission System, to implement continuous monitoring of certain airborne pollutants as a condition of the project’s approval.
At the same time, however, the agency said it would agree to Iroquois’ request to amend its application to allow for greater releases of carbon monoxide, a potent gas which contributes to global climate change. 
As a result of the later change, DEEP said it would launch a new public comment period, giving critics and supporters 30 days to weigh in on the amended project. That will effectively delay a final decision until later this year, at the earliest, as regulators will again have to take time to review and respond to any comments.
“Our position [is that] transparency is very important to us,” Acting DEEP Commissioner Emma Cimino said in an interview on Monday. “Public participation is key to our permitting processes, and so we decided to go back out to notice so that the public could review and provide comment on these carbon monoxide numbers.”
While the decision left open the door for DEEP to eventually approve Iroquois’ application, it was welcomed by critics who have called for greater scrutiny over the project’s design. 
In a post on social media announcing the decision on Friday, Brookfield First Selectman Steve Dunn said that the town will be able to request a new, more robust public hearing in addition to the public comment period — which could add further delays to the project timeline. He also suggested the town would continue pushing for additional revisions, including the use of all-electric compressors that do not release any emissions.
“At this point, a final decision has NOT been made to require Iroquois to use electric compressors,” Dunn said. “However, this is a WIN for Brookfield and our residents who have been fighting for changes.”
A spokesperson for Iroquois was not immediately available for comment. 
The Brookfield project is a key component of Iroquois’ compression-only expansion of its 414-mile pipeline running from the Canadian border to its terminus in New York City. The project will increase the capacity of the pipeline by about 8%, or an additional 125 million cubic feet of gas each day.
In order to increase the flow of gas without actually expanding the size of the pipeline, Iroquois owners want to build two additional gas turbine compressors at an existing compressor station in Brookfield. The new compressors will be fueled by burning some of the gas within the pipeline, releasing emissions of carbon and other pollutants.
The expansion project had been projected to cost $272 million before the last changes announced by DEEP.
Much of the criticism of the project, particularly in Brookfield, has focused on the issue of local pollution, as well as the site’s proximity to a nearby middle school. More broadly, the project has encountered opposition from environmental groups who argue Connecticut officials have pledged to wean the state off planet-warming fossil fuels and this instead doubles down on those.
Gov. Ned Lamont, who has spoken favorably of gas expansion in the past, met with Dunn in April to discuss the local opposition to the project. He later told the Connecticut Mirror that he would not interfere with DEEP’s review of the project’s air quality permits.
DEEP received a total of 428 responses during its initial public comment period, resulting in several delays as agency staff worked to prepare a response.
One recurring criticism that appeared in those comments, according to the agency’s response, was that Brookfield — along with the rest of Fairfield County — already struggles with poor air quality as a result of out-of-state pollution that blows in from the west. Other commenters pointed out that Iroquois’ proposed increase of smog-forming nitrogen oxide, or NOx, emissions fell just below the 25 ton-per-year threshold that would have triggered a more extensive permitting process.
Without a way to constantly monitor the facility’s actual emissions, critics argued, it would be all-but impossible to determine whether those limits are being met.
“Those comments were well taken,” Cimino said. “Upon reviewing them, we decided that [the continuous air monitoring] requirements were appropriate here, and they will just allow for real-time nitrous oxide, NOx, emissions testing from each turbine, which will allow both the permit holder to ensure that they’re staying under the cap, and will ensure that DEEP has very complete information about what’s coming out of the stacks of this facility.”
Even with the anticipated increase in NOx emissions, the expanded facility should be able to operate under its current permit levels for those gases — around 42 tons per year — because it has historically operated well below its limit, according to Jaimeson Sinclair, director of engineering at DEEP’s Bureau of Air Management.
The expansion is also expected to result in a reduction of CO emissions from the Brookfield facility because Iroquois is planning to retrofit its existing equipment with more modern pollution-control equipment, in addition to constructing two new turbines, Sinclair said. 
Iroquois’ original application would have resulted in a 90% reduction in allowable CO emissions, Sinclair said. However the company’s revised application, if approved, will result in a reduction closer to 69%.
Jessica Roberts, an attorney with the environmental nonprofit Save the Sound, said she and other advocates remained concerned about the project’s impacts on air quality and public health. While she said she was still reviewing the agency’s responses to the initial round of public comments, she said the agency made the right decision to continue fielding input on the project.
Roberts was involved in a lawsuit earlier this year that unsuccessfully sought to block DEEP from issuing a final ruling on the project. 
“I’m very pleased to see that DEEP’s accepting comments on the entire permit as a whole, rather than the new modifications,” Roberts said. “So yeah, I do see that as a win, absolutely.”

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Haitian immigrants brace for end of protected status
text: WASHINGTON — Hundreds of thousands of Haitian immigrants could lose their legal status as early as Tuesday, subjecting them to deportation after the U.S. Supreme Court last month allowed the Trump administration to proceed with terminating their humanitarian protections. The incoming loss of Temporary Protected Status for between 330,000 and 350,000 immigrants comes amid the Trump administration's deportation campaign and continued attacks on TPS recipients who hail from countries deemed too unsafe for return. The State Department highly advises against any visit to Haiti due to kidnappings and violence by gangs. The Department of Homeland Security has already urged those who are set to lose their TPS to self-deport. “Temporary protected status is exactly that — TEMPORARY,” DHS said in a Monday social media post. “For those with terminated TPS: it’s closing time. You don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.”Several media reports have indicated that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is planning for aggressive enforcement of Haitian immigrants who lose their legal status, starting with the large population in Springfield, Ohio. The state's Republican governor, Mike DeWine, told CBS News on Monday he was not aware of those plans from DHS, and called any enforcement actions against Haitians a "mistake."Lower court stayThe exact timing of the loss of status is complicated by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., who has yet to apply the Supreme Court ruling in the case and lift an earlier stay that bars the administration from ending TPS for Haitians. A decision, potentially issuing another stay while the court hears other arguments, is expected this week. The U.S. Department of Justice has proposed a briefing schedule to continue arguments in the District of Columbia trial court, with the last brief due Nov. 6. Attorneys for Haitians with TPS plan to file a brief by Friday laying out their legal arguments in the wake of the high court's decision.Federal judges have paused TPS terminations for nationals from Burma, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Before the second Trump administration began last year, there were roughly 1.3 million immigrants on TPS hailing from 17 countries. Businesses, families in fluxImmigration advocates and business leaders have criticized the administration’s policy to revoke TPS.“Most adult TPS holders are active participants in the labor force, working in industries that already face persistent worker shortages,” Rebecca Shi, CEO of American Business Immigration Coalition Action, said in a statement. “Removing these workers doesn't just upend lives, it weakens industries that are already struggling to meet demand.”The Haitian Bridge Alliance, which advocates for Haitian TPS holders, said in a statement that the loss of deportation protections will lead to family separation, as many recipients have U.S. citizen children.“What we could witness will be one of the largest family separation events in modern day history,” the Haitian Bridge Alliance said.Other avenues closingSome TPS recipients can apply for another immigration status, such as asylum, though not all can apply or qualify. For example, noncitizens with TPS due to a natural disaster are unlikely to meet the criteria for asylum, which includes fear of persecution “on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion,” according to federal law. Additionally, the Trump administration issued a rule Tuesday that will allow for asylum officers to immediately send asylum seekers to appear before immigration judges without conducting an interview or including key evidence of the applicant's credibility, leading to a quick denial and deportation. The new rule, coupled with the loss of TPS, means that recipients are unlikely to have a strong chance of winning asylum claims. High court rulingLast month, the Supreme Court ruled that courts were barred from reviewing if the decision to end TPS designation made by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem followed the proper procedures.Even though the case was brought by TPS recipients from Haiti and Syria, the decision could also impact other TPS-related challenges to the Trump administration’s efforts to end the designation.Following the high court’s ruling, attorneys representing TPS recipients in courts across the country are amending their complaints. They argue that the termination of TPS status, including work authorization, is a violation of the U.S. Constitution’s 5th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which says the government cannot deprive a person of their “life, liberty or property” without following certain procedures. Lawyers have also argued that the TPS terminations were based on racial animus rather than because country conditions improved. They cite President Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign statements that falsely accused Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, of eating house pets.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Professor offers ‘modest proposal’ to accompany Mississippi’s Confederate Heritage Month
description: The Mississippi Legislature in 1890, the year a constitutional convention formed with the stated goal of disenfranchising Black people. Several provisions of that constitution have been the subject of lawsuits in recent years, most recently a requirement that statewide candidates capture a majority of state House districts to win election.
text:
This essay is part of Mississippi Today Ideas, a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share fact-based ideas about our state’s past, present and future. You can read more about the section here.

Gov. Tate Reeves is a big proponent of understanding and celebrating Mississippi’s history, sentiments that I heartily agree with. Take for example his recent Confederate Heritage Month proclamation, which mentions the importance of coming “to a full understanding that the lessons learned yesterday and today will carry us through tomorrow if we carefully and earnestly strive to understand and appreciate our heritage and our opportunities which lie before us.” 
Christopher Norment Credit: Courtesy photo
Although Gov. Reeves’ ambiguous language cleverly manages to say everything while simultaneously saying nothing, we still should ask what he means by urging Mississippians to “earnestly strive to understand and appreciate our heritage.”
After all, he is governor of a state that celebrates Robert E. Lee’s Birthday on the same day as Martin Luther King’s Birthday, Confederate Memorial Day and Jefferson Davis’ Birthday.
These state holidays are part of Mississippi’s heritage, along with its 1861 justification for secession from the Union, which includes the statement that “our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” A keen social analyst and purveyor of unintended irony, Reeves has proclaimed April as Confederate Heritage Month while also insisting that there is “not systemic racism in America”. 
But now to my modest proposal. Given Gov. Reeves’ appreciation for Mississippi’s history, I urge him to proclaim an annual “Jim Crow Heritage Month” as a companion to Confederate Heritage Month.
Identifying the most appropriate month for this recognition might require waiting until the GOP-dominated Mississippi Legislature redraws legislative districts to diminish Black voter power. Symbolically, though, November would be an excellent choice for Jim Crow Heritage Month, because in November of 1890 Mississippi adopted its post-Reconstruction constitution, which used a poll tax and literacy tests to disenfranchise Black voters. As the president of the convention, S. S. Calhoon said, “We came here to exclude the Negro. Nothing short of this will answer.” Consequently, the percentage of registered eligible Black voters in Mississippi decreased from 67% in 1867 to less than 6% in 1892. 
Now, that’s heritage.
Given the Supreme Court’s April 2026 Louisiana vs. Callais decision, one of the “opportunities that lie before us” – in terms of  Mississippi’s racial history – is the chance to suppress Black voting power throughout the South. According to the Supreme Court’s majority opinion in Callais, which was written by Justice Samuel Alito, “Because the Voting Rights Act of 1965 did not require Louisiana to create an additional majority-minority district, no compelling interest justified the state’s use of race … and that map is an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.”
Curiously, the Supreme Court’s Callais decision functionally implies that majority-white gerrymandered districts are constitutional, a form of fantastical legal logic that could lead to the end of multiracial democracy in the South.
This predication has been verified in Tennessee, where the state Legislature and governor quickly acted to gerrymander Memphis and eliminate the state’s only Black-majority congressional district – supposedly in the name of partisan politics, although the means and ends appear undeniably related to race in a state that celebrates Nathan Bedford Forrest Day, which honors the founder of the Ku Klux Klan.  Louisiana recently followed suit by eliminating one of two Black-majority congressional districts, while Alabama also is preparing to eradicate one of its two majority-Black congressional districts – a move that GOP governor Kay Ivey praised by observing that “For years, we have fought for this outcome, and I am proud to celebrate this win for Alabamians.” 
Well, some Alabamians. 
One small step for Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama, one giant step for the GOP in its quest to consolidate power in the South, with each state doing its best to channel Nina Simone’s lyrics to “Mississippi Goddam.”  
Bob Thompson (1937-1966), Homage to Nina Simone, 1965. oil on canvas. Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund, 89.83  © Estate of Bob Thompson, Courtesy of Michael Rosenfeld Gallery LLC, New York, NY Credit: Photo courtesy of Mississippi Museum of Art
Alabama and Tennessee (and Louisiana) have gotten me so upset, and Mississippi will likely follow.
Given Gov. Reeves’ politics and selective view of his state’s heritage, as illustrated by his 2013 speech to the Sons of Confederate Veterans, which he gave in front of an immense Confederate battle flag; the Republican-dominated state Legislature; and a pile on by GOP candidates for state offices, including Shad White (state auditor) and Michael Watson (secretary of state), it is likely that Mississippi will follow the lead of Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama, with Congressman Bennie Thompson’s district being an obvious target.
Poll taxes and literacy tests are out for the time being (bad optics, I suppose), but the effects of white-biased gerrymandering on Black voting power could be similar. 
Heritage, y’all. History and opportunity, right? So, how about November as Jim Crow Heritage Month in Mississippi? 
Of course, there is a different way forward for Mississippi, a possible future that pushes back against the state’s legacy of chattel slavery and Jim Crow laws, and its host of racist governors, from James K. Vardaman to Theodore Bilbo and Ross Barnett. Mississippi could refuse to follow the lead of Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama.
Instead, “A full (and truthful) understanding (of) the lessons learned yesterday and today” could invoke the heritage of Hiram Rhodes Revels (the first African American from Mississippi to serve in the U. S. Congress), Medgar Evers, James Meredith, the Freedom Riders, Robert Moses, Fannie Lou Hamer, William Winter and the Legislature’s 2020 decision to remove the Confederate battle flag from the state flag.
This noble and courageous heritage could propel Mississippi toward a more equable distribution of political, economic and social power. But that’s wishful thinking and appears unrelated to how Tate Reeves and the GOP leaders in Mississippi imagine the “heritage and … opportunities which lie before us.” 
So, cue Nina Simone. 

Bio: Christopher Norment holds a PhD in Systematics and Ecology from the University of Kansas and is an emeritus professor of environmental science and ecology at the State University of New York–Brockport. During his career he published over 50 peer-reviewed scientific papers and three science-related books of creative nonfiction, and received awards from the State University of New York for teaching and scholarship. He now lives in Jackson.

title: Douglas County sees continued rise in cyclospora infections
description: OMAHA — The number of parasite cyclospora infections among residents in Nebraska’s most populous county continues to climb — rising to 45 confirmed cases this past Saturday. That’s up from 27 confirmations as of just five days earlier. The Douglas County Health Department, in a media release Tuesday, said its investigation into the sudden increase continues[...]
text:
Nebraska's Douglas County Health Department on Monday notes a sudden rise in cyclospora infections among county residents. On July 17, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it has linked an outbreak of cyclosporiasis in five states to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taco Bell restaurants. (Photo courtesy Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)OMAHA — The number of parasite cyclospora infections among residents in Nebraska’s most populous county continues to climb — rising to 45 confirmed cases this past Saturday. That’s up from 27 confirmations as of just five days earlier.
The Douglas County Health Department, in a media release Tuesday, said its investigation into the sudden increase continues as federal health officials have now broadened their cyclospora outbreak probe to include nine states, up from five about a week ago. 
Nebraska is not yet officially part of the multistate outbreak involving about 2,000 people who reported getting sick, said Dr. Justin Frederick, Douglas County’s deputy health director. He said his team is working closely with the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. Food and Drug Administration to determine whether Douglas County illnesses are associated with the same contaminated iceberg lettuce identified in the federal investigation.
Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes the intestinal illness known as cyclosporiasis. Symptoms begin typically about a week after consuming contaminated food or water and typically include prolonged watery diarrhea, stomach cramps and nausea. The CDS says the number of people affected by the outbreak is likely much higher than the reported count, as many people recover without medical care and are not tested.
“Public health investigations evolve as new information becomes available,” said Frederick, also Douglas County’s chief of infectious disease epidemiology and preparedness. “Our priority is identifying the source of illness, preventing additional infections and keeping the public informed as the investigation progresses.”
Without treatment, illness can last for several weeks or months. 
The FDA has told consumers to avoid eating the shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico that has been recalled, county officials said.
People with questions can contact the Douglas County Health Department at 402.444.7471.

title: Indiana attorney general loses appeal in Haitian trafficking investigation
description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita can’t compel an Evansville manufacturer and migrant support group to cooperate with a human trafficking investigation in the absence of a specific allegation, the Indiana Court of Appeals ruled Monday. The three-judge panel’s opinion affirms an earlier ruling from the Vanderburgh Superior Court denying Rokita’s petition t[...]
text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita lost an appeal to compel Evansville manufacturer Berry Global and a migrant support group to cooperate with a migrant labor trafficking investigation. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita can’t compel an Evansville manufacturer and migrant support group to cooperate with a human trafficking investigation in the absence of a specific allegation, the Indiana Court of Appeals ruled Monday.
The three-judge panel’s opinion affirms an earlier ruling from the Vanderburgh Superior Court denying Rokita’s petition to enforce civil investigative demands against Berry Global Group and the Haitian Center of Evansville in a 2024 trafficking investigation.
Judge Nancy H. Vaidik, who authored the opinion, found the attorney general’s demands were “unauthorized, invalid and unenforceable” due to a lack of particularized evidence.
“The record makes clear that the Attorney General is at most trawling for evidence of wrongdoing — looking for information that might eventually trigger an investigation, based on his alleged concern that someone, somewhere might be involved in labor trafficking,” she wrote.
Story continues below.
Opinion (13)
 
The attorney general issued the investigative demands, or CIDs, seeking documents and formal written responses from officials at Berry Global and the Haitian Center in November 2024 as part of a purported labor trafficking investigation, but neither complied.
Petitions to compel cooperation cited the increased arrival of migrants and refugees “vulnerable to human trafficking and forced labor,” but did not identify a specific suspect, victim or incident justifying an investigation, the court found.











Instead, the attorney general’s office claimed it had reasonable cause because Berry Global “is a large, sophisticated employer that actively recruits refugees and migrants and works with various migrant resettlement nonprofits” and support groups like the Haitian Center, according to the opinion.











Asked in trial court, state attorneys could not identify a suspect or act of human trafficking either, according to the opinion.
The court held that allowing Rokita to enforce CIDs in the absence of a specific suspect or allegation would violate First and Fourth Amendment protections and burden business.
Indiana law “authorizes the issuance of a CID only if an ‘investigation’ is being conducted,” Vaidik wrote in her opinion Monday.
“For an investigation to exist, there must be a factual predicate — an articulable reason to suspect that particular wrongdoing may be afoot. A mere hunch will not suffice. Here, the Attorney General has not shown that he has information of any sort, he is searching for something to investigate. Therefore, the CIDs issued to Berry Global and the Haitian Center were unauthorized, invalid and unenforceable.”
A spokesperson for the Office of Attorney General said the agency is evaluating the decision as it considers next steps for the investigations.
Thousands of Haitians living in Indiana under temporary protected status this week lost their work authorization after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to revoke TPS.

name: Michigan Advance
title: State of the Race: Democratic U.S. Senate race pits old guard, vanguard in battle for party’s soul
description: In August, Michigan Democrats will once again be asked to vote in a bellwether statewide election that could also determine the future electoral prospects of the national party. Whether voters choose the progressive Abdul El-Sayed or center-left U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham on the Aug. 4 ballot could be a key determinant for whether […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, left, and former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, right, participate in a U.S. Senate candidate debate during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)In August, Michigan Democrats will once again be asked to vote in a bellwether statewide election that could also determine the future electoral prospects of the national party.
Whether voters choose the progressive Abdul El-Sayed or center-left U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham on the Aug. 4 ballot could be a key determinant for whether Democrats or Republicans control the upper chamber of Congress for the next two years. 
It could also reveal how purple of a state Michigan really is. Voters in the Great Lakes State last elected a Republican U.S. senator in 1994. However, the lone Republican in the race, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake, is endorsed by President Donald Trump and seen as the GOP’s best bet for beating the Democrats’ 25-year lock on Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat.
Democratic voters’ decision on whether they’ll send El-Sayed — who they rejected in his 2018 gubernatorial run in favor of Gretchen Whitmer — or Stevens into the ring with Rogers in November will ultimately be a decision on which kind of candidate they want in that fight. 
Gretchen Whitmer quickly becomes Haley Stevens’s most prominent ally after a late game endorsement

El-Sayed has run as one of the race’s most progressive candidates, endorsed by progressives including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens, meanwhile, has drawn support from nearly every corner of the Democratic Party establishment, from Whitmer to the retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, who Stevens is seeking to replace.
The choice between the two may also have implications in the national debate over which faction rules the Democratic Party.
“It is certainly going to be seen that way nationally,” Matt Grossmann, a political scientist, author and director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research, told Michigan Advance. “This would be the first test of, ‘well, this succeeded in a swing state.’ Or it will be taken as a sign that swing state victories are harder. People do have some concerns about the electability of further left candidates.”
That was especially true in Michigan, as the candidates are most clearly reflective of the factions they represent.
“A victory will not happen without a massive African American advantage for Stevens, so it would play into the traditional problems that the left has as being identified as the white part of the party, or at least one that has trouble, especially, with African American voters,” Grossmann added. “But El-Sayed has overperformed expectations in terms of not just demonstrating excitement and support, but in being able to appeal to a broader range of voters than when he ran for governor.”
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Both candidates are raising big dollars in the final stretch
The August primary will also test the role of big money in politics in a heated intraparty contest.
Federal Election Commission filings show both campaigns are well-funded heading into the Aug. 4 primary. Between April 1 and June 30, El-Sayed raised $4.57 million and spent $4.37 million, leaving him with $2.7 million cash on hand. Stevens raised $2.09 million, spent $2.06 million and reported $3.41 million in the bank. Pre-primary filings covering July 1-15 show Stevens had $2.79 million cash on hand after raising $920,859 and spending $1.54 million, while El-Sayed reported $2.55 million after raising $2.3 million and spending $2.48 million.
Outside groups have spent at least $47 million on the race, with the vast majority benefiting Stevens. Nearly $24 million has been spent to support the congresswoman, including more than $9.7 million from the AIPAC-affiliated United Democracy Project and $12.9 million from A Stronger Michigan PAC. 
Outside groups have spent about $2.5 million supporting El-Sayed, while nearly $10 million has been spent opposing him—almost all of it from the United Democracy Project — which is directly connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
Even in the face of steep spending disadvantage, Grossmann said that El-Sayed has shown strong fundraising support to fight against Stevens-backed outside spending. It also shows that Stevens’ campaign has not manufactured an effective negative narrative against him.
“I think all those things make it harder for the money to matter,” Grossmann added. “That said, it still is the case that outspending is associated with success in primaries. It does matter if the electorate is buying the message that’s been sent with all the money.”
AIPAC’s spending in the race, however, has been a clear advantage for Stevens in terms of media access. As of last week, AIPAC through United Democracy Project told the FEC that it had purchased $4.87 million in advertising for the final week of the race. The group has also spent a quarter of a million dollars on direct mail against El-Sayed as of July 21. 
Both of those purchases pushed United Democracy Project’s spending in the primary past $24 million, funding additional resources to boost Haley and target El-Sayed.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens holds an output carrier at the General Motors Romulus Propulsion Systems plant. May 9, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
AIPAC becomes a major faultline in Michigan
The debate over whether AIPAC should have such sway on American elections has been particularly fierce in Michigan.
Grossmann said that Michigan was a major battleground for that debate mostly due to the state’s large Arab and Muslim population. 
A wide swath of Arab and Muslim Michiganders voted uncommitted in the 2024 primary in protest of former President Joe Biden for supporting Israel in its war with Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks that left more than a thousand Israeli citizens and other civilians dead and more than 250 people kidnapped by Hamas fighters. While it had no real effect on Biden in the primary, many of those voters swung to support President Donald Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris, who became the nominee after Biden dropped out.
Stevens’ connection to AIPAC could swing those voters toward El-Sayed in the 2026 primary, giving him a powerful hedge to the strong Black vote that Stevens is likely to net in Southeast Michigan.
Progressives have been more forceful in making the case to move support away from Israel, causing another liability for Stevens, who is very much aligned with Israel in its foreign policy. AIPAC’s spending on Stevens has only bolstered those associations.
“There’s all kinds of places where you know AIPAC has come in, and they want to attack El Sayed, but that’s not really the main story,” Grossmann said. “The story is that this is the most AIPAC identified candidate that is available, and long standing and not trying to run away from it.”
A cautionary tale of Democrats supporting Israel 
AIPAC most notably began supporting Stevens during the 2022 primary race she ran against former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin after the pair were placed into the same district when new congressional maps were drawn. Levin, who is Jewish, favors a two-state solution between Palestine and Israel, saying that while he firmly supports Jewish statehood, Israeli military occupation of Palestinians has been toxic to both sides. 
Levin, who has endorsed El-Sayed, told the Advance that despite holding views shared by Republican and Democratic presidential administrations alike, AIPAC went on the attack.
“That was obviously unacceptable to AIPAC,” he said. “The irony is that this particular position isn’t that radical. This is important — this is a Jewish thing to me. Thirty-six times in the Torah it says, in one version or the other, to treat the other as you want to be treated. If you’re serious as a Jew and the obligations of theology, if you’re honest, the ‘other’ to the Jewish people, especially for the Jewish state, is the Palestinian people.”
Rep. Andy Levin on the night he lost his primary to Halay Stevens, Aug. 2, 2022 | Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance
As AIPAC has continued to heavily back Stevens this year, Levin has campaigned with El-Sayed, who has called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel, supporting Palestinian statehood and curbing AIPAC’s influence in American politics.
Levin also said AIPAC would likely be comfortable with either Stevens or Rogers winning in November.
Pro-Israel groups, donors and many Democratic supporters have often equated opposition to military aid for Israel or criticism of its war in Gaza with antisemitism. Levin rejected that view.
“This whole thing about antisemitism and criticism of Israel gets so mixed up in ways that are really harmful to both,” Levin said. “I’m pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel. To most people, Zionism means support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his policies, and it’s horrifying, right? I agree with all that. But if you want to go back to the very basics of Zionism as the idea that the Jewish people have a right to self-determination in the Holy Land, I’ll go all the way there, too.”
All guns blazing as the race winds down
Aside from the AIPAC controversy, the race overall was mostly cordial during the year-long buildup to the Aug. 4 contest. Attacks between El-Sayed and Stevens have only intensified, however, since fellow Democrat, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), suspended her campaign earlier this month. Her name will still appear on the ballot.
Stevens has focused her attack lines on the fact that El-Sayed’s net worth is more than $1 million, painting him as a hypocrite for attacking the wealthy on the campaign trail. That was confirmed Monday when El-Sayed finally released his financial disclosures, showing his net worth could total as much as $2.1 million, which Stevens used as an attack line in the pair’s final debate.
“You talk about getting money out of politics and putting money in people’s pockets, but still no one knows who’s putting the money in your pocket,” Stevens said, referencing close to $300,000 El-Sayed listed as “other income.”
El-Sayed’s campaign has focused on Stevens’ connections to corporate funding and her AIPAC backing and argues she has misled voters by emphasizing her ties to former President Barack Obama.
Stevens’ team has invoked Obama throughout the primary and her association with his auto industry rescue efforts during the late 2000s recession. Mailers from outside supporters of Stevens’ campaign have drawn connections to past support from Obama, even though he has not officially endorsed her in 2026. There has been much debate over whether those mailers were a deceptive tactic to convince Black voters that Obama was backing Stevens.
El-Sayed’s campaign noted another recent example of Stevens’ campaign potentially misleading voters when it sent out a notice designed to appear as though it came from El-Sayed’s campaign, touting an endorsement from Rogers, even though it came directly from Stevens’ communications office.
El-Sayed wants the FEC to investigate the email as potentially violating federal election law. Stevens spokesperson Joetta Appiah told the Advance that it was simply a parody.
Email sent by the Hayley Stevens campaign designed to look like an endorsement alert from Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign. El-Sayed has asked for an FEC investigation into its creation.
 
All things considered, Grossmann said he doesn’t believe the race is as dirty as it could have been. As Stevens calls El-Sayed a major liability against Rogers in the fall, Grossmann said the attacks show how much of a threat he is to Stevens’ shot at winning the nomination.
“It’s harder to make that argument when it seems like a last ditch effort,” Grossmann said of Stevens throwing everything her campaign had at El-Sayed to blunt him before Aug. 4.
Mike Rogers patiently waits in the wings
Meanwhile, Rogers’ campaign is watching this all unfold with good feelings about the divisions within the Democratic Party with a little more than three months until the general election.
Rogers — who lost his 2024 race against current U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) — has faced no real primary challenge and is waiting in the wings for his opponent, raising steady cash for the race ahead. Rogers’ pre-primary FEC filing shows that he has $4.41 million cash on hand.
“Mike Rogers is happy,” Grossmann said. “It wasn’t initially a top-tier Senate race for Republicans because people assumed that if it was a Democrat year, Michigan would be trending toward the Democrats. Now, I think it will be a top-tier Senate race because if El-Sayed wins, he’ll be viewed as more vulnerable, and if Stevens wins, she’ll be viewed as having trouble coalescing support from her own party, even in the general election.”
Both of those scenarios are likely being viewed as net positives for Rogers’ campaign.
“Right now, Republicans are already gearing up to spend a lot more in this race than they otherwise would have,” Grossmann said. “They’ve moved it up in the potential for contests they can win. Stevens is making a big deal out of the fact that Rogers said he was happy to run against El-Sayed, and I think that is sincerely the case.”
Although Stevens has yet to win a statewide race, she did flip the former 11th Congressional District seat away from Republicans in the 2018 bid that sent her to Congress. She has consistently won in subsequent races, and won perhaps her toughest contest in 2020 against Republican Eric Esshaki — Stevens won by a little more than 2 percentage points.
El-Sayed has also never won a statewide race, let alone any electoral victory, putting him at a disadvantage against Rogers, who served two terms in the Michigan Senate and seven terms in Congress representing his mid-Michigan district.
“This has been a race where people will have a harder time buying that disadvantage,” Grossmann noted. “Even if they did buy that, there’s a general trend that shows they wouldn’t necessarily believe it. Mike Rogers’ campaign does believe that it’s true.”
Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake) walks with his wife Kristi Rogers after he filed signatures in Lansing in his bid for the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate. April 17, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance
‘Don’t let history repeat itself’
Either way, the Democratic Party will have to reckon with the possibility that too much bad blood has been spilled during the primary race, and that both Stevens and El-Sayed will move into the general election as wounded warriors. Not only will the party need to bridge divides between progressives and establishment forces who have been at each other’s throats online, it will need to focus on the task at hand; beating Rogers in November.
State Rep. Tyrone Carter (D-Detroit), who is firmly behind Stevens, has been a surrogate for the congresswoman appearing at some of her more recent Detroit events. Following a meet-and-greet event organized in Detroit just hours after Whitmer endorsed Stevens, Carter told the Advance that the divisions among Michigan Democrats is a real concern if they want to hold their 30-year streak of electing only Democrats to the U.S. Senate.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’ve watched it before,” Carter said. “I hate to say it, but labels do matter when you have different factions of the Democratic Party, the socialists, the progressives working in Lansing with them. It cannot be all or nothing.”
Carter said control of Congress was ultimately at stake.
“Compromise within your own party is not a bad word because getting the gavel is what matters,” Carter said, reflecting on the Democratic trifecta that party commanded in the state Legislature during the 2023-24 session. “I know what it’s like not to have a gavel for four years, and to get the gavel and be able to move the agenda on some things. Watching little kids eat breakfast at school, that’s huge. That wouldn’t have happened. We put all of our differences aside.
“Even the uncommitted understand what uncommitted did to communities. If they did get a lesson from what ‘uncommitted’ meant, it is: Don’t let history repeat itself.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas governor votes, celebrates first time in 22 years she’s not on the ballot
description: TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly voted Tuesday morning, offering a laughing “halleleujah” when she was asked about seeing a ballot that didn’t have her name on it.  “I have told you that I would never run again for an office, and, other than school board, I’m going to stick to that,” she said. “I will […]
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly fills out a ballot July 28, 2026, voting early in the Kansas primary election on Aug. 4. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector) TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly voted Tuesday morning, offering a laughing “halleleujah” when she was asked about seeing a ballot that didn’t have her name on it. 
“I have told you that I would never run again for an office, and, other than school board, I’m going to stick to that,” she said. “I will see how that goes as time goes on. This is the first time I voted in 22 years, 23 years, my name has not been on the ballot, and it’s nice.”
Kelly spoke to reporters after voting at the Shawnee County Election Office. She began her political career in 2004 when she was elected to the state Senate, and then was elected as governor in 2018 and 2022.  
Kelly said she cast a vote for gubernatorial candidate Ethan Corson, whom she formally endorsed in November. Corson and Cindy Holscher, both state senators from Johnson County, as well as Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog, are competing in the Aug. 4 primary for the Democratic nomination for governor.
Gov. Laura Kelly speaks to reporters after voting in the Kansas primary election on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Kelly said this election cycle has been different than the last two when she ran for office. During those campaigns, she highlighted the effect former Gov. Sam Brownback had on the state. 
Today, she said, candidates are looking at the influence of the federal government on Kansas. 
“Our problems are really coming from the federal government and a lot of the policies that the Trump administration is forcing down on states,” she said. “That’s impacting a lot of people, really taking away a lot of our autonomy as a state to make our own decisions about things.” 
Many of the decisions also are “cruelly” taking funds the state uses to build roads, and take care of people who are elderly and disabled, Kelly said. 
“It’s important, at this point, to be fighting back bad, and to know that whoever becomes governor will fight back and stand up for Kansas,” she said.
