name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Lawmakers, workers plan to keep pushing for Pennsylvania to raise the minimum wage
description: State Sen. Christine Tartaglione (D-Philadelphia) rises at the end of every legislative session with one message for lawmakers.  “It’s been 7,309 days since Pennsylvania last raised the minimum wage,” she said at the end of the session on July 12, immediately after the legislature passed this year’s budget without a wage increase.  “This year marked […]
text:
Pennsylvania Department of Human Services (DHS) Secretary Dr. Val Arkoosh speaks during a press conference announcing an increase in funding for direct care workers on April 21, 2026. (Photo from PACast)State Sen. Christine Tartaglione (D-Philadelphia) rises at the end of every legislative session with one message for lawmakers. 
“It’s been 7,309 days since Pennsylvania last raised the minimum wage,” she said at the end of the session on July 12, immediately after the legislature passed this year’s budget without a wage increase. 
“This year marked 20 years — 20 years — since Pennsylvania last raised its minimum wage,” Tartaglione told the chamber. “Twenty years of rising rent, rising grocery bills, rising utility costs, rising healthcare expenses. Twenty years in which every one of our neighboring states recognized that working people deserve better.” 
Pennsylvania’s minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since a federally mandated increase in 2009. The state hasn’t raised it on its own since 2006, when Tartaglione negotiated a bill raising the wage to $7.15. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
All of its neighboring states, from West Virginia to New York, have raised their wages higher than the federal minimum in that time. 
“The system is not set up to help the working class anymore,” said Lynn Weidner, a home care worker from Allentown. She makes $16.26 an hour as a paid caregiver for her partner, who has cerebral palsy. She’s also an unpaid caregiver for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s disease. 
Caregivers like Weidner only get a wage increase if they receive money from the state budget. The 2025-2026 spending plan included a $21 million increase in funding for direct home care workers, which allowed workers like Weidner to receive a pay hike. 
There is no such increase in this year’s spending plan, meaning caregivers won’t be getting another raise. And while they’re making above minimum wage — largely thanks to the lobbying efforts of their unions — they still struggle with basic needs, and some make too much to qualify for certain state and federal benefits. 
Caregivers are not alone in their struggles to make ends meet. According to the state Department of Labor and Industry’s most recent minimum wage report, just under 43,000 workers across the commonwealth made $7.25 or less in 2025. 
Over 510,000 others made between $7.26 and $15 an hour — all well below Pennsylvania’s average living wage, which is over $22 an hour. 
Legislative efforts
Tartaglione was sworn in as a state senator in 1995 and introduced her first minimum wage legislation that year. It never advanced to a full vote. 
“I have introduced one every session for the past 32 years,” she said. She’s been reminding senators how long it has been since a wage increase on the floor of the Senate since before Gov. Josh Shapiro took office.
Sen. Christine Tartaglione (D-Philadelphia) speaks at a press conference on raising the minimum wage on June 30, 2026 (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
This year’s legislation proposed a gradual increase of the minimum wage, peaking at $15 an hour by 2029, and incorporated an annual cost of living increase starting in 2030. It passed the state House in March but never advanced from the Senate Labor & Industry Committee. 
Tartaglione called the minimum wage a “moral issue,” emphasizing the economic benefits of ensuring working-class constituents have a stable, living income. 
As the cost of living and inflation continue to increase, workers are struggling to live comfortably, even as Tartaglione said Senate Republicans have alleged “nobody’s making $7.25 an hour anyway.” 
“My comeback is, ‘Well, tell that to my single mother who’s working three jobs because she needs to pay rent, she needs to put food on the table,’” she said. “How about the people that sweep the streets? How about the people that serve you the food when you go somewhere? They’re all making $7.25 an hour. And we’re telling them they’re not important.” 
Shapiro has been vocal about his desire to raise Pennsylvania’s minimum wage, making it a legislative priority in each of his budget addresses during his first term as governor. 
But each year’s measure has stalled in the Republican-controlled Senate. Democratic lawmakers from both chambers have expressed frustration with their GOP counterparts and emphasized that raising the wage remains a legislative priority. 
“It’s shameful that Pennsylvania Senate Republicans have refused to raise the minimum wage for decades while every state around us has done so,” Alex Peterson, a spokesperson for Shapiro, wrote in a statement. “The Governor will continue to stand up for the working women and men of Pennsylvania and calls on Senate Republicans to put this up for a vote.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On the Senate floor on June 30, Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) said he has “made it very clear publicly and privately that we are prepared to talk about meeting in the middle” to raise the wage. 
Tartaglione said that in conversations with Pittman, “he says maybe $11 [or] $12 an hour” could be a reasonable minimum wage compromise that could pass both legislative chambers. 
Pittman’s office did not respond to a request for comment for this story. 
Workers’ struggles continue
Suzzanne Ott, a caregiver who lives in Venango County, received a wage increase earlier this year. She was previously making $12.91 an hour — above minimum wage, but not enough to make ends meet. 
“It makes it hard for people to survive,” she said. “If we make enough that we’re over welfare, we don’t get food stamps, we don’t get medical [care]. So sometimes it comes to a point where it’s like ‘Oh, I can’t go to the doctor because my kids need food.’”
Caregiver Suzzanne Ott speaks during a press conference on April 21, 2026. (Photo from PACast)
Ott now earns $17.50 an hour, which she said has made a big difference in how she and her family live, from being able to pay bills on time to saving money for the first time in years. 
“I’ve made so many sacrifices in the last few months,” she said. “Everything isn’t perfect for me. But it’s a lot better than it was.” 
Weidner agreed — noting her wage increase helped her keep her health insurance. But, she said she and many other workers are still struggling.  
Some, who got a raise but still make under $15 an hour, have been disqualified from Medicaid and face high prices from Pennie, the state health insurance, Weidner said. 
“Workers lost their health insurance because of the lack of subsidies, and we’re in this weird limbo area of not making enough but making a little too much to get any assistance,” she said. 
Tartaglione urged Republicans to vote on minimum wage legislation for the sake of Pennsylvania workers.
“Everyone deserves to make a livable wage,” Ott said. “Raising the minimum wage doesn’t make it a livable wage.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: As federal teen pregnancy prevention grants get cut, efforts in Ohio try to keep helping
description: The federal government is taking swipes at funding for teen pregnancy prevention, causing concerns in Ohio and elsewhere as advocates attempt to keep helping teens. The cuts are also bringing about discussion when it comes to teens who are already parents. Rosemary Oglesby-Henry was a teen mom herself three decades ago, and from what she’s […]
text:
Getty Images.The federal government is taking swipes at funding for teen pregnancy prevention, causing concerns in Ohio and elsewhere as advocates attempt to keep helping teens.
The cuts are also bringing about discussion when it comes to teens who are already parents.
Rosemary Oglesby-Henry was a teen mom herself three decades ago, and from what she’s seen, not a lot has changed in terms of the perception of teen pregnancy.
“I chose to parent, and when I chose to parent there were no resources to teach me how to be a mother,” she told the Capital Journal.
In 2016, Oglesby-Henry founded Rosemary’s Babies Company, a Cincinnati-based nonprofit aimed at helping teen parents learn not only parenting skills, but also how to reach educational goals, gain workforce skills, and delay having further children.
The founder and CEO hopes to be part of the supports that might not be as needed down the road.
“Basically saying okay, we understand you have a child, but … you can still go back to school, you can wait until you build your family to have another child, and in that way you’re getting back on target so that you’re not dependent on the government, and you don’t end up on that economic cliff, especially our young girls” she said.
Rosemary’s Babies is a donor-based nonprofit that also receives state funding, something that she said is hard to get in the area of teen pregnancy support, but means the most when it comes to bolstering a population that is often weighed down by trauma, abuse, and a lack of other supports, including sex education.
“It helps to reduce the stigma, so that organizations like my own can now seek out support in saying, ‘I don’t promote teen pregnancy, but once these young people have these children, we need to help them before they get caught up in the system,” Oglesby-Henry said.
The U.S. Health and Human Services agency recently announced a plan to cancel 53 of 67 grants meant for the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program, amounting to about $68 million in eliminated funding.
Federal health agency cancels most of its teen pregnancy prevention grants

Stateline reported that President Donald Trump took a similar action in his first term, changing grant funding for more than 80 recipients, before a judge stopped the action, ruling in favor of legal advocacy group Democracy Forward in a lawsuit claiming agency regulations violations.
The most recent actions are also the subject of a lawsuit, with Democracy Forward again among the parties suing the Trump administration to stop the cuts.
Nationwide Children’s Hospital’s research institute was named as one of the federal grant recipients between 2020 to 2023, receiving more than $860,000 for a program called “Changing the Landscape for Adolescent Health Equity and Access in Central Ohio,” according to the HHS website.
Representatives for the hospital were unavailable for comment.
Nationwide Children’s still houses a Teen and Pregnant Program, which provides prenatal and postpartum care for pregnant women up to age 21.
According to the program’s website, the Teen Pregnancy Clinic allows pregnant individuals to meet with medical professionals, participate in group meetings, learn about infant care and sign up for public programs including federal food assistance, and receive education on birth control for the future.
According to the Health and Human Services agency’s own data in an objective it calls “Healthy People 2030,” babies born to teen mothers “are more likely to be premature, have a low birth weight, and even to die.”
“Having a baby can also negatively impact teen mothers’ health and their educational and job opportunities,” the HHS data states. “Although teen pregnancy and birth rates have gone down in recent years, disparities by race/ethnicity remain.”
The department also states “evidence shows that a variety of outreach and educational programs can help reduce teen pregnancies.”
State data from 2024 showed 69 babies born in Ohio to mothers who were younger than 15, more than 1,300 who were born to individuals aged 15 to 17, and nearly 4,000 who were born to mothers who were 18 to 19 years old.
The most recent state data is still considered preliminary, according to the Ohio Department of Health’s database, but 2025 numbers showed 52 children born to Ohioans younger than 15, and more than 1,000 born to children between the ages of 15 and 17. Those aged 18 to 19 represented more than 3,700 births in 2025.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The CDC’s most recent data on teen births is from 2024. Ohio’s teen birth rate in that year was 14 per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, down slightly from the year before, when it was 14.6 per 1,000 female Ohioans.
Funding related to teen pregnancy is also part of state grant efforts, particularly through the program established by Gov. Mike DeWine, called the Governor’s Office of Faith-Based and Community Initiatives.
The money historically comes from federal and state contributions to the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program (TANF).
The Ohio General Assembly’s most recent operating budget allowed up to $26.8 million for the governor’s office initiatives over 2026 and 2027.
A spokesperson for DeWine did not specifically comment when asked about the cuts to federal teen pregnancy prevention programs, but said the governor’s office and the state Office of Budget and Management “continuously monitor federal funding decisions throughout the year.”
The most recent executive order from DeWine directing TANF dollars for 2026 and 2027 said one of the purposes of the TANF program was to “prevent and reduce the incidence of out-of-wedlock pregnancies and establish annual numerical goals for preventing and reducing the incidence of these pregnancies.”
Following the most recent cuts, HHS put out new grant programs, called “Replicating Effective Teen Pregnancy Prevention Programs,” and “Rigorous Impact Evaluation of Programs to Prevent Teen Pregnancy and Achieve Optimal Health,” according to the agency’s website.
The Trump administration also plans to put money toward abstinence education and an emphasis on marriage, with grant application language similar to concepts supported by conservative groups, which discourage contraception, among other ideas.
  Sex education and the ‘success sequence’ 
The state has been criticized for lacking a standardized sex education program over the years, which advocates say contributes to the teen pregnancy rate.
The sex education advocacy group SIECUS gave Ohio a failing grade in a national ranking of state sex ed programs.
The group decried the newest development in the state’s sex education program, called the “success sequence,” which requires school to teach students that they should graduate high school, get a job, and get married, consecutively, before having a baby.
Under the new law, the “success sequence” would be a graduation requirement.
A 2021 study commissioned by the federal Health and Human Services agency found that though completing high school, getting a full-time job, and getting married did make people less likely to experience poverty, the order of events was not necessarily important.
“For the association between milestones and economic self-sufficiency at ages 35-40, our results suggest that the individual milestones, regardless of sequence, appear to be the main factors associated with economic outcomes in adulthood,” the study stated.
For Oglesby-Henry, the information provided through the “success sequence” and other measures can be helpful, even just as a conversation starter.
“It teaches about economics and the impact that happens when we make these decisions, and it teaches about consequences,” she said.
But there still needs to be lessons at higher levels about the consequences of promoting pregnancy without providing the support that’s needed.
“As this administration is pushing the need for families to have more babies and things such as that, we have to evaluate, okay, can people afford daycare if we’re cutting benefits, can people afford housing,” Oglesby-Henry said.
Having just opened Holloway House for housing support, workforce training, and other programs for teen parents, the founder of Rosemary’s Babies is attempting to strike at an increase in homelessness among young mothers as well, making funding even more important.
“We’re looking at how can we continue to assist these families, where, if we get them through our program, we get the training that this administration is (encouraging) … but when they complete all of that, they can’t afford housing, or they can’t still afford to live,” Oglesby-Henry said.
Support for teens who are pregnant and prevention for the future isn’t easily funded, she said, but education and the money to continue that education will bring about more results.
“Prevention always costs less than the actual epidemic or the actual problem,” according to Oglesby-Henry.

title: Advocates puzzled after HIV is left off of Georgia’s ‘medically frail’ list for Medicaid work rules
description: Low-income Georgians living with HIV would not be counted as “medically frail” under a state proposal still under consideration and would therefore have to satisfy work requirements to qualify for Medicaid coverage. As of now, state officials plan to exclude HIV from a list of medical conditions that would exempt Georgians from Medicaid work requirements, […[...]
text:
State officials did not include HIV to a list of conditions that exempts low-income Georgians from work requirements for Medicaid coverage. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderLow-income Georgians living with HIV would not be counted as “medically frail” under a state proposal still under consideration and would therefore have to satisfy work requirements to qualify for Medicaid coverage.
As of now, state officials plan to exclude HIV from a list of medical conditions that would exempt Georgians from Medicaid work requirements, and that omission has been met with concerns from Georgia health advocates. 
The new proposed state policy is aimed at aligning Georgia’s Pathways to Coverage, a partial Medicaid-expansion with work requirement components, with new federal changes to Medicaid eligibility that were included in President Donald Trump’s tax break and spending cuts package that passed last year. A waiver authorizing the Pathways to Coverage program’s work requirement is set to expire at the end of this year, and the new federal work requirement takes effect early next year.
States gird for new Medicaid ‘medically frail’ rule

Under Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance released in June, able-bodied adults must complete 80 hours of work, community service or education per month to keep their healthcare coverage, something that is already required in Georgia. 
But now the state will have to provide exemptions to people deemed “medically frail,” with the federal government’s guidance specifically citing HIV/AIDS alongside cancer, end-stage renal disease and sickle cell disease as potential examples of medical conditions states could include.
The Georgia Department of Community Health released its proposed rule in July, with one list of conditions that automatically qualifies a recipient and another list of conditions that will be considered on a more case-by-case basis. 
When Georgia Equality executive director Jeff Graham saw the proposal, he said he was perplexed. He said in an interview that the state’s program that helps people living with HIV access their medication struggles financially, and ensuring this population has access to Medicaid could help lower those costs. He also said that excluding HIV could worsen health outcomes with increased hospitalizations and emergency care.
“Ultimately the state of Georgia would save money by having more people living with HIV having access to Medicaid,” Graham said. “And again, by being able to ensure that there are the needed exemptions from the community engagement criteria or the work requirements, as people really know it, is not just good for people living with HIV, it would clearly be in the best interest financially for the state of Georgia.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A public comment period ended on July 21, and the DCH board will consider those comments at its Aug. 13 meeting, where they can make changes to the rule before voting to approve it.
In a letter submitted during the public comment period, Metropolitan Atlanta HIV Health Services Planning Council, an advisory body established by federal law, asked the state agency to add HIV to the list of conditions that automatically exempt a person from work requirements.
“We do not raise this as a question of state policy preference. We raise it as a question of the correct application of a federal standard,” Graham and Daniel Griffin, chair of the Metro Atlanta HIV Health Services Planning Council, wrote in the letter.
25 Democratic-led states sue Trump administration over Medicaid work requirements

According to the letter, “Georgia continues to be at the epicenter of the ongoing epidemic in the United States,” with 2,485 people newly diagnosed with HIV in 2024, the most recent year with available data. A total of 66,896 Georgians are living with HIV.
Fiona Roberts, spokesperson for the department, said they “are reviewing the public comments and will address any changes to the public notice at our next Board meeting.” 
Despite these concerns, changes to the state program under the new federal law may still lead to more Georgians being covered by Medicaid.
While the new federal changes could decrease coverage in states that have fully expanded Medicaid, especially for the ill and disabled, those changes could actually expand coverage in Georgia, according to Leah Chan, director of health justice at the left-leaning Georgia Budget and Policy Institute.
The state’s Pathways to Coverage program, which has only enrolled about 30,000 Georgians since 2023, according to a GBPI tracker, currently doesn’t have exemptions for those considered medically frail. Its current exemptions for work requirements, like being a parent to a Medicaid-enrolled child under the age six, are more narrow than the federal guidance. Under the new exemptions, parents of Medicaid-enrolled children under 13 are exempt from work requirements, as well as those who were formerly in foster care.
“One of the biggest opportunities for more Georgians to get access to healthcare is some of these other exclusions that are more broad,” Chan said. “Those are just broader categories that more people fit under.”
Laura Colbert, executive director for Georgians for a Healthy Future, a patient advocacy group that advocates for full Medicaid expansion, said that some of the changes the state proposed will decrease some of the paperwork challenges people face, calling those “smart choices” by state officials. 
But she said she is worried about what the state has not included in its proposal, like information about the process the state used to update the medically frail list or how the department will communicate with people affected by these changes.
“Right now, the public has not seen that plan,” Colbert said. “DCH’s board will vote on this rule without knowing whether and how the people it affects will receive the information they need.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Here’s how the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative got politicians from both parties on board
description: In a time of political polarization, it’s easy to forget that the vast majority of Americans of all backgrounds and beliefs — 80% or more, depending on the poll — value environmental conservation. However, this support is not easily or often translated into successful, popular initiatives. One success story is the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative. Since […[...]
text:
Lake Erie from Kelley's Island. (File photo from Getty Images)
In a time of political polarization, it’s easy to forget that the vast majority of Americans of all backgrounds and beliefs — 80% or more, depending on the poll — value environmental conservation. However, this support is not easily or often translated into successful, popular initiatives.
One success story is the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative. Since 2010, it has provided over US$5 billion to improve the quality of the region’s environment, with an overarching goal of cleaning up the water in the Great Lakes watershed. And it has survived multiple attempts to reduce its funding or eliminate it altogether.
As a water policy and politics expert and a former leader in the Great Lakes advocacy community who has worked on and analyzed the initiative, I worked with environmental historian and Great Lakes expert Marc Gaden along with a team of graduate students to comprehensively assess the initiative and determine useful lessons learned for other projects in conservation and beyond.
 A bit of background

The Great Lakes contain approximately 20% of the world’s available surface freshwater, providing drinking water to over 40 million people in the U.S. and Canada and billions of dollars annually in economic activity and ecological productivity.
Throughout most of the 20th century, the ecosystem in and around the lakes was degraded and contaminated due to raw sewage, industrial waste, invasive species, loss of natural habitats and runoff pollution from development, among other issues.
Many problems remained even after the major environmental and Great Lakes laws of the late 20th century took effect. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has funded more than 8,000 specific projects, focusing on cleaning up especially toxic locations, controlling invasive species, restoring natural habitat and educating the next generation of leaders.
Government reports, public opinion polls, economic analysis and many other accounts suggest that the initiative has not only been successfully implemented and popular but has led to positive results for water quality, habitat restoration and wildlife while boosting the local and regional economy.
 Deep connection

But these results didn’t happen by accident, and they weren’t inevitable. Our research team identified converging forces, some unique to the Great Lakes but many broadly applicable, that led to this success.
Underlying each force is the iconic status of the waters themselves. People in the region feel a deep attachment to the lakes and the quality of life they enable, with more than 50% of residents engaging in walking/hiking, swimming, boating or simply being with family and friends along the lakes. As U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga, Republican co-chair of the Great Lakes Congressonal Task Force, said in mid-July 2026: “The Great Lakes aren’t a Republican issue or a Democratic issue. They’re an economic engine, a source of drinking water for millions of people, and part of our way of life here in Michigan. Protecting them is something we can all rally around.”
A 2024 poll of a random sample of more than 2,500 Americans and Canadians found 96% of the region’s residents think it’s important for governments to invest in protecting the Great Lakes – a level of near-unanimity unheard of for other issues.
 A prominent launch

Shared identity and popular support are not enough to launch a major government effort without a spark and a plan.
In 2004, President George W. Bush – in part driven by the swing state electoral power of the Great Lakes region – signed an executive order declaring the Great Lakes to have “national significance” and launching the Great Lakes Regional Collaboration Strategy. Developed over the course of a year through work groups involving more than 1,500 people combined with public input sessions, the strategy laid out common goals for restoration and prioritized a list of needs, such as funding to clean up toxic hot spots and sewage overflows, which was critical to securing congressional support for funding.
 Diverse allies

A plan for restoration – even for an iconic resource – will not garner billions of dollars in federal funding without significant bipartisan support from all levels of government and strong community support.
Those speaking up for the new program were “not simply one group or one voice. It was governors, mayors, the NGO community and tribes,” David Naftzger, executive director of the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Governors & Premiers, which works with all the chief state and provincial executives across the region, told our research team.
Business leaders have been particularly crucial backers. They relay to lawmakers the economic value of restoration projects, providing political cover for a program that increases government spending.
The broad range of support continues today and has helped the initiative weather various efforts to reduce or eliminate its funding.
Most famously, in 2019, President Donald Trump proposed cutting the initiative’s funding by 90%. Three weeks later, while traveling with Trump to a political rally in Michigan, three Michigan congressional Republicans explained how critical the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative is to the region’s identity and economy, and how popular it is. At the rally, Trump reversed course and announced he would support keeping funding levels at US$300 million per year, promising to “make the Great Lakes great again.”
At a Washington, D.C., event celebrating the Great Lakes in 2023, I saw JD Vance, then a Republican U.S. senator from Ohio, and U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow, a Michigan Democrat, proclaim that while they may not agree on much, they are united in their support for the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative.
 Clear communication

Our analysis found that initiative supporters have been organized and disciplined about how they talk about the program and the overall goals. State officials, local leaders, tribal nations, nonprofit groups and businesses all deliver a “coordinated, consistent kind of beating of the drum,” Erika Jensen, executive director of the Great Lakes Commission, told our research team.
This includes not only the many positive stories of success but also the economic benefits. A University of Michigan study that showed the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative boosts the region’s economic output by more than $3 for every dollar of federal spending is used often to make this case.
These coordinated messages allow political leaders to tie the initiative into their priorities and build support across diverse audiences. One key reason for this kind of powerful communication is that the initiative funds work in every congressional district in the Great Lakes watershed, so every member of Congress in the region can say they brought home federal money to make significant improvements in their own districts.
 ‘Secret sauce’

The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative pays for community-based work on local lands and waterways – it does not regulate industries or tread into particularly controversial territory.
Everywhere has places that need help, cleanup and care. These ecosystems are relatively easy to build support for, and when connected with other projects across a wide region, these smaller efforts can make a significant difference in environmental quality and quality of life while building political and community support for even bigger undertakings.
I believe that many of the core lessons and converging forces that make up the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative’s “secret sauce” can be applied not only to the future of the Great Lakes but to conservation initiatives across the U.S. and the world. And they may even be able to help restore bipartisanship to at least some parts of U.S. politics.
Mike Shriberg, Professor of Practice & Engagement, School for Environment & Sustainability; Director of the University of Michigan Water Center, University of Michigan

name: Maryland Matters
title: Old hands return to Blueprint board, new judges and a Pepco veteran to PSC, in political notes
description: It’s as if they never left. When the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board meets Thursday in a virtual session, board members Isiah “Ike” Leggett and Robin Werner will be back in their seats, after they were reappointed by Gov. Wes Moore (D) to new six-year terms. Leggett’s and Werner’s previous appointments expired […]
text:
Blueprint for Maryland's Future Accountability and Implementation Board Chair Isiah "Ike" Leggett, left, at a September hearing with AIB Vice Chair William "Brit" Kirwan. Leggett, who has been on the board since its creation, was recently reappointed to it by Gov. Wes Moore. (File photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)It’s as if they never left.
When the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board meets Thursday in a virtual session, board members Isiah “Ike” Leggett and Robin Werner will be back in their seats, after they were reappointed by Gov. Wes Moore (D) to new six-year terms. Leggett’s and Werner’s previous appointments expired July 1.
Leggett, the first Black county executive in Montgomery County, has served as the Blueprint board’s chair since it first convened in November 2021. Werner, a director of teaching and learning for public schools in Talbot County, was appointed in August 2025 to replace Mara Doss, a former associate vice president for teaching, learning and student success at Prince George’s Community College.
Leggett and Werner were among 29 people who applied to serve on the board, which is charged with overseeing implementation of the state’s multiyear, multibillion-dollar education reform plan, the Blueprint. The list of applicants was narrowed down to four finalists by the AIB Nominating Committee last month and sent to the governor, who makde the final selection.
When the board meets online Thursday, its agenda includes proposed updates to the Blueprint comprehensive plan, which serves as a guide for state agencies, the 24 school districts and other stakeholders to follow and help implement the statewide plan. Any updates to the plan must be done annually by Aug. 1. Some of the changes include new or revised policies adopted by the General Assembly during the 90-day session.
The board will not meet in August but then reconvene on Sept. 17.
From Pepco to the PSC
The Maryland Public Service Commission’s new communications director hails from Pepco, the Exelon electric company that serves the District of Columbia and parts of Maryland.
Maryland may have to go to court to fight for $20M in annual relief for electric customers

Tony Ruffin, who worked at the utility for 16 years, including as external affairs manager covering Prince George’s County, replaces Tori Leonard, who retired at the end of June after more than a decade at the commission.
“I am honored to join the Commission as well as work with Chair [Kumar] Barve, each Commissioner and Commission staff on the important issues before the MD PSC,” Ruffin said in a statement issued Friday. “It’s also a privilege to succeed Tori, whose long, impressive tenure and commitment to excellence sets a high bar but I am confident that the legacy she has left and the incredible talent within the Commission will allow me to make a smooth transition.”
Ruffin, a Washington D.C. native, previously worked in communications roles at Anne Arundel County and Prince George’s County public schools, according to a news release from the commission. He also served as chairman of the Board of Directors of the Prince George’s Chamber of Commerce from 2024 to 2025.
“We are very pleased to welcome Tony to the Maryland Public Service Commission,” said Barve, the chair of the PSC. “Tony brings years of utility, communications, and government affairs experience that we believe will be valuable in this role, and we look forward to his leadership in helping to shape and strengthen public engagement and outreach.”
District judges named
Gov. Wes Moore (D) announced the appointments Monday of six people to serve in the district courts of Prince George’s and Washington counties.
Daniel Kyungmin Kim, Julia Simone Gagne Rupert, Jessica Lowell Garth and William Carl Isler II will serve as judges in Prince George’s, while Travis William Poole and Mikhaila Miriam Eugenia Mc Nicolls will serve on the Washington County bench. Moore said that with their “years of experience and guided by a wealth of legal expertise, I know all of them will serve our state well.”
Kim currently works in the Prince George’s State’s Attorney’s Office as the assistant chief of the homicide and strategic investigations units. Prior to that,  he worked for 11 years at the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office and spent the majority of that time as an assistant state’s attorney. Kim received a law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law.

Rupert is an assistant attorney general in the criminal appeals division of the Maryland Attorney General’s office. She has also served as \an assistant section chief in the District of Columbia Office of the Attorney General, an assistant state’s attorney in Prince George’s and a law clerk for Circuit Judge Nicholas E. Rattle. Rupert graduated from the University of District of Columbia’s David A. Clarke School of Law.
Garth has worked in the Prince George’s State’s Attorney’s Office for more than 12 years, which includes work as an intern, the office’s legislative policy director and an assistant state’s attorney. She is currently chief of the office’s special victims unit. She received a law degree at the George Washington University Law School.
Isler has worked for more than 11 years as program counsel in the Office of Compliance and Enforcement for the Legal Services Corp., an independent, nonprofit organization that helps provide legal aid for providers to help low-income residents. Before that, Isler worked as counsel to the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission. He received a law degree from the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law.
According to the governor’s office, Poole serves as an assistant attorney general and became the supervising attorney for the Western Maryland region, whose work includes representing the Department of Human Services and the Washington County Department of Social Services. In March, the county’s Board of Commissioners unanimously voted to reappoint Poole as a legal representative to the county’s Animal Control Authority. He earned his law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law.
Mc Nicolls is a co-managing partner at the Hagerstown law firm, Hutchison & Mc Nicolls, established in 2024. Mc Nicolls, originally from Trinidad & Tobago, worked as a public defender in Washington County and also worked in private practice. She received her law degree from the Howard University School of Law.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Health experts: State’s high vaccination rate is keeping spread of measles in check
description: Just seven months into the year, confirmed measles cases Maryland are already four times higher that they were for all of last year, but health officials say the situation could be much worse if the state did not maintain a relatively high measles vaccination rate.
text:
Maryland health officials and public health experts urge Marylanders to vaccinate against measles amid nationwide surge in cases. (Photo by Jerry Saslav/U.S. Ari Force)Just seven months into the year, confirmed measles cases Maryland are already four times higher that they were for all of last year, but health officials say the situation could be much worse.
Almost all of the 12 cases recorded so far this year — up from three for all of 2025 — were “imported” into Maryland after out-of-state or international travel. But once here, the infections have not spread further, which experts say is a sign that the state’s relatively high vaccine coverage at 96% is protecting residents from the potentially fatal illness.
“This is higher than many previous years, but it doesn’t represent sustained transmission within Maryland,” said Dr. William Moss, director of the International Vaccine Access Center at Johns Hopkins University. “We have now had repeated importations into the state without sustained transmission.”
It’s a trend that he and public health officials hope to protect amid growing vaccine skepticism as new state data shows more parents opting their children out of required school vaccinations.
Approximately 96% of Marylanders have lifelong protection from measles due to being vaccinated, above the national average of 93%, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Other Marylanders who have already been sick with measles are also considered immune.
The recommend vaccination coverage rate to considered necessary to protect a community from measles is 96%, but as regions across the United States struggle with outbreaks, the dozen cases identified in Maryland reflect those challenges.
Of the 12 cases identified by the Maryland Department of Health this year, nine were detected after the resident returned from out-of-state travel, while two cases were detected after international travel. The most recent case, announced June 23 by the health department, did not indicate where the individual may have picked up measles.


But Moss says that the lack of sustained community transmission is “a signal of the strength of our immunization program and our really good measles vaccine coverage.”
That coverage may be slipping, as more Maryland families cite religious reasons to opt their kids out of vaccinations that are otherwise required to enter kindergarten through religious exemptions. The Maryland Department of Health reports that during the 2025-2026 school year, 2.1% of kindergartners had religious exemptions from the vaccinations, up from 1.7% the year before.
That’s more than 1,300 of the 65,500 kindergartners enrolled in the 2025-2026 school year. It’s the highest percentage since 2019-2020, when the religious exemption rate was 2.7% amid disruptions in the school year due to COVID-19.
That said, overall vaccine coverage among kindergarteners was still at least 95% in every Maryland county, even in counties where religious exemptions were higher like Allegany and Worcester, according to the health department’s most recent data.
“High vaccination rates in schools are crucial for preventing outbreaks and maintaining community immunity,” the Maryland Department of Health said in a written statement Monday. “Maryland maintains a strong safety net with 96.7% of kindergarteners reported as vaccinated in the 2025-2026 school year.”
Dr. Andrea Berry is an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and a pediatric infectious disease specialist at University of Maryland Golisano Children’s Hospital. She says that over the last few years, there’s been growing confusion and vaccine skepticism among parents, which leads them to opt their kids out of vaccines, including the measles vaccine.
“There is a very close relationship between vaccination rates and the likelihood of an outbreak,” she said. “Overall, Maryland does a really great job getting children vaccinated, but the increase in these exemptions stems from vaccine hesitancy.”
Meanwhile, the number of measles cases climbs across the United States with 2,318 cases confirmed as of July 23 this year. Those cases have reached 44 states and Washington, D.C., with Maryland’s neighbors among the states with the largest measles outbreaks currently, with Virginia facing 176 measles cases and Pennsylvania facing 134 cases.
Measles cases have reached a 35-year high, CDC reports

Despite Virginia’s high vaccination rate at 96%, the measles outbreak it’s facing occurred in two rural counties where vaccination rates are less than 75%. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s statewide vaccination rate is 92%.
Moss warns that the growing measles cases in neighboring states create a greater chance of exposure when Marylanders are visiting those regions, especially in communities with lower vaccination coverage. He says Maryland is “not immune to having local transmission.”
“I suspect that we have communities here in Maryland that have lower vaccine coverage … but fortunately, these imported cases have not made it into those communities yet,” he said. “Traveling to a place where there’s ongoing measles virus transmission … the most important thing is to make sure you’re protected against measles.”
Berry noted that anyone past the age of 6 months can get a measles vaccination. She urges Marylanders to get vaccinated if they are not already protected through prior illness from measles, especially as cases rise in neighboring states.
“Now that there are so many outbreaks all throughout the United States, it’s more likely that somebody is going to travel to those places or speak to somebody who did travel those places,” she said. “With the vaccine, you’re much less likely to get measles, and when people do get measles, it is not as severe.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s hypocrisy about election integrity
description: If leaders want credibility when they condemn Trump’s attacks on democracy, they must also be willing to confront corruption, intimidation, and election abuse in Bridgeport.
text:
While Trump is wrong to use election fraud in the City of Bridgeport as a prelude for restricting voting rights, Connecticut leaders are also wrong when they respond by pretending that election fraud is only a right-wing talking point. 
In Bridgeport, election fraud is very real.
To me it is personal because in 2023, I stood with other Bridgeport residents after a mayoral primary stolen by absentee-ballot abuse. As some may recall, I was peacefully protesting near Boca Oyster Bar, holding a sign that read “Joe Gotta Go!” when Bridgeport police ordered me to leave. I was on publicly accessible property and exercising my First Amendment rights. I was arrested. A Superior Court judge later dismissed the criminal case against me.
That experience proves what Bridgeport residents already knew: when political machines feel threatened, they do not always answer criticism with facts. Sometimes they answer it with intimidation.
That is why the recent press conference in Hartford defending Connecticut elections cannot be the end of the conversation. The Secretary of the State is right that Connecticut elections depend on “people, paper, and proof.” But in Bridgeport, proof exists that people forged paper and stuffed the ballot box.
A Connecticut Superior Court judge overturned the results of Bridgeport’s 2023 primary after finding that the volume absentee ballots seen on video being stuffed, called the result into serious doubt. The judge wrote that the evidence was “shocking” and that the court was unable to determine the legitimate result of the election.
That was not a wild right wing nut conspiracy theory. That was a court ruling.
The investigation that followed deepened public’s concerns. Five people were charged with election-related crimes relating to the 2023 primary. The guilty pleas and trials have begun.
Bridgeport’s crisis did not begin in 2023. In the 2019 mayoral election cycle, absentee-ballot misconduct also became the subject of criminal charges.
So when Bridgeport residents say that two consecutive mayoral races were stolen from people of color, that claim should not be dismissed. Any talk of election integrity should at least give mention to Bridgeport’s woes. Marilyn Moore, a Black woman and longtime Bridgeport leader, challenged the machine in 2019. John Gomes, an immigrant from Cape Verde, challenged the machine in 2023, and his campaign’s challenge led to a court-ordered redo after absentee-ballot misconduct came to light.
I reject Trump’s attempt to turn election integrity into a weapon against voters. I oppose restrictions that make it harder for lawful voters to register, vote by mail, or participate fully in democracy. Trump’s executive order sought changes that were overly burdensome, especially Identification requirements for married women and the federal overreach into states sovereign rights to administer elections.
Real election integrity should not suppress voters. It should prevent fraud without using fraud as an excuse to silence communities, restrict access, or centralize power in the hands of one president.
Rejecting Trump does not require us to pretend what happened in Bridgeport did not happen.
In fact, if leaders want credibility when they condemn Trump’s attacks on democracy, they must also be willing to confront corruption, intimidation, and election abuse when it happens inside Democratic cities, under Democratic leadership, and within Democratic political machines.
Bridgeport is Connecticut’s largest Black and brown city. Our votes should never be treated as property of a political organization. When absentee ballots are mishandled, and when critics are arrested or intimidated for speaking out, the damage goes far beyond one candidate or one election.
The damage is to democracy itself. I have said before that public criticism is not a crime. Police and personnel systems should never be used as weapons against people whose message those in power dislike. It is a message that should be echoed at press conferences about election fraud.
Voters should not have to choose between Trump’s false, self-serving narrative and a Democratic establishment that wants to minimize Bridgeport’s pain. The Lamont administration needs to tell the truth
The truth is that overall our elections are safe and Bridgeport has suffered real election scandals that deserve serious accountability.
The truth is that election integrity and voting rights are not mutually exclusive
If Connecticut leaders want claim the moral high ground and stand against Trump, they must prove that their commitment to democracy does not ignore Bridgeport corruption. They must defend voters from federal overreach while also defending Bridgeport residents from local machine politics and having their votes stolen.
Anything less is hypocrisy.
Connecticut does not need press conferences about trusting democracy. Connecticut needs democracy worthy of trust.
Joseph Sokolovic lives in Bridgeport.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Judge halts Minnesota ban on prediction markets
description: A federal judge halted a new Minnesota law aimed at stopping the massive expansion of gambling via prediction markets on sites like Kalshi and Polymarket. The two companies and the Trump administration sued Minnesota to invalidate the new law, and federal Judge Katherine Menendez granted a preliminary injunction to stop the law from taking effect […]
text:
A federal judge halted a new Minnesota law aimed at stopping the massive expansion of gambling via prediction markets on sites like Kalshi and Polymarket.
The two companies and the Trump administration sued Minnesota to invalidate the new law, and federal Judge Katherine Menendez granted a preliminary injunction to stop the law from taking effect during the ongoing litigation. She determined the companies and the federal government were likely to prevail and face “irreperable harm” should the law — the first of its kind in the nation — to go into effect.
Prediction markets, which have soared in popularity in recent years in part thanks to regulatory relief from the Trump administration, allow people to bet on almost anything, including whether Gov. Tim Walz will finish his term or Jonathan Ross will be charged in the killing of Renee Good.
The companies have successfully persuaded the Trump administration that they are not gambling sites but a platform for futures contracts — a common financial instrument for buying or selling something at a fixed price in the future, which helps investors hedge against risk. Except, instead of speculating on the price of, say, a barrel of oil, the companies allow people to predict a sports or political or pop culture outcome.
News stories about suspected insider trading on Kalshi and Polymarket — when people use inside information not available to the general public — are a near daily occurence. President Donald Trump’s teleprompter operator made more than $100,000 betting on the content of his speeches, ABC News recently reported.
The judge ruled that federal law gives the CFTC “exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions” involving the futures contracts known as swaps, Menendez wrote in her 44-page ruling.
Congress gave the CFTC more robust authority after the global financial crisis of 2008, when unregulated contracts known as credit default swaps sank some massive financial firms when they bet wrong.
Here’s how NPR described credit default swaps back in 2008:
“Let’s say there’s a guy named Frank and he has a life insurance policy. When he dies, the beneficiary gets a million dollars. Now imagine a whole bunch of other people saying, “I want a million dollars if he dies, too.” And so they take out life insurance policies on Frank. Now imagine Frank dies, and all those people bought their policies from the same company. That company, more or less, was AIG.”
Now, paradoxically, the Trump administration is using the CFTC’s authority — which was intended to limit the economy’s exposure to massive risk-taking — to ban Minnesota from limiting people’s ability to take on extreme risk by, say, betting their life savings on whether Costco will increase hot dog prices before 2027.
Rep. Emma Greenman, a Minneapolis Democrat, told MPR she’s disappointed by the ruling but considers it just the start of the litigation around Minnesota’s law.
“If it walks like a duck and if it quacks like a duck, it’s gambling,” Greenman said. “It’s a duck and we should be able to regulate it in the public interest.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: ‘Government edit’? Two lawsuits challenge state’s description of WA income tax measure
description: Legal wrangling on the income tax initiative could reach the state’s high court before Washington voters consider it this November. Sponsors of Initiative 645 on Monday formally contested a statement drafted by state attorneys that says the initiative would decrease funding for Washington’s budget, saying it “is inaccurate and would create prejudice against[...]
text:
A volunteer for Let's Go Washington unloads boxes of petitions for Initiative 645 that were turned in to the secretary of state's office on July 2, 2026. The measure seeks to repeal Washngton's new income tax on high earners. Differences on how to describe the fiscal effects of the measure passing has sparked legal fights that could reach the state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield / Washington State Standard)Legal wrangling on the income tax initiative could reach the state’s high court before Washington voters consider it this November.
Sponsors of Initiative 645 on Monday formally contested a statement drafted by state attorneys that says the initiative would decrease funding for Washington’s budget, saying it “is inaccurate and would create prejudice against the measure if it were allowed to be placed on the ballot.”
Lawyers for Let’s Go Washington argued in a petition filed in Thurston County Superior Court that passing the initiative would in fact lead to increased funding for the budget. 
The statement “must be corrected” because that is the only effect that the initiative would have on the current state budget, wrote Callie Castillo, attorney for the conservative political committee led by Brian Heywood. 
In its court filing, Let’s Go Washington proposed completely new language for what is known as the public investment impact disclosure.
The state Attorney General’s Office had not seen the petition as of 5 p.m. Monday.
“We’ll review it and respond in the appropriate venue,” said Mike Faulk, deputy communications director for the state Attorney General’s Office.
Let’s Go Washington’s action comes days after an open government activist filed his own lawsuit contending the requirement for the public investment statement is an unconstitutional infringement on the citizen initiative process.
Arthur West, who filed the suit in Thurston County Superior Court, is seeking an injunction that, if granted, would bar the “public investment impact disclosure” for Initiative 645 from appearing on ballots.
A hearing is set for Aug. 7, after which a decision could be appealed directly to the state Supreme Court.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and Attorney General Nick Brown are named as defendants. A Hobbs spokesperson referred questions to the attorney general’s office.
Controversy centers on 15 words
A 2022 law requires disclosure statements of 15 words or less be placed on ballots if a measure repeals, levies or modifies a tax or fee, and if it would cause a net change in state revenue. State attorneys write the one-sentence that gets tacked on after the ballot title.
Initiative 645 would repeal the 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year that Gov. Bob Ferguson signed into law in late March. The tax is slated to take effect Jan. 1, 2028, with payments due the following year. The state Department of Revenue estimates it would bring in roughly $2.7 billion for the fiscal year that ends June 30, 2029.
The public investment statement for I-645 drafted by Brown’s office reads: “This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare).”
Anyone objecting to the language had until 5 p.m. Monday to appeal. 
Let’s Go Washington argues that if the measure passes, it will result in savings for the state, which translates to an increase in available funding for the budget that runs through June 30, 2027. It criticizes the state-drafted language for projecting potential fallout for future budgets, which is not the purpose of the statement, Castillo argued.
The statement is intended to let voters know the immediate impact of a measure, not to “describe future hypothetical impact on a future hypothetical budget that will never take place if the measure goes into effect,” she wrote.
Let’s Go Washington proposed this rewrite: “This measure would increase funding for the 2026-2027 state general fund, which primary investments are medical assistance-programs, public instruction, and higher education.”
‘Government edit’
Similarly, West argues in his suit that the language proposed by the state is not neutral, as required by the law. Rather, it is prejudicial and likely to push voters toward opposing the measure. He cited a 2023 poll that found early signs of opposition to the three measures on the 2024 ballot when voters were told about fiscal effects. Service Employees International Union 775 and Washington Conservation Action paid for the poll.
He also said the content is not factual because only the Legislature can decrease funding for any of the areas the statement mentions.
The public investment statements, he said, essentially give the state the last word in the initiative process, well after people like himself, who signed a petition, and the sponsors, Let’s Go Washington, who gathered more than 500,000 signatures, get the measure on the ballot.
This ability “to alter the official ballot presentation of a completed initiative petition after petition circulation has concluded exceeds the Legislature’s authority,” he wrote.
It is, West wrote, “a government edit to a document the government had no further authority to touch.”
In an interview Monday, West said the law violates the state’s separation of powers doctrine that protects the legislative, executive and judicial branches from each other’s overreach. If the legislative deliberative process is protected from the people, he said, “why is the people’s power of the initiative not protected from incursions” of the legislative and executive branches?
In his filing, West said if the court is not inclined to grant an injunction, it should consider ordering the statement removed from ballots and put in the voter’s pamphlet.
Andrew Villeneuve, founder of the Northwest Progressive Institute, helped develop and then lobbied hard to pass the 2022 law as a means to ensure voters understand the fiscal consequences of initiatives and referendums. He described West’s effort as “a deeply misguided attack on a vital transparency law.”
“The creation of these essential materials and their dissemination to voters does not infringe on anyone’s right to petition, short circuit the people’s right to pass laws at the ballot, or violate the separation of powers doctrine,” Villeneuve wrote in an email. 
“He is asking the courts to invent a new restriction on official representations of ballot measures, one that doesn’t exist in the Washington State Constitution,” he wrote. “West’s case is wholly without merit.”
This isn’t the first time this issue has been before a judge.
Two years ago, state Republican Party Chair Jim Walsh sued to block statements, which he described as warning labels. These appeared with initiatives to scrap Washington’s cap-and-trade system, end its capital gains tax, and make the WA Cares long-term care program optional. Voters defeated all three measures, which were also sponsored by Let’s Go Washington.
The state Supreme Court rejected Walsh’s lawsuit primarily because he sought “ancient, rare and extraordinary” remedies rather than follow the usual course of action in trying to block a state law.
West said he’s doing just that by focusing on the legality of the statute.
“The constitutional question the state would now like this court to believe was settled in 2024 was, in fact, the one question the 2024 court went out of its way not to touch,” he wrote.

title: WCU political scientist Chris Cooper on the ongoing battles over election laws and voting rights
description: With the 2026 midterm elections less than 100 days away, it a great time to check in with one of the state’s foremost experts on politics and elections, Western Carolina University Professor of Political Science, Chris Cooper. text:
Western Carolina University political scientist Chris CooperWith the 2026 midterm elections less than 100 days away, it a great time to check in with one of the state’s foremost experts on politics and elections, Western Carolina University Professor of Political Science, Chris Cooper.
This past week, Newsline got a chance to catch up with Cooper for an extended conversation in which we delved into an array of front burner topics. In Part One of our chat, we focused on the issue of our elections, themselves – how they’re run, how President Trump has repeatedly sought to sow distrust in their honesty and how they’re run, and how Trump’s Republican allies in North Carolina have taken a number of recent actions that they say will improve voting and elections, but that critics argue are really just thinly disguised efforts to discourage participation by voters the GOP fears will vote for Democratic candidates.
In Part Two of our conversation, Cooper shared some of his thoughts on the career of longtime South Carolina U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham in light of his recent passing, as well as his take on the state of two high-profile North Carolina races on the ballot this fall – the U.S. Senate Race between Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley and western North Carolina congressional race between Chuck Edwards and Jamie Ager.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Army Corps of Engineers uses released water from Dworshak Reservoir to cool river temperature
description: Hot temperatures across western Idaho and southeastern Washington have been heating up river temperatures, which can be dangerous for salmon and steelhead. The Army Corps of Engineers has responded by releasing cold water from the reservoir behind Dworshak Dam.  The Clearwater River, near Orofino, had a water temperature of 79.7 degrees on July 25, according[...]
text:
In this undated photo, Chinook salmon spawn in Snake River. River temperatures rose this month, which can be dangerous for salmon and steelhead. (Photo by Natalie Fobes/Getty Images)Hot temperatures across western Idaho and southeastern Washington have been heating up river temperatures, which can be dangerous for salmon and steelhead. The Army Corps of Engineers has responded by releasing cold water from the reservoir behind Dworshak Dam. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Clearwater River, near Orofino, had a water temperature of 79.7 degrees on July 25, according to a press release from the Corps of Engineers. The Snake River, at a point about 25 miles southwest of Lewiston, reached 74.4 degrees that same day, the release said. 
The Clearwater and Snake rivers converge at Lewiston, and hot water mixing is dangerous for steelhead and salmon, which prefer cooler water temperatures, the release said. 
“Above about 68 degrees, they start showing signs of stress, migration delay, and, if temperatures go higher, mortality can start to occur,” Chris Peery, a Corps of Engineers fish biologist, said in the release. “Water that flows into the lower Snake River and the Lower Granite Dam reservoir comes from Hells Canyon and other tributaries and is always warmer than 68 in summer.”
The Corps responded by releasing cold water on July 25  from the Dworshak Dam reservoir near Orofino. The water release kept river temperatures behind Lower Granite Dam at 66.1 degrees or cooler, the press release said. 
The Corps manages the dam, and performed the water release in consultation with the National Marine Fisheries Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the release said.
Dworshak is 600-feet deep, according to the release, and the bottom of its reservoir stays 42 degrees year-round. The dam, standing at 717 feet tall, is the third tallest in the U.S and has the capacity to store more than 3.4 million acre-feet of water. That’s enough to cover the state of Connecticut with 1 foot of water, according to the release. 
“If we manage it carefully, we can help cool the Snake River so it stays around 68 degrees in the tailrace of Lower Granite Dam, but there is a limited amount of water that we can release from Dworshak,” Peery said 
Dworshak Dam near Orofino. (Photo from Army Corps of Engineers)
 Dams can both help and hinder salmon and steelhead 

Dams, agricultural or industrial water use, habitat quality, and climate conditions like drought, annual snowpack and precipitation can all affect river temperatures. Because of varied conditions, releasing water from the dam cannot eliminate high temperatures throughout the river system, the release said. 
“(The dam) can, however, provide operational flexibility and help improve conditions in portions of the Clearwater and lower Snake rivers during periods of elevated summer temperatures, aiding salmon and steelhead,” the release said. 
Other dams along the Snake River contribute to the warming waters, according to advocates for salmon restoration. A 2024 Hot Water Report from the conservation coalition Save our wild Salmon, or SOS, noted that Dworshak reservoir releases helped cool waters but the report also said, “the benefit of this cold water does not last long in the summer heat and does not cool the other three downstream reservoirs on the lower Snake.” 
The coalition argued that, “with a free-flowing lower Snake River, cold water releases from Dworshak Dam during the summer months would further help keep temperatures cool and healthy for fish from Lewiston (ID) downstream to where the Snake River joins the Columbia River in south-central Washington State near the Tri-Cities.” 
Construction of the dam, which began in 1966, blocked salmon and steelhead trout’s migration to their natural spawning grounds and removed some of the fishes’ habitat. The height of the dam made it impossible to build a fish ladder, according to Fish and Wildlife. The Dworshak National Fish Hatchery was built to mitigate fish losses, according to the Corps. The hatchery is operated by U.S. Fish and Wildlife and the Nez Perce Tribe.
