name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide
description: Connecticut's primary election will take place on Aug. 11. Here's what to know about how to register, vote and know who's running.
text:
Connecticut Primary Election 2026Voter Guide
How to register, vote, and know who’s running.

IN THIS GUIDE:    KEY DATES    CANDIDATES    FAQ    GENERAL ASSEMBLY    COVERAGE
Connecticut residents will head to the polls on Aug. 11 to cast ballots in party primaries for governor, U.S. Congress and state legislative and constitutional races. Many will have questions about where to vote, how to vote and for whom to vote when Primary Election Day rolls around. The Connecticut Mirror, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization, is here to help with this primary voter guide — a comprehensive look at the key dates to know ahead of Aug. 11, a one-stop-shop for election-related information. 

KEY DATES FOR THE 2026 PRIMARY ELECTIONS


July 21
First day absentee ballots are issued


August 3
First day of early voting


August 6
Last day to register to vote by mail


August 9
Last day of early voting


August 10
Last day to request an absentee ballot and register to vote in person


August 11: Primary Election Day! Polls open 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.

FAQ
Any questions we haven’t answered here? Send us an email and we’ll try to answer them for you.
Am I eligible to vote? What if I’m unaffiliated with a party?
Connecticut residents are eligible to vote if they are a U.S. citizen and turn 18 on or before Nov. 3, 2026. If a person has been convicted of a felony, they must also have completed confinement.
You must be registered with a party to vote in that party’s primary elections. If you are unaffiliated with a party, you can register with one until 12 p.m. on Aug. 10. The deadline to change your affiliation from one party to another has passed.

How do I register to vote?
Those eligible to vote can visit the state’s online voter registration portal to sign up, apply in person to your town clerk or registrar, or download a paper form in English or Spanish and mail it in to your town’s registrar of voters office. 
The deadline to register in person is 12 p.m. on Aug. 10. For voters affiliated with a party, the deadline to register by mail is Aug. 6, and your application must be postmarked or received by this date. The deadline for new voters and unaffiliated voters to register by mail was July 24. 

What if I miss the deadline? Can I vote on primary election day or during early voting?
You can register every day at an early voting location from Aug. 3 through Aug. 9. Same-day registration is not available for primary elections.

Tell me about early voting. Who can vote? When does it begin? Where do I go?
Anyone eligible to vote in the primary election can vote during the early voting period. Early voting begins on Aug. 3 and runs through Aug. 9. Early voting locations will be posted on a rolling basis on the state’s Early Voting Locations page.
If you are unaffiliated with a party and wish to vote during early voting, you must register with a party by 12 p.m. on July 31.

Are polling locations the same on primary election day as they are during early voting?
No. Early voting locations can and will be different from regular polling locations. To find out where to cast a ballot on primary election day, registered voters can visit the secretary of the state’s voter registration lookup and polling place locator here.

What time are the polls open on primary election day?
Polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. If you are in line at 8 p.m., you will still be able to vote.

Do I need to bring an ID to vote? 
No, but you can. Before you receive a ballot at the polls, you will be asked to provide a government-issued ID, a different ID with your name and photo, or a document such as a utility bill or checkbook that has your name and address. You may use your current driver’s license at the polls even if it is marked “not for federal identification.”
If you can not provide any of these, you will be asked to sign an affidavit instead.

Can I vote by using an absentee or mail-in ballot? 
For the first time this year, anyone eligible to vote in the primary election can request an absentee ballot. Voters can submit requests through the Online Absentee Ballot Request Portal, or mail or hand-deliver a printed ballot to their town clerk. Voters no longer need to specify reasons for requesting an absentee ballot. The deadline to request an absentee ballot is Aug. 10.
Absentee ballots will be issued and mailed to voters starting July 21. The ballot must be returned to the voter’s town clerk by using the United States Postal Service, in person at the town clerk’s office or in a drop box in their town. Voters must return their absentee ballot in the same envelope that housed the ballot and ensure that they print and sign their name on the envelope. 
All ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Aug. 11 to be counted. Voters can check if their ballot has been received on the state’s Voter Registration Lookup and should contact their town clerk if their ballot has not been received.
For additional questions about absentee voting, contact the state Legislation and Election Administration at LEAD@ct.gov or (860) 509-6100.

I’m a college student. How do I vote? 
Students eligible to vote in the primary can do so in one of two ways: vote by absentee ballot in your home town or register to vote in your college town.

GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATES
The Democratic primary for governor is the only statewide primary this year and the first challenge to a governor for their party’s nomination since 1978, when Lt. Gov. Robert Killian failed to wrest the top spot from Gov. Ella T. Grasso.
Gov. Ned Lamont, a fiscal centrist and social progressive who is seeking a rare third term, is being challenged from the left by state Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden.
Lamont, 72, of Greenwich is waging his fifth statewide campaign and his fourth for governor. Making national news as anti-war candidate in 2006, he won a Democratic primary against U.S. Sen. Joseph I. Lieberman in 2006, but Lieberman won his fourth and final term as an independent candidate. Lamont lost a gubernatorial primary to former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy in 2010.
Elliott, 41, was elected to the state House of Representatives in 2016, running with the backing of the Working Families Party for the seat then held by House Speaker J. Brendan Sharkey. Ultimately, Sharkey did not seek another term. Elliott helped resurrect the progressive caucus in the House. This year, Elliott is hedging his bets, running for reelection to the House while challenging the governor.

CT CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT CANDIDATES


All five of Connecticut’s U.S. House seats are on the general election ballot in November. But there are only three primaries in August: a Democratic primary in the 1st District and Republican primaries in the 4th District and the 5th District.
Democrats hold all five seats and have advantages again this year. The 1st District is the most heavily Democratic in the state, with a Republican last winning in 1956. Republicans haven’t won the 4th District since 2006 or the 5th since 2004. The 5th District is considered the most competitive in Connecticut.
Here’s who’s running in the congressional primaries:




Democratic primary in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District
The district is centered around Hartford, wrapping around up to the northwest toward Torrington and down and over to Bristol. It is currently represented by Democrat John B. Larson.
Luke Bronin is the former mayor of Hartford, serving between 2016 and 2024. He served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve and was deployed to Afghanistan in 2010. Before becoming mayor, he worked in the Obama administration and served as general counsel to former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy. He won the party’s endorsement at the nominating convention.
Ruth Fortune is an estate lawyer and first-time candidate for elected office. She’s an appointed member of the Hartford Board of Education. Fortune failed to win enough support from local delegates at the nominating convention, but she secured the signatures needed via petition to get a spot on the August primary ballot.
Jillian Gilchrest is a state representative from West Hartford who has been in office since 2019 after unseating a longtime incumbent. Before her tenure in the General Assembly, Gilchrest served in leadership positions for the Connecticut Coalition Against Domestic Violence, NARAL Pro-Choice Connecticut and the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence.
Larson has represented the district since 1999. He serves as the ranking member of the Ways and Means’ Social Security Subcommittee. Prior to Congress, he served in the Connecticut Senate and worked as a history teacher before his time in politics. This is the first time he’s faced a primary in his 28-year congressional tenure.
Republican primary in Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District
The district covers the southwestern corner, including Stamford and Bridgeport. It is currently represented by Democrat Jim Himes.
Michael Goldstein is a physician and attorney who has run to represent the district multiple times. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the GOP nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. In this year’s primary, Goldstein is the party-endorsed candidate.
Daniel Miressi is a former professional hockey player who coaches youth hockey and has worked in the hospitality industry. He’s run for elected office before, including in an unsuccessful race to unseat state Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, in 2022.
Republican primary in Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District
The district spans the western part of the state, including sections of Fairfield, Litchfield, New Haven and Hartford counties. It is currently represented by Democrat Jahana Hayes.
Republican challenger Chris Shea is a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy SEAL. He founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders. Shea is the party-endorsed candidate.
Republican challenger Jonathan De Barros has worked as a mentor for at-risk youth. He shot and killed a man in 1996 and was convicted of murder, but it was overturned on appeal. He was granted an “absolute pardon” in 2022. He filed a defamation lawsuit against Republicans who have called him a murderer.

CT GENERAL ASSEMBLY CANDIDATES
The only Democratic primaries for state legislative nominations are in two Senate and seven House districts currently represented by Democrats. In all nine districts, whoever wins the primary is favored to prevail in November.
Two races to watch involve challenges to incumbents: Sen. Doug McCrory of Hartford in the 2nd Senate District and Rep. Patricia Dillon of New Haven in the 92nd House District.
McCrory’s role in delivering earmarks is the subject of a continuing FBI investigation. Dillon is the longest-serving member of the House seeking reelection and faces a generational challenge.
A third Democratic primary is a bit of an oddity. Rep. Jill Barry of Glastonbury lost the Democratic endorsement in a caucus to Moise “Moses” Carelus. He now faces a primary, but not from Barry. She is running as an independent.
On the Republican side, the only primary getting attention turns on the Republican Party working to defeat convention-endorsed candidate Jadon MacCormack of Brooklyn over his homophobic statements.
Rep. William Pizzuto of Middlebury is the only Republican incumbent facing a primary.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Company at center of NJ voter registration scandal has multiple state contracts
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill has blamed state contractor Idemia for allowing non-citizens to register to vote. The company has three multimillion-dollar contracts with New Jersey.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill has blamed state contractor Idemia for allowing non-citizens to register to vote. The company has three multimillion-dollar contracts with New Jersey. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The French company under fire after Gov. Mikie Sherrill blamed it for allowing non-citizens to register to vote holds three multimillion-dollar contracts with the state of New Jersey.


Besides the contract with the state Motor Vehicle Commission that is at the center of the voter registration debacle, the company, Idemia, also holds contracts to handle fingerprinting for the New Jersey State Police and a third one to provide fingerprinting, background searches, and other services for various state agencies, state records show.


State taxpayers have paid the company about $61.1 million so far total, the records show.


A spokesman for Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who said last week that her administration is moving to terminate Idemia’s contract with the motor vehicle agency, declined to say whether the other two contracts are in jeopardy. Idemia, which has denied responsibility for registering non-citizens, did not respond to a request for comment.


Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex), who is among the Republicans who has called for a bipartisan legislative committee to investigate the voter registration matter, said it doesn’t make sense for the Sherrill administration to target only Idemia’s contract with the Motor Vehicle Commission.


“If Idemia really was the problem here and lost the state’s confidence, why would we be concerned with that and not actual background checks?” she said.


Sherrill last week announced that about 6,600 non-citizens had been added to the state voter rolls for a year starting in June 2023 because of what she called a software glitch on Idemia’s part. She said non-citizens who were prompted at the agency to say whether they were citizens would respond no, but the software identified them as citizens anyway. About 400 of them cast ballots, she said.


Sherrill said Thursday that the motor vehicle commissioner had moved to end Idemia’s work with the agency because the company “was at the heart” of the agency’s failures.


“The commissioner was already in the process of removing them for their incompetence,” Sherrill said.


Idemia’s contract to assist with enhanced driver’s licenses was issued in January 2010 and ends in January 2027. It has been paid $35.7 million so far, records show.


It also holds a contract with the State Police related to an electronic fingerprinting system, a contract that started in January 2019, runs through January 2027, and has cost the state roughly $3.8 million so far, the records show.


Another contract that began in May 2019 and expires in May 2027 allows Idemia to provide electronic fingerprinting for background checks and other “noncriminal justice purposes” for agencies across state government. New Jersey has spent about $21.6 million on that contract to date, the records show.


Fantasia thinks moving to sever Idemia’s contract now would be a mistake. She said she does not believe Sherrill’s story that the 6,600 non-citizens were registered because of a software error.


“Without an investigation, I think we’re setting ourselves up for a serious lawsuit,” Fantasia said. “If the flag we’re carrying is we’re getting rid of them because of this software glitch, that has yet to be proven. That’s an assertion by the governor. The vendor denies it. So to me, that’s hardly irrefutable evidence.”


The company is also a contractor with the federal government. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat, last week requested a government-wide audit of every federal contract involving Idemia, suggesting there could be a deeper problem as the company “sits at the center of the federal government’s identity, screening, and border infrastructure.” He pointed to contracts for TSA PreCheck, U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s biometric entry-exit system, and identity operations at the U.S. Department of Defense, including contracts with driver’s license systems in 36 states.


“A ‘small’ software issue like what happened in New Jersey could, right now, be allowing improperly vetted individuals to enter our airports and board our airplanes,” Gottheimer told federal budget officials last week.


Sherrill has blamed the administration of her predecessor, Phil Murphy (D), in addition to Idemia because the problem started when he was governor. Sherrill took office in January.


Murphy spokesman Mahen Gunaratna said Friday that Murphy was unaware of this issue before Sherrill brought it to light this week.


The registration matter has drawn national attention, including criticism from President Donald Trump. The Trump administration is suing New Jersey over the state’s refusal to hand over unredacted voter roll information. U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has alleged that more than 35,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in New Jersey.
Dana DiFilippo contributed.

title: Warren County eyes slaughterhouse as solution for NJ’s road-weary livestock farmers
description: New Jersey's livestock farmers often travel hours for meat-processing, because of a statewide lack of USDA-approved slaughterhouses.
text:
New Jersey's livestock farmers typically travel hours out of state to take cattle, poultry and other animals for meat-processing, because of a statewide lack of facilities approved by the USDA to butcher and package meat for individual sale. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Third-generation farmer Chad Muckenfuss raises cattle, pigs, and chickens on his sprawling farm in Medford, continually rotating livestock around 120 acres in a regenerative approach that keeps both the animals and the pastures healthier than factory farming.
It’s a model that has kept the Muckenfuss family farm successful, with a steady stream of customers devoted to organic meats. There’s only one problem.
“All of my meats are processed two-plus hours one-way over in Pennsylvania,” he said.
New Jersey has no slaughterhouse certified by the U.S. Department of Agriculture where the state’s livestock farmers can get animals butchered for individual cuts, a shortcoming that forces farmers to haul them long distances to out-of-state facilities that are so backlogged many have monthslong waits.
Industry advocates are trying to change that, with plans to open a meat-processing center in rural Warren County by late 2028.
But it has been slow going.
More than a decade ago, Rutgers University researchers warned of a “sharp decline” in slaughter plants since the mid-20th century and its economic toll especially on smaller livestock farmers. In 2019, New Jersey agriculture officials landed federal funding to study the feasibility of creating a centrally located regional processing facility or on-farm processing and inspections. And Warren County commissioners, calling in a 2021 resolution for a slaughterhouse to be sited there, noted the county’s status as the state’s top livestock producer and warned the absence of a processing plant was “unsustainable.”
Joe Labarbera, director of the agriculture and economic development program at Warren County Community College, blames the poky progress on “a cultural misunderstanding” about agricultural development. Public officials at every level of government have prioritized preservation and lost focus on supply-chain economics, he charged.
“They’re saving the farmland, but they’re not saving the farmer,” Labarbera said.
But some state officials who support the Warren County proposal are working to change that.
Sen. Doug Steinhardt (Hal Brown for New Jersey Monitor)
Sen. Douglas Steinhardt (R-Warren) introduced three bills last month that would speed up permitting, expand the workforce, and create tax incentives for slaughter plants and other projects that support agriculture.
New Jersey Agriculture Secretary Ed Wengryn anticipates construction will be underway within the next 18 months.
“This is really critical for our livestock industry,” Wengryn said.
 A decades-long decline
Suburban sprawl gobbled up so many agricultural acres in the Garden State since the 1970s that the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2011 named New Jersey the nation’s leader in farmland loss.
As farms disappeared, so did their support industries like slaughterhouses.
Policymakers scrambled to preserve farmland, permanently protecting about 250,000 acres in the past 45 years, even as the state auditor found the state should be doing more.
Ben Spinelli, executive director of the New Jersey Highlands Water Protection and Planning Council, agrees the state’s work is far from done. The state-created council, which protects natural resources and oversees development in a hilly and forested 1,300-mile stretch of North Jersey, supported the Warren County slaughterhouse proposal with a $150,000 planning grant in 2023.
“I believe that we have come to the end of the decline of agriculture in New Jersey, and we’re in a place where agriculture is going to rebound,” Spinelli said. “Now we have to take a look and see where the opportunities are to bring back not just the farmers and the farming, but the support industries that make what they do possible.”
Vegetables, soybeans, and fruits may be New Jersey’s biggest agricultural commodities, but more than 24,000 cattle graze on Garden State farms, according to USDA data. Farmers here also raise hogs, chickens, turkeys, and other animals for their meat.
The USDA listed about 45 slaughter plants and markets in New Jersey in 2021, the most recent data available, but most were rendering plants (that handle animal bones and other byproduct after meat is cut), bulk butchers (that don’t cut and package for individual sale), and specialty services (like halal butchers).
Chad Muckenfuss is a third-generation farmer who must haul his animals more than two hours from his farm in Medford to meat-processing plants in Pennsylvania, because New Jersey has no USDA-approved slaughterhouses that butcher meat for individually packaged sale. (Photo courtesy of Michael Paras Photography)
With no in-state slaughter plant to take his animals for individual cuts, Muckenfuss treks his cattle to a butcher in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, and his poultry to a plant in Gettysburg. The trips stress the animals, add time and costs that ultimately inflate meat prices for customers, and require scheduling that can impact his whole year and beyond, he said.
“I have to commit to all of the animals that I’m going to process a year in advance with these processors, because they’re so backed up,” he said. “But the flip side of that is, we had a very harsh winter this past winter, so most of the cattle lost a little bit of weight. In order to meet my deadlines, I can’t just magically have them gain weight, so I have to cancel reservations that I had. And you only get a certain number. Once you give up slots, it’s very difficult to gain them back again for the following year.”
The butchers’ backlog means that Muckenfuss and other livestock farmers often have limited cuts for sale. Customers who try to order Muckenfuss’ meat online sometimes “just see ‘out of stock,’ and it could be out of stock for four months,” he said.
In Hillsborough, such challenges drove Lima Family Farms to take the unusual step of opening its own private USDA-inspected slaughterhouse on site in 2023.
“During Covid was when we decided that we needed to open our own facility, because if they were closed down, we couldn’t get our animals in. And our customers still wanted the meat,” said Abigail Blanchard, who manages the farm’s store. “Now the animals don’t have to leave the property, which is great for them.”
But that’s a solution out of reach for many farmers, because it’s expensive. The USDA requires inspectors to have their own office and bathroom on site and to observe processing from start to finish.
Muckenfuss hopes the public’s growing concerns about the path meat takes before it appears in store refrigerator cases will spur change.
“‘Buy local,’ and the pushback on lab-grown meats is a real driver for people wanting to know where their meats come from. It is becoming more and more of a political agenda item, as opposed to before, where everyone was like, ‘Well, if they got to drive to Pennsylvania, then let them drive to Pennsylvania,’” he said.
He supports the Warren County plan but also thinks the industry needs multiple slaughterhouses around the state.
Cows graze on pastures at the Medford Cattle Farms in South Jersey. (Photo courtesy of Chad Muckenfuss)
 From litter to livestock
In Warren County, the proposal known as the Northwest Jersey Processing and Innovation Center may be closest to completion, with a site identified, partnerships cemented, and seed funding secured.
Still, even those who welcome the center have voiced environmental, cost, and other concerns.
The 21-acre site, where the old Covanta trash incinerator and recycling plant operated for 30 years in Oxford, has contaminated soil that requires remediation. That’s underway, said Jason Hahn, a spokesman for Reworld, formerly known as Covanta.
Funding uncertainties also have held up development.
Construction will cost $12 million, Labarbera estimated. That is not yet funded.
The center last spring landed $980,000 in federal funding, earmarked for Warren County Community College to expand programs to train butchers and food sanitation workers and buy instructional equipment. That’s an annual grant for four years, totaling close to $4 million, Labarbera said.
And one of the bills Steinhardt introduced would provide $3 million in state funding to further expand vocational training. Industry insiders say a longstanding labor shortage in the meatpacking industry, which historically has relied on immigrant workers, is likely to worsen as the Trump administration carries out its mass deportation mission.
Who ultimately will own the site and center also has proven controversial. The county owns the site and plans to donate it to the community college, with the commissioners passing a resolution in April to do so despite objections from residents about smell, traffic, foreign laborers, and cost.
Commissioner Jason J. Sarnoski shared some residents’ concern about removing the property from the tax rolls and voted against the resolution, saying he supported the plan in concept but opposed giving away publicly owned property.
“It is an asset and giving away an asset is not in the best fiscal interest of the taxpayers and not the best fiscal interest of the county,” Sarnoski said.
Labarbera told the New Jersey Monitor that such an “obsession with rateables” does not serve the broader economy well.
“Anytime you try to do anything in New Jersey, you come up to this combination of a fight over rateables and a fight over ‘Well, we don’t want this in our town.’ Almost like a town is an HOA instead of a town,” Labarbera said.
He expects the critics will quiet down as they learn how the slaughterhouse will help New Jersey’s livestock farmers.
The center is expected to handle 6,000 animals in its first year and as many as 17,000 by its fourth year, employ 55 people, and train the next generation of meat-processing professionals, he said. He envisions the college eventually opening satellite slaughter plants elsewhere in the state, with an overarching goal of growing the industry.
“This is bigger than just a meat processing plant,” Labarbera said. “This is truly a benefit for the entire state of New Jersey. This is going to give New Jersey a sustainable local supply chain that is going to be able to withstand economic disruptions, power surges, and pandemics.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Critics call for more details about Stratos data center in Utah’s west desert
description: Critics of the Stratos data center are pushing for more details on the plan and criticizing the rapid pace of early approvals for the project.
text:
The sun rises over a part of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, near the proposed Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for 40,000 acres of land, on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Rhonda Lauritzen returned earlier this month to the beach on the northern tip of the Great Salt Lake where she splashed around as a kid. But this time, she was surrounded by dry mud, with no water in sight. 
Lauritzen brought reporters to Monument Point as she and other critics made their case against the proposed Stratos data center in the neighboring Hansel Valley. They wanted to see more than the lake, though, including information on potential environmental costs and which company would move in. The rapid rollout of the project backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary of TV’s “Shark Tank” was also top of mind.  
“The lack of transparency makes me insane,” Lauritzen told Utah News Dispatch. “I mean, that is not what we stand for as a society in America, in Utah, it’s not how we should be doing business, and it just feels like that pendulum has swung so far that maybe it finally swung far enough to wake people up.”
Rhonda Lauritzen and her brother Val Anderson are pictured near Monument Point in Box Elder County on July 13, 2026. They brought a large photograph of their father, taken in the same area decades ago. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
As more data centers have cropped up across the country, they’ve brought up concerns including rising power bills and water contamination, transforming the concept of artificial intelligence from something abstract to a topic of discussion at the kitchen table, said Christabel Randolph, associate director of the nonprofit Center for AI and Digital Policy, based in Washington, D.C.
“And at the same time, it’s a real transparency and democratic governance issue,” Randolph said. “People want to know why their leaders are approving these projects when folks are not sure what they’re getting in return.”
In Box Elder County, a citizens’ group has gone to court to pursue a referendum allowing voters to undo the county’s approval.
Stratos developers say the project would bring an initial $30 million to the county and a permanent 2,000 skilled jobs, higher than the 50 jobs data centers typically provide, according to a 2024 Virginia legislative audit of the industry in that state. 
In terms of water, backers say the project wouldn’t draw directly from the Great Salt Lake and would use two kinds of cooling systems to keep servers from overheating: a closed-loop system circulating liquid and air-based cooling. 
They’re also seeking water rights for more than 13,000 acre-feet — enough to supply 26,000 households per year — saying those rights are attached to the land they’re buying. But they contend the data center would use less water than the ranchers there do now. 
Abandoned buildings are pictured at Locomotive Springs on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Lauritzen, a resident of neighboring Weber County, who with her brothers runs a business extracting minerals from the lake for use in supplements, said she has concerns the data center’s water consumption will actually be higher. 
“We’re adding to an ecosystem that’s already beyond crisis,” she said. 
Utah lawmakers are doing their own research. At the state Capitol in May, a natural resources panel voted to study impacts from data center development on water, wildlife and air quality  ahead of the 2027 legislative session, though they didn’t name Stratos and haven’t analyzed the issue publicly yet. 
This is the first year Utah is requiring large data centers to report their water use to the state, but the numbers will be reported to the public in the aggregate under HB76. The law allows data centers to raise claims of business confidentiality to keep their information from being broken out individually.

In April, the data center proposal cleared an initial round of approval from Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA. Hundreds protested 10 days later at a meeting of the three-member Box Elder County Commission, which did not take public comment before it gave unanimous support to the project, while others have converged on the Utah Capitol in opposition. 
Rhonda Lauritzen speaks during a rally at the Utah Capitol against the 40,000-acre Stratos data center in Box Elder County. (Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch)
In response to outcry across the state, Gov. Spencer Cox signed an executive order he said would raise the bar for how Utah evaluates data center proposals, noting they need permits tied to air and water quality. And O’Leary made a concession, halving the project size in response to demands from Senate President Stuart Adams, who had earlier voted to advance it as chair of the MIDA board. 
MIDA, for its part, is pledging a transparent process, to include the creation of a Box Elder County development review committee. The authority said through a spokesperson that the project’s developers would carry out every environmental test required by the state and federal government. 
But an attempt to put a referendum on the ballot and a separate lawsuit filed against MIDA by the left-leaning Alliance for a Better Utah have complicated its path forward. 
“Out of respect for the referendum process and litigation, MIDA is paused on Stratos,” the authority’s spokesperson, Kristin Kenney Williams, said in a statement. 
Adams went on to lose his legislative seat in the Republican primary, a stunning political upset for one of Utah’s most powerful politicians. But as the political dust settles, it’s still not clear exactly how and when Utahns will learn more about the evolving plan. 
Adams had announced early in June that a new source of information on the proposal was on its way, saying “to ensure transparency and public accountability, a centralized public-facing website will be created in coordination with state agencies, so Utahns have access to project information, review materials, environmental analyses and updates as policymakers do throughout the process.” 
While the state hasn’t put up a new portal, Stratos developers have launched their own website aimed at sharing information with the public, but haven’t committed publicly to any schedule of updates. O’Leary Digital did not respond to a request for comment from Utah News Dispatch.
Rhonda Lauritzen and Ben Abbott of Grow the Flow speak with journalists at a stock tank in rural Box Elder County on July 13, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
After a Utah State University professor warned in May of the “extreme” heat the project and its gas power plant could generate — raising temperatures by upward of 20 degrees at night — Stratos backers and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox rejected those estimates as inaccurate. 
Ben Abbott, executive director of conservation group Grow the Flow, said he questions why the developers didn’t fill the information gap first by releasing their own numbers and a plan to manage the effects. 
“This kind of rollout really harms public trust and makes it difficult to do things the right way,” Abbott said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Raising state revenues is essential to protecting vital services for Michiganders
description: State policy and budget leaders have finalized the fiscal year (FY) 2026-2027 state budget, and, while it contains some important investments that are worth celebrating, it also leaves out something that is essential to protecting vital services for Michiganders: ways in which to raise revenue. This is especially important in the wake of the passage […]
text:
Flags atop Michigan State Capitol Building | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceState policy and budget leaders have finalized the fiscal year (FY) 2026-2027 state budget, and, while it contains some important investments that are worth celebrating, it also leaves out something that is essential to protecting vital services for Michiganders: ways in which to raise revenue.
This is especially important in the wake of the passage of the so-called “One Big, Beautiful Bill Act” by Congress last year, which has left the state and those who live here bracing for significant federal funding cuts to essential social safety net programs like Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
These cuts, which were made to give significant tax breaks to the wealthiest among us, will shift insurmountable costs to Michigan and cause harm to people living in every county across our state. This includes many of the estimated 40% of Michigan households already struggling to afford basic needs.
With SNAP benefits paused, Michigan recipients, advocates and lawmakers determine how to respond

Federal changes have already resulted in very real budget impacts in states like Michigan. For example, the state has had to invest more funding in SNAP for administrative costs as well as hiring costs for new staff who can work to make sure that new federal eligibility requirements are met. And the negative impact on the state’s budget will only continue to grow because changes are slated to be implemented over several years.
It’s important to recognize that raising revenues is critical to addressing Michigan’s present-day and future budget challenges; however, we here at the Michigan League for Public Policy understand it won’t be easy. One thing that is important to keep in mind when it comes to exploring revenue options is that, while Michigan was once considered a high-tax state, that is no longer the case.
Policy changes have reduced the so-called “tax burden” here. In fact, when you combine the total state and local taxes as a percent of personal income, Michigan currently ranks 38th in the nation, below any other state in the Great Lakes region.
The Headlee Amendment, which passed in 1978 with the approval of Michigan voters, also shows how Michigan’s revenues have room to grow. As a part of this constitutional change, Michigan’s total state tax collections are capped at 9.49% of personal income. However, this revenue limit was last met back in 2000.
If state tax collections would have simply kept pace with personal income since 2000, the state would have an additional $14 billion for the critical needs of Michiganders right now. These critical needs include things like healthcare, food assistance, education and childcare.
Options for raising state revenue include raising taxes on profitable corporations, ensuring flow-through businesses pay the same tax rate as traditional corporations and considering the various policy solutions that would increase taxes for the wealthiest Michiganders. Michigan currently doesn’t have any wealth taxes and they are seldom used in our country despite their revenue raising potential.
Raising the capital gains tax rate higher than the income tax rate, expanding the real estate tax,  installing a progressive mansion tax rate, and decoupling from the federal estate tax and implementing either a state inheritance or estate tax are just a few ways Michigan can ensure that wealthy Michiganders are paying their fair share and reduce inequality in the state.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
We at the League have also long advocated for the state to enact a graduated income tax, so those who earn the most pay a fairer share of their income in taxes. Right now that is not the case as Michigan has a flat income tax of 4.25%, meaning that everyone from all income groups pays the same tax rate. This is deeply unfair for Michiganders earning the least in our state — they pay the largest share of their income in taxes.
Tax increases on commodities like tobacco and gambling to increase funding for healthcare are also great examples of common sense ways in which the state could raise revenue while improving the health and well-being of Michiganders. We lauded Gov. Gretchen Whitmer for proposing this in her executive budget earlier this year and we were disappointed to see that it was not included in the state’s final budget agreement.
These are just a few of the avenues in which state lawmakers could address current and forecasted state budget challenges to ensure vital services for Michiganders do not need to be reduced or cut completely. It’s important for our legislators to understand that there are ways for the state to adequately and equitably raise revenues so the services that Michiganders depend upon do not continue to be placed in jeopardy.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Parents worry WA developmental disabilities program is about to get axed
description: Parents of children with developmental disabilities fear the unexpected and potentially imminent elimination of a Washington state support program they’ve come to depend on. As the state deals with budget troubles, Washington officials say the Parent to Parent program’s future isn’t guaranteed past August. Parent to Parent provides support and resources for[...]
text:
The Washington state Capitol in Olympia on March 7, 2026. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)Parents of children with developmental disabilities fear the unexpected and potentially imminent elimination of a Washington state support program they’ve come to depend on.
As the state deals with budget troubles, Washington officials say the Parent to Parent program’s future isn’t guaranteed past August.
Parent to Parent provides support and resources for families of children with autism and other developmental disabilities. The program’s name comes from its pairing of newer parents with more experienced ones to help guide them through the complicated system of resources, as well as provide support and community. It also features “sibshops” to support siblings of people with developmental disabilities.
The first Parent to Parent program in Washington was established in 1980 in King County. Today, it serves families of children and adults in all of Washington’s 39 counties, with tens of thousands of calls and emails for assistance every year.
Parents believe the program, costing about $900,000 a year, is invaluable, and can’t be replicated or recreated if state funding disappears. 
“We fill in the gaps for areas where government really can’t provide this kind of support,” said Stacy Dym, executive director of The Arc of Washington State, an organization advocating for people with developmental disabilities. The Arc oversees the statewide program under a contract with the state Department of Social and Health Services.
‘Completely taken aback’
This comes as Gov. Bob Ferguson has pledged not to propose tax increases in his two-year budget proposal later this year. Instead, the first-term Democrat says he’ll rely on cuts as the state faces another, potential multibillion-dollar shortfall. He has specifically cited programs created or expanded after 2019 as possible targets for reductions. Lawmakers will pass a new budget working off the governor’s blueprint next year.
Parent to Parent received funding in the current budget. But advocates are worried the Department of Social and Health Services is letting contracts lapse, trying to get ahead of budget talks. Dym was “completely taken aback.” 
“It’s destructive, and it doesn’t make a lot of sense, and probably would cost more to rebuild the infrastructure,” said Cathy Murahashi, advocacy and policy specialist at The Arc.
Agency spokesperson Jessica Nelson said “no funding decisions have been made for Parent to Parent or any other DSHS program.”
“Budget conversations are ongoing and must consider our state and federal funding,” Nelson said in an email. “Our goal is to meet the challenge of the moment in a way that sustainably protects core services and ensures that Washington has a solid financial foundation for the long-term.”

She said the agency doesn’t have a timeline for a decision on the future of Parent to Parent, but the program’s contract only runs through August. Initially, it was only through July, but state officials extended it another month.
Dym is frustrated with the process, as usually decisions on spending cuts are subject to public hearings in the Legislature.
“We didn’t get any of that notice,” she said. “We just got told that the contract is under review, and there’s a good chance it won’t be renewed. “
‘It’s everything to our family’
Jenna Vogel first encountered the program at a “breaking point” when her son, Jonah, was 2  years old. Jonah has Level 2 autism and complications from being born premature. Unable to find support for her child, she felt she was failing. Vogel’s husband was working extra hours, as she left her job.
Parent to Parent, which Vogel accessed through Children’s Village in Yakima, made her feel for the first time her family wasn’t alone. 
“They understand everything that you’re going through, the grief and the joy that exists in every day, and they walk through it with you,” Vogel said. “It’s everything to our family.”
Services the program can connect parents to include therapies, doctors to get an official diagnosis, caregiving, educational and employment help, Social Security support for people with disabilities, and other safety net resources. 
Vogel, for example, was able to get caregiving services for Jonah, now 7. After leaving her career as an accountant, helping connect families to Parent to Parent has become her purpose. Its end is unimaginable, she said.
Parent support groups have also been helpful for Claudia Ramirez, whose 9-year-old son has autism. Like Vogel, she felt isolated, like no one understood what she was going through. Hearing from parents with similar experiences made her feel seen. They’ve become her best friends. 
“We hang out and we talk and there’s no judgment,” Ramirez said. “I tell my husband ‘I don’t have friends that don’t have kids with disabilities’ because I don’t feel comfortable, because they don’t understand.”
Without Parent to Parent, families will still need services, but it’ll just be harder to find them, advocates say.

“You can cut us,” Dym said, “but the people and the issues and concerns they have don’t go away.”

title: Reproductive Freedom for All announces six-figure Michigan canvassing investment
description: Reproductive Freedom for All, one of the largest reproductive rights nonprofits nationwide, announced Monday a six-figure investment in a Michigan canvassing effort in advance of the November midterm elections.  The investment is part of the organization’s “My Body. My Ballot.” campaign — $23.5 million going to the group’s “largest-ever midterm electoral pro[...]
text:
A sign at the Michigan Pride rally in Lansing on June 26, 2022. | Photo by Laina G. StebbinsReproductive Freedom for All, one of the largest reproductive rights nonprofits nationwide, announced Monday a six-figure investment in a Michigan canvassing effort in advance of the November midterm elections. 
The investment is part of the organization’s “My Body. My Ballot.” campaign — $23.5 million going to the group’s “largest-ever midterm electoral program and will focus on persuading and mobilizing voters – including independents, soft Republicans, and split-ticket voters – whose support for abortion access puts them at odds with Trump and his endorsed candidates.” 
Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, currently represented by Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte, was listed as one of the campaign’s top-tier targets. 
“Even with the protections we fought hard to pass here in Michigan, we know our reproductive freedom is not safe from extreme anti-abortion Republicans. We still feel the nationwide attacks on funding and access. Reproductive freedom will be a defining issue in November, and Michigan voters deserve to know exactly where the candidates stand,” Reproductive Freedom for All Director of Michigan Campaigns Shanay Watson-Whittaker said in a press release.
The group specifically named Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the frontrunner for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination in the Aug. 4 primary, as well as Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, who are the Democratic nominees for Secretary of State and Attorney General, respectively, as “champions for reproductive freedom.” The press release did not name any candidates in highly contested Democratic primaries — including for the 7th Congressional District and the U.S. Senate. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group also announced on Monday that its president and CEO, Mini Timmaraju, will travel to Michigan in August to join candidates, organizers and advocates.
The press release also specifically targeted Barrett and fellow Republican U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, who is running for governor with the endorsement of President Donald Trump in a primary against businessman Perry Johnson, for their support of “devastating Medicaid cuts that threaten reproductive, preventive, and essential health care, while standing with a movement determined to push abortion care further out of reach,” Watson-Whittaker continued.
The press release cited an internal study based on a focus group and survey of voters who did not vote for Kamala Harris but who voted “Yes” on abortion referendums in Arizona, Michigan, or Nevada. It found that, among battleground voters, 43% considered a politician that supports a national abortion ban to be a dealbreaker — just a slightly lower percentage than a politician who supports raising taxes on middle class families or cutting Medicaid. 
“Most battleground voters are not hearing about the issue of abortion, so while many express concerns about Republican policies that restrict access to abortion, they also believe these policies are unlikely to happen,” a summary of the survey results said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: After voucher data leak, Missouri treasurer’s office pointed at its contractor
description: Newly released emails show that when the Missouri State Treasurer’s Office learned in April that spreadsheets on its website unintentionally exposed the names of students receiving private school vouchers, it downplayed the leak to families and drafted a statement blaming its software contractor. That provider says that is not where the problem started. And[...]
text:
Missouri State Treasurer Vivek Malek, pictured testifying in a Missouri Senate committee hearing in January 2024, has shared concerns about edtech company ClassWallet. When his office learned that a public report contained MOScholars student information, staff shifted blame toward the software provider in statements sent to educational assistance organizations. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)Newly released emails show that when the Missouri State Treasurer’s Office learned in April that spreadsheets on its website unintentionally exposed the names of students receiving private school vouchers, it downplayed the leak to families and drafted a statement blaming its software contractor.
That provider says that is not where the problem started. And the file itself carries markers suggesting it passed through a treasurer’s office employee’s computer before it was published.
Missouri treasurer’s office posted MOScholars student data on its website for nearly a year

The data — student names, parents’ email addresses, the schools and vendors paid through the program and each scholarship amount — sat on the treasurer’s website in downloadable spreadsheets for months.
These reports are required by a 2024 state law that mandates certain demographic information about MOScholars participants be published each year while ensuring “no personally identifiable information of any student” is disclosed.
One file presented the required figures in a table built with Microsoft Excel’s PivotTable function. The underlying records were reachable from that table in a few clicks.
The treasurer’s office said in its statement that the vulnerability was “fully resolved immediately upon notification.” It took several days to get the file pulled from internet archive sites.
Emails obtained by The Independent under the Missouri Sunshine Law show the office sent the seven educational assistance organizations that administer MOScholars a draft statement on April 20 — two business days after being told about the leak. Those organizations are families’ main point of contact with the program.
“Recently, the contracted application and fiscal management platform confirmed that the underlying data set generated for publication could potentially be manipulated to view unpublished information,” the statement began.
The Independent alerted the treasurer’s office the morning of April 16, minutes before the organizations’ monthly meeting, and published a story April 21 that did not reveal the specific route to find this information.
 A change in providers

At the time of the data leak, the treasurer’s office used a company called ClassWallet to facilitate payments and track student enrollment with ClassWallet’s partner FACTS Management. ClassWallet is the largest software provider in the school-choice space, with contracts with the nation’s largest voucher programs like Florida and Arizona.
The company has drawn scrutiny before, most notably in Arizona where a permissions error let a parent view payment requests of other users, prompting an investigation by the Arizona Department of Homeland Security. Last year, State Treasurer Vivek Malek talked about letting ClassWallet’s contract expire, which eventually happened last month after a competitive bidding process.
But Missouri’s leak was not inside ClassWallet’s interface. It was on the treasurer’s own website.
The file downloaded from the treasurer’s website gives the name of the data source: a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet called “MoScholars Distro Amounts,” with a sheet labeled “All Time Raw Data.” The path also points to the account of Trent Blair, the treasurer’s director of programs.
The office, which has said little publicly, has not said whether it created the document.
Asked about the data in April, Malek’s chief of staff, Jackson Bailey, said: “The spreadsheet was compiled by the third‑party application and fiscal management platform that houses and maintains the data and is contractually obligated to provide expenditure information for publication.”
ClassWallet spokesperson Jason Hart said the platform provides “complete, unredacted exports of the data to the client for use at their discretion.
“How that data is then handled, shared, or reflected in any public-facing report,” he added, “is a determination made solely by the client.”
Nothing in the contract requires that the downloadable reports be ready for public posting, Hart said.
That contract, signed in 2022 prior to the law requiring certain annual reports, has two parts: the request for proposals from the state and ClassWallet’s offer. ClassWallet’s response characterizes the data’s purpose as “compliance monitoring and preparing for the audit.”
The request for proposals has few requirements for the data, though it notes that confidential information should be encrypted.
“We have a number of privacy measures in place designed to protect student information within the platform,” Hart said. “However, once data is exported and submitted to the treasurer’s office, it falls outside of the scope of our contract.”
In April, the office entered a contract with edtech company Odyssey after a bidding process led by the Missouri Office of Administration.
The bidding process this time around included additional requirements for the software provider, saying it should “allow the MOScholars program administrator to create ad-hoc reports” and “provide customizable dashboards and reports, including data updates.”
“The contractor shall use safeguards designed to prevent the inappropriate use or disclosure of the state’s proprietary or confidential information,” the office’s request says.
The contract’s definition of “state data” includes personally identifiable information, which it says is “any information that identifies an individual, such as an individual’s social security number or other government-issued identification number, date of birth, address, telephone number, biometric data, mother’s maiden name, email address, credit card information, or an individual’s name in combination with any other of the elements listed herein.”
The office now publishes the reports as PDFs, as most states with similar programs do.
 ‘Directory information’

The statement the organizations were asked to pass along to parents described the exposure as “limited to directory information,” which it said “United States Department of Education guidance acknowledges is not generally considered harmful or an invasion of privacy if disclosed.”
The records went further than that. They paired student names with parents’ email addresses. And the scholarship amounts carried something more: students with an individualized education plan qualify for 160% of the base award, so the figure indicates which children have disabilities.
Under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, schools are allowed to provide student directory information. But there is a requirement that schools give notice about what it considers directory information and allow parents to opt out.

title: Former DOJ lawyer blames Missouri senators for inciting death threats against her
description: WASHINGTON — Former Justice Department lawyer Elizabeth Oyer has posted a video to YouTube blaming Missouri Republican Sens. Eric Schmitt and Josh Hawley for an onslaught of hate messages and death threats she has received. “Hey everybody,” Oyer said in the video. “I started getting death threats after I testified against Todd Blanche last week.” […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt speaks to reporters after the Governor's Ham Breakfast at the Missouri State Fair in Sedalia in August 2024 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).WASHINGTON — Former Justice Department lawyer Elizabeth Oyer has posted a video to YouTube blaming Missouri Republican Sens. Eric Schmitt and Josh Hawley for an onslaught of hate messages and death threats she has received.
“Hey everybody,” Oyer said in the video. “I started getting death threats after I testified against Todd Blanche last week.”
Blanche has been nominated to be attorney general by President Donald Trump, and Schmitt and Hawley sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee, which must make an initial vote on his nomination.
Oyer’s video shows images of several emails she received, many of which came from fake email addresses and contained messages such as, “Die in hell you pos,” “I hope you die tragically,” “Let’s hope somebody murders your family and gets clemency,” and other threatening messages containing obscenities.
“Two Republican senators with a political agenda rage-baited their followers into believing nasty and dangerous lies,” she states, referencing Hawley and Schmitt.
The committee’s July 16 hearing had five witnesses, including Oyer, who was the pardoning attorney for the Department of Justice for 13 years. In her written testimony to the committee, Oyer said she was fired by Blanche after she refused to restore firearm rights for actor and filmmaker Mel Gibson, a close friend of Trump.
The hearing was meant to consider the pending nomination of Blanche. Schmitt and Hawley, however, did not ask Oyer about Blanche. Instead, they drilled her about the recommendation she made to President Joe Biden to commute 40 people’s federal death sentences to life in prison without parole.
“You personally recommended commuting all 40 death sentence cases, an even broader action than Biden took,” Schmitt said in the hearing.
Biden commuted 37 of the death sentences.
Schmitt was unable to be immediately reached for comment, but a spokesperson commented on his behalf.
“(Liz Oyer’s) disgraceful clemency recommendations ignored the victims’ families’ concerns and were so extreme that even Joe Biden’s autopen handlers couldn’t stomach them,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
Hawley confronted Oyer with photos of the parolees, many of whom committed violent acts of rape and murder. He showed photos of the victims and referenced them by name. In an interview with the Missourian, Hawley said that these were the real victims, not Oyer.
“The people who were murdered, and devastated and raped by the criminals that she recommended that President Biden give clemency to, those folks are the real victims here,” Hawley said. “I was proud to tell their stories.”
In her video, Oyer said that Hawley had misrepresented her by claiming that she had sympathy for the perpetrators of the crimes.
“That is dangerous misinformation, and Josh Hawley knows it,” Oyer said in the video.
In response, Hawley said that he had read from memos that Oyer sent.
“She tried to weasel her way out of it, and say she hadn’t said this or that,” Hawley said. “We have the memos, and I put them in the record.”
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Missouri Independent
title: The weird world of Missouri campaign B-roll
description: It’s one of my favorite times of the election year: B-roll season. Across Missouri, candidates are posting B-roll — the wordless, context-free footage ad-makers layer under narration — so the political action committees they’re legally barred from coordinating with can stumble upon it and cut it into ads. All of it perfectly legal, thanks to […]
text:
Candidates bury raw footage online so independent political committees can turn it into TV ads — producing some of Missouri politics’ strangest videos (Getty Images). It’s one of my favorite times of the election year: B-roll season.
Across Missouri, candidates are posting B-roll — the wordless, context-free footage ad-makers layer under narration — so the political action committees they’re legally barred from coordinating with can stumble upon it and cut it into ads. All of it perfectly legal, thanks to the U.S. Supreme Court’s touching faith that money spent “independently” can’t corrupt anyone.
They don’t make it easy to find, often burying footage in unlisted YouTube videos, public Google Drive folders and campaign website pages coded so search engines pretend they don’t exist — public enough to be found, hidden enough that no actual voter will ever stumble across it.
But to those bored enough to dig, the results are often hilarious.
Do you want to watch Republican 5th Congressional District hopeful Taylor Burks chat in slow motion with an unidentified gentleman in front of a tank, accompanied by what I presume is royalty-free blues rock?
We got that B-roll.
What about Democrats Gina Mitten and Steve Butz, running against each other for a St. Louis-based seat in the Missouri Senate, marching down courthouse steps or thumbing through family photos?
We got that B-roll.
Or perhaps you’d prefer 15 seconds of Democratic St. Louis County executive candidate Brian Williams smiling into the camera, followed by 15 seconds of him turning very serious?
We got that B-roll.
Missouri didn’t invent this. In 2014, Mitch McConnell’s campaign posted two minutes of the senator silently smiling at the camera; Jon Stewart turned it into a meme (“McConnelling”), and a pro-McConnell PAC was airing the footage within 10 days.
The genre has flourished ever since — and Missouri has contributed some classics.
Among my all-time favorites: Jay Ashcroft making what appears to be a peanut butter and jelly sandwich in slow motion during his 2024 campaign for governor. Slow motion makes everything feel more profound.
I remain fond of State Treasurer Vivek Malek leaning against the border wall in Texas while the sun sets behind him. For sheer quantity, there’s 48 minutes of former Attorney General Andrew Bailey driving a tractor, fixing a barbed wire fence and standing confidently with arms folded in an alley.
But the B-roll that makes me laugh hardest came from the 2024 Democratic primary for a Kansas City seat in the Missouri Senate between Patty Lewis and Pat Contreras.
Designed, presumably, for the PAC backing Contreras, it is mostly nine minutes of people claiming to have no idea who Patty Lewis is.
The first 30 seconds alone feature an unnamed woman saying:
“Rep. Patty Lewis? Who’s that? I’ve never heard of her. Patty Lewis? She’s just another politician in Jeff City getting nothing done. Wait, who’s running for Senate? Patty Lewis? I’ve never heard of her. I think she’s a do-nothing politician. Rep. Patty Lewis? Who’s that? I’ve never heard of her. Patty Lewis? I’ve never heard of her. Patty Lewis? Has she accomplished a single thing in Jeff City?”
Nine minutes.
Someone wrote that script. Someone assembled that cast. Someone watched stranger after stranger pretend not to know who Patty Lewis is and said, “Perfect — but can we get one more?”
Lewis won the primary with more than 67% of the vote.
Ordinary campaign ads are polished attempts to manipulate voters. B-roll lets us see the raw ingredients before the manipulation begins: the candidate walking through a factory, the candidate listening intently to a farmer, the candidate laughing slightly too hard at something a small-business owner has said.
No dialogue. No context. Just hours of candidates opening doors, examining equipment and reacting warmly to comments we cannot hear.
Eventually, an independent political committee may take these images and transform them into an advertisement explaining that the candidate is either the only person capable of saving Missouri or an immediate threat to the republic.
The campaign, of course, will have had no role in that decision.
It merely posted an hour of professionally filmed, high-definition footage online, organized around the candidate’s preferred themes, for anyone who happened to need it.
Independently.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: What’s worse, an Oklahoma public official that spreads misinformation or one lacking compassion?
description: I can’t decide which Oklahoman should win top prize for biggest disconnect with reality.  Should it go to our former U.S. senator-turned-Homeland Security chief Markwayne Mullin, or to lame duck Gov. Kevin Stitt? In one corner of the ring, we have Mullin, a former MMA fighter, who had the gall to threaten to prosecute elections […]
text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, at the time a senator from Oklahoma, speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newroom)I can’t decide which Oklahoman should win top prize for biggest disconnect with reality. 
Should it go to our former U.S. senator-turned-Homeland Security chief Markwayne Mullin, or to lame duck Gov. Kevin Stitt?
In one corner of the ring, we have Mullin, a former MMA fighter, who had the gall to threaten to prosecute elections officials who refuse to “participate in securing the elections” ahead of November’s general election. His bullying came just hours after his boss, U.S. President Donald Trump, gave an unhinged speech designed to implant distrust in the security of our nation’s democratic elections by suggesting that we’re vulnerable to foreign cyberattacks and meddling.
In the other corner sits Stitt, who – during an interview with Oklahoma Voice’s sister outlet, Stateline – suggested that maybe we need to return to a time not so long ago when poor people were stigmatized for needing help feeding their hungry families. He also had the gall to suggest that churches, food banks and other charities, not the state and federal government, should bear the burden of ensuring Oklahomans are fed.
Holy guacamole, Batman. I’m so torn.
Is it worse to spread misinformation about the outcomes of our elections and threaten to imprison the very folks who are doing their best to make sure our election system functions without interference? 
Or is it a bigger sin to show so little empathy for the least among us and to demonstrate that you have a blind spot a mile wide about the realities of poverty that continue to grip every corner of this state?
Maybe it’s a tie: both of these Republican standouts are equally appalling.
In his prime time address, Trump vaguely suggested that Oklahoma was among states that had voter rolls “compromised” by supporters of the Chinese government four years ago, NPR-affiliate KOSU reported. That’s based on a document released by the federal government claims that someone affiliated with the Chinese government downloaded Oklahomans’ voter information from a commercial website. Trump cited that as a reason that states need to strengthen election security.
Even as Mullin was threatening to prosecute election officials, our state’s top election leader argued China didn’t obtain their records from Oklahoma’s own database. The Chinese government actor accessed them from a commercial site — that means a business independent of the state Election Board.
For the record, China probably couldn’t do much with that information anyhow other than annoy us with more useless mailers promoting candidates. 
You know why? That information is already publicly available, and it’s why you already get so much political junk mail as it is, so who is to say which are from foreign meddlers versus campaigns or dark money PACs?
But Mullin bizarrely insists that foreign adversaries can “change voter registration and your vote.”
That’s wrong.
So what if they get my information? They can’t vote with it because we require voter identification. They can’t tamper with my ballots because we use paper ones, which allows for recounting. If someone changes my voter registration, I receive a card in the mail reflecting that. Our voting machines don’t link to the internet, so they can’t hack them to mess with the outcomes. We also allow candidates to audit the results.
In short, running elections is one of the things Oklahoma does best, despite Mullin’s insinuations to the contrary.
Mullin, as it turns out, is also concerned about noncitizen votes canceling out those of Americans. Noncitizens are barred from voting in Oklahoma, just like they are in federal elections nationwide. 
Yet we’ve got a trusted official, hailing from our state, spouting rubbish and misinformation that’s designed to stoke fear in November’s election outcomes.
What Mullin should be doing is raising the alarm about the fact that about 1 in 5 Oklahoma voters couldn’t even exercise their right to vote for candidates in our primary elections this year. Why isn’t Mullin worried about the fact that our legislators are disenfranchising independent voters by holding closed primaries? Talk about canceling out votes.
But then we’ve got Stitt, who is yet again proving that he has no compassion for struggling Oklahoma families and no grasp of how congressional changes to the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program, better known as SNAP, are affecting them. Among the changes to the federal program: New eligibility standards, work requirements and penalties for states that overpay and underpay food stamp recipients.
Stateline reported four million Americans have already lost access to their food benefits, which has increased pressure on food banks.
Yet Stitt insists that “nobody’s going to go hungry in Oklahoma” 
“…I can assure you people were eating, getting married, graduating from high school before we even had anything called SNAP benefits,” he said.
Again, pesky facts get in the way of Republican rhetoric: People are going hungry in Oklahoma.
In fact, the Food Bank of Eastern Oklahoma reports that 14.5% of Oklahomans are food insecure, meaning they’re not sure where their next meal is coming from. We’re only 1 of 5 states that has a rate that high.
Still, Stitt insists churches and food banks and other entities will fill the gap.
With what?
Is Stitt suggesting the Legislature begin funding these programs. These charities are not boundless founts. They rely on the generosity of donors to survive, and they’re supposed to be safety net programs, not permanent replacements for federal and state programs that our tax dollars are paying for to help lift people out of poverty. 
In 2024, the U.S. Census Bureau reported that 14.9% of Oklahomans were impoverished — well above the national rate of 12.1%.
One wonders if perhaps Stitt would have more empathy if he or his children were going hungry, or if he truly understood how the federal programs work and the role that nonprofits play in this state.
So, which man is more deserving of the prize? I don’t know.
I do know that neither of these men currently is a living embodiment of the Oklahoma Standard. That philosophy – born in 1995 during the response to the Oklahoma City bombing – is supposed to promote a “culture of caring citizens” who embrace the pillars of honor, kindness and service. 
So here’s hoping moving forward that both Mullin and Stitt remember what they’re supposed to stand for.
Honor, kindness and service go a long way toward making this world a better place.

name: WyoFile
title: New data forecasts not enough workers to fill new Wyoming jobs
description:
Businesses already struggle to find workers with projected job growth on the horizon.
The post New data forecasts not enough workers to fill new Wyoming jobs appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Many Wyoming businesses already struggle to hire and retain workers. Recent data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and Wyoming Department of Workforce Services project more challenges ahead as Wyoming jobs increase and the unemployment rate rises.
It’s not a case of no jobs. Instead, it’s too many jobs without enough people to work them. 
Labor statistics
Wyoming has continually lost mining jobs, which includes the oil and gas industry, over the last several years. This isn’t new, as employment in the mining sector peaked in the fourth quarter of 2008 and has declined since. 
Wyoming’s average monthly employment in mining, oil and gas measured from the first quarter of 2015 through the fourth quarter of 2025. (Wyoming Department of Workforce Services)
However, according to the 2026 Wyoming Workforce Annual Report the number of jobs in Wyoming has remained unchanged due to growth in other fields. What has changed? The unemployment rate — or the percent of people unemployed out of the total labor force. 
Wyoming’s unemployment rate increased from 3.1% to 3.4% between 2024 and 2025, and has stayed at that rate since, according to Workforce Services. 
Wyoming’s average overall monthly employment measured from the first quarter of 2015 through the fourth quarter of 2025. (Wyoming Department of Workforce Services)
“People aren’t working for whatever reason: They’re in school or they’re taking care of a loved one or they’re for whatever reason they’re just not participating in the labor market here in Wyoming,” said Michael Moore, a research supervisor for the Workforce Services Research and Planning Division. “And so that way, we have a smaller pool to draw from with workers.”
Business impact
This smaller pool of workers is a challenge for businesses. Currently there are more jobs than workers, which hinders hiring and employee retention, Wyoming Business Alliance President Renny MacKay explained. 
“There are challenges getting the talent that businesses need. 
And so then that affects the ability for business to put in a new bid on a new project, to bring in more revenue or something,” MacKay said.
Part of these challenges can be attributed to Wyoming’s decreasing labor force, MacKay said. Wyoming’s aging population, combined with an exodus of young people from the state, makes it more difficult for businesses to fill job openings. While some people from other states have moved to Wyoming, it isn’t enough to fix the labor shortage. 
The Wyoming Business Alliance identified several factors that make it harder for  businesses to hire employees. A lack of affordable housing, a need for more educational opportunities and difficulties securing childcare impact workforce numbers. 
Problems and solutions
Housing is one of the hurdles to working in Wyoming. Some employers will make a job offer and have it accepted only for a person to not be able to find housing, specifically affordable and available housing. 
To solve this, the Wyoming Business Alliance advocates for less regulations around zoning and permitting to make it faster and easier for developers to build housing. This past session, the Legislature passed House Bill 2, “Fast Track Permits Act,” which sets specific deadlines for local governments to respond to residential building permit applications. 
Rep. Lee Filer, R-Cheyenne, seen during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne, sponsored the Fast Track Permits Act in an effort to encourage more housing development. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
Another problem is a mismatch between the jobs employers are trying to fill and the skills people have. Sometimes the right training programs aren’t offered in Wyoming or there are too few spots available. 
Gov. Mark Gordon created the Wyoming Innovation Partnership to help solve this problem. The partnership works to establish training programs in nine different categories including healthcare, energy and agriculture. Some of the programs develop degree programs at community colleges and the University of Wyoming. 
Affordable childcare is also a problem. Some families can’t afford childcare, leading people to care for their children instead of entering the labor force.  According to MacKay, it’s more affordable to open a childcare business out of a home, but zoning regulations can prohibit it. Currently the Wyoming Business Council, Wyoming Community Foundation, the Department of Family Services and Department of Workforce Services are exploring solutions. 
Wyoming outlook
Wyoming is projected to gain over 6,000 new jobs from 2025 to 2027 and over 28,000 new jobs from 2024 to 2034. The largest increase in jobs is predicted for the construction industry and specifically the speciality trades. The arts, entertainment and recreation industry is predicted to have the largest percent increase in jobs with agriculture following close behind. 
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, much of Wyoming’s job growth has been in the construction industry, Moore said. Many of these jobs are temporary and vanish once the construction projects are completed. 
Construction workers brace the facade of a historic home in Jackson in October 2024. (Ryan Dorgan)
Workforce Services’ Research and Planning Division puts out long and short-term Wyoming job market projections. The projections are based on historical trends going back decades. More emphasis is given to recent years, so if the projections are prepared during an economic downturn, the projections show slow growth or job loss. If they’re prepared during rapid economic growth, more job growth will be projected. Projections do not account for unforeseen events, such as economic collapse, a pandemic or natural disaster. Taking those limitations into account, these projections help businesses and workers make informed decisions. 
“That really gives people a way to dig in and get an idea of what jobs are in demand and what the requirements are to enter jobs,” Moore said. 
“The occupational projections in particular have a lot of value to them because those also include what it typically takes to enter an occupation, what education you need, what training you need, what type of experience you may need.”
